The Western water crisis has a simple solution

Stop giving the majority of the water away to farmers for almost nothing!

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 25
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Any time I read about water scarcity issues in the United States, I get kind of annoyed.

For starters, the United States is a land of relatively abundant water. Our freshwater resources per capita are above average globally, and while we’re no Canada or Brazil, we easily outpace the world’s other major states in terms of water availability.

We do have a problem, though: While on the whole the United States is quite wet, a significant region of the country is quite arid.

The good news is that a sizable majority of the population lives in the well-watered Eastern United States. Indeed, if you look at a map of the United States at night, the divide is striking. You can trace I-35 from Fort Worth up through Oklahoma City and Wichita, then northeast to Kansas City, Des Moines, and Minneapolis. Way more people live east of that line than west of it, and this historical settlement pattern basically comes down to water availability.

But the Western United States is quite beautiful, and the advent of air conditioning means that places like Las Vegas and Phoenix are now livable, which has created more and more issues around water scarcity in the dry part of the country. A lot of the water used in this dry region comes from the Colorado River and is managed carefully as a critical natural resource. Unfortunately, there just isn’t enough water in the Colorado River to meet demand, and this drives most of the conflicts around water use.

Last week the Trump administration sharply cut the water available to Arizona, California, and Nevada. This is, as far as I can tell, the right thing to do. But it’s going to make those conflicts even more intense.

Part of my annoyance with this discourse is that the relatively small minority of the population that lives in the relevant part of the country has managed to inflict its various water-related neuroses on America as a whole. You often get the sense from policy debates that the United States in general suffers from critical water shortages and that we all need to spend a lot of time worrying about this.

Even worse, the whole Western water conflict has an incredibly simple solution: End federal law’s current stipulation that a huge share of the available water must be sold at very low prices exclusively for the purpose of agriculture.

The issue here is well known, well understood, and not particularly controversial. It’s just that nobody seems to want to actually fix it.

Water, water everywhere

The American Prospect is not normally where I turn for advocacy in support of free markets and strong property rights. And yet Ryan Cooper, in a casual aside in an article advocating that we completely drain the Lake Powell reservoir to reduce wasteful evaporation, points out the actual problem here is that “cattle feed farmers paying $30 an acre-foot (or about 0.009 cents per gallon) while cities pay between $500 and $2,000 per acre-foot is preposterous.”

As Cooper says, “give something extremely valuable away for almost free, and people will waste it.”

Back in 2022, Shawn Regan wrote a big National Review article about Lake Powell running dry, and he mentioned somewhat casually that agricultural water prices in the West are low — sometimes only a few pennies per thousand gallons — “owing in part to federally subsidized water projects and limitations on transferring water to municipal uses that are valued more highly.”

Way back in 1986, when the problem of acute Western water scarcity was largely hypothetical, Reason magazine ran a piece lambasting the region’s then very right-wing politicians for their failure to appreciate prices and markets. Vincent Carroll argued that “before the job of conservation is everywhere turned over to the regulators, Western states — which, after all, give conservatives some of their most lopsided political victories — might try pricing water at its true cost and uprooting obstacles to its free exchange.”

All of this is correct. There’s nothing new or interesting to say about it.

Water is both rivalrous and excludable. If you don’t want people to waste it, you should create economic incentives to conserve it. Either it should be expensive for people to buy water, or else they should be able to sell the water they save to someone else. Obviously the option you pick makes a lot of difference to the interest group politics involved. But conceptually “you can use a ton of water for your farm if you want but it will cost you dearly” and “here’s a bunch of free water for your farm but also you can sell it to someone else if you want to” are the same solution.

The point, either way, is to shift the scarce water to high-value uses and to shift low-value water-intensive activity to other parts of the country where water is plentiful. But even though I can cite numerous articles from progressive magazines and right-wing think tanks all advocating the correct solution, it keeps not getting implemented.

It’s the alfalfa, stupid

I came to this originally as a lifelong Northeasterner and housing guy.

Over here, “but the water!” as an objection to new housing is almost purely pretextual. It is true that if a given area lacks a municipal water and sewer system, that limits how much housing it’s feasible to allow before wells run dry or get contaminated by sewage. But that just goes to show that if there’s meaningful housing demand, you should build a water and sewer system (in New England, some places refuse to build out sewers in order to block housing).

That’s not the situation in the West, though. The amount of water available for Western suburbanites is genuinely constrained by scarcity.

But that’s not because household water use is especially high. Here’s a great graphic reproduced from a Nature article by Brian Richter et al. that shows that total use of Colorado River Basin water for all household and industrial uses is less — a lot less — than the use of water for growing alfalfa.

“The whole crisis is because of alfalfa” sounds ridiculous, in part because alfalfa is a funny word. But also because it’s so random. Wheat? That’s in bread and pasta. Everyone loves wheat. Cotton? That’s my shirt, I get why we need cotton.

But alfalfa?

Alfalfa is grown as animal feed. But the particular absurdity of the situation is that it’s grown precisely because it’s a smart choice when water is cheap. The great thing about alfalfa is that it’s a perennial plant and you can harvest it by machine, so the cost structure of alfalfa cultivation is dominated by water. Note, though, that the high alfalfa share here isn’t because alfalfa is a particularly thirsty crop. It’s not like the almond situation where the water-intensity is through the roof. There’s just been a big pivot to alfalfa because demand for alfalfa — from Western dairies but also from places like Saudi Arabia and China — is high.

So I want to be clear that I’m not scapegoating the alfalfa farmers. The issue is that Western water rights are governed by a mix of “prior appropriation” (places that claimed water early get to keep using it) and “beneficial use” (if you’re using the water, you get to keep it, but if you’re not, someone else can have it) and this incentivizes agricultural rights-owners to use water as if it were plentiful even though it isn’t.

A rational allocation would be better

I remember the first time I went to Arizona and was a little shocked to see cotton farming. I asked a guy, “Isn’t this the desert?” and he pointed out that in a lot of ways the desert is the ideal place to farm. After all, plants need sunshine. Rain and cloud cover are bad for crop growth. If you think about the history of agriculture, the cradles of civilization were along riverbanks in Iraq and Egypt — i.e., the desert — because the optimal place to farm is a place that has water but no rain. Indeed, to this day Egypt has some of the most productive agriculture on Earth on a per-acre basis.

So on some level, I get it. Farming in the most arid part of the country isn’t a totally crazy idea.

But in the modern world, this is just not a very high-value industry. The entire American alfalfa crop is worth about $8 billion in revenue. Even in a bad year, the casinos of Las Vegas earn more than twice that. Arizona has attracted tens of billions of dollars’ worth of investment in semiconductor manufacturing. New housing in California is, obviously, incredibly valuable.

It makes no sense that because agricultural users got to the water first, it has to be used for agriculture forever.

In some sense, the most reasonable thing would be to just charge everyone the same amount for water. That would be a financial windfall for the residential users throughout the region and would cause a natural shrinkage of the agricultural footprint, as much of the current farming activity would become uneconomical.

The real point here, though, isn’t that the farmers are living high on the hog and need to be taken down a peg. You could easily let them keep their windfall water rights but turn those rights into property that they’re able to sell. Then existing cities or industrial users or real estate developers looking to build new housing or whoever else could just buy out the alfalfa farmers. The land currently under cultivation could shift to less water-intensive uses. Even a golf course uses significantly less water per acre than an alfalfa farm. Much of the land would, of course, turn into housing, but some could become non-irrigated parks with native vegetation.

Farming activity would shift to the parts of the country that have less sunshine but more water — which historically of course is where most farming has happened, with situations like the Nile being exceptional.

Toward water abundance

There’s even more that can be done beyond rational allocation of property rights.

The United States is a water-rich country with some arid regions. But there are plenty of countries that are entirely arid. In the United Arab Emirates and Israel, around 80 percent of their freshwater comes from desalination plants. In Singapore, it’s 25 percent.

In America, there’s no reason to contemplate desalination on that scale. But it could make a lot of sense in Southern California, where many people live and where many more people will live in the future if recent statewide YIMBY legislation is efficacious. Southern California is very nice and, as evidenced by the extremely high cost of land, tons of people would like to live there. If that became possible, housing-wise, I’m sure they’d be happy to pay a modest price premium for desalinated water rather than the current astronomical premium for scarce land.

But the last time someone tried to build a desalination plant there, it got blocked by the California Coastal Commission.

The larger story is that desalinating water takes electricity, and part of the case for energy abundance is that it lets you overcome water scarcity.

For now, though, I still think this kind of focus on larger solutions is probably unnecessary or at least premature. The overwhelmingly dominant issue in the arid West is that water is moderately scarce — not U.A.E. scarce, but scarce enough to cause problems — yet a huge share of the available water is set aside for agriculture on terms that encourage agricultural users to deploy it as if it’s not scarce.

This is a silly way to allocate resources, and everything is downstream of that.

I get that the current approach is deeply rooted in the traditions of the American West, but this is just another example of complicated customary property rights being worse than simple ones. If you don’t want to take away the farmers’ windfalls, then let them formalize their windfalls by selling the rights. The problem will then be solved for an indefinite span of time, giving us ample opportunity to work on desalination and other issues.

READ IN APP
 

I still remember the first time I set foot on Market Street. I was a freshman in college, and big cities were still a very new thing to me. It felt like I was swimming through an ocean of foot traffic; the towering shops and hotels seemed like they were built by giants.

That Market Street is gone now. In its place is a giant empty field of asphalt in the center of San Francisco — a desolate gray waste baking in the sun, empty except for the occasional bus and a tiny smattering of bicycles.

On either side of this yawning wasteland are giant sidewalks with only a few pedestrians, boarded-up stores, and the occasional small, sad retail chain. At midday on a Monday, what was once the bustling commercial heart of San Francisco feels abandoned.

What happened? In fact, Market Street was destroyed by several things:

  1. The city’s decision to close the street to cars (but not buses), enacted in 2019

  2. The crime wave of the early 2020s

  3. The pandemic, and the shift to remote work

The second and third of these, together, are known as the “Doom Loop”. It’s been talked about a lot, so let’s just cover it briefly.

The pandemic, and the economic and social changes it brought, came out of the blue. But San Francisco was particularly vulnerable to the shock. As in many American cities, 20th century urban planning and zoning rules concentrated office buildings in the downtown area and put housing farther out. This meant that once people stopped going downtown for work, the neighborhood was just a lot more empty, because almost no one lives there. This is in contrast to big cities in Europe and Asia, where downtown neighborhoods are typically mixed-use. (SF also had a stronger shift to remote work, because of the heavy presence of the tech industry.)

The crime wave was another shock. Although SF escaped the destructive rioting that hit other West Coast cities like Seattle, Portland, and Los Angeles in 2020, it had plenty of looting in downtown areas — especially around Union Square and the San Francisco Centre mall on Market Street. Even after the pandemic ended, San Francisco suffered especially hard from the statewide wave of “smash-and-grab” store thefts. It got so bad that American Eagle actually sued the San Francisco Centre for being negligent toward crime, reporting over 100 serious incidents of violence and harassment in its downtown store.

Crime and emptiness fed on each other. Less foot traffic meant fewer “eyes on the street” to discourage property crime. Property crime and reduced foot traffic forced stores to close. Fewer stores meant less foot traffic, and so on. The collapse of downtown culminated in January 2026 with the closure of the San Francisco Centre, the iconic mall that had formed the commercial heart of Market Street, but which had been gutted by the Doom Loop. It now stands as a looming, empty, boarded-up structure dominating the area around the Powell Street train station:

The intersection of Powell Street and Market Street, once bustling and alive with tourists, shoppers, and street vendors, is now virtually empty, except for a forlorn line of people waiting to get on the iconic streetcar:

But recent years have seen the first glints of recovery from the Doom Loop. For one thing, crime has begun to fall. 2025 alone saw a 27% decrease in property crime, including a 29% decrease in burglaries, a 22% decrease in larceny (including retail theft), and a 24% decrease in robbery. 2026 has seen further drops. The reasons for this are interesting, but I’ll go into them another time. Suffice it to say that this has made downtown SF feel much safer and more orderly. The stereotype of SF as being overrun by drug addicts and dangerous vagrants still holds true of a few areas of the city, but from Powell Street to the bay, the city no longer feels like a post-apocalyptic movie.

Meanwhile, the business district is showing a few sluggish signs of life. The AI boom is causing a (modest) rebound in the demand for office space. Some office buildings are being converted to housing, raising hopes that SF’s downtown can finally become a mixed-use neighborhood. A concerted effort to revive Union Square after the devastation of 2020 is beginning to bear fruit. And both companies and the SF city government are mandating return-to-office policies.

And yet Market Street remains a dead zone. Weekday foot traffic is still down by half compared to 2019:

The wounds inflicted by the Doom Loop will take lots more time and effort to heal. Retail businesses have to be encouraged to open. Defunct buildings have to be torn down and rebuilt. Crime has to be reduced even further, and so on. This will all take years.

But there’s one other factor contributing to the death of San Francisco’s most important street, and it began before the pandemic: The ban on cars.

In recent years, a number of cities around the world have experimented with car-free zones and traffic reduction policies in their downtown areas. The most famous of these is Paris, with its Limited Traffic Zone, its expansion of pedestrian malls, and its road closures during Sundays and holidays. Shortly before the pandemic, San Francisco decided to enact a plan its leaders thought was in the same spirit: closing downtown Market Street to all car traffic:

But although Market Street was closed to cars, it wasn’t closed to buses, delivery trucks, and licensed taxis. This was in keeping with the general “transit good, cars bad” thinking of modern progressive urbanism. But a bus will kill a pedestrian just as easily as a car will, which is why Market Street remains empty of pedestrian traffic. This mathematically guaranteed that Market Street would become a more empty place: Cars were subtracted, but pedestrians weren’t added.

The direct cost of this policy is pretty obvious. When people can’t park in a parking garage on Market, and when Uber and Lyft can’t pick people up and drop people off on the street, it makes businesses on the street less attractive to visit. Sure, people could bike or take the train, but not everyone wants to do that; instead, they’ll just go to restaurants or stores in other areas. In addition, restaurants on Market Street now can’t deliver food, cutting them off from an important source of revenue. That probably helps explain why Market has suffered more from the Doom Loop than other areas.

But what did SF gain by deleting cars from Market Street and adding nothing at all in their place? Cars create a little bit of pollution (though modern cars are very clean), so that was removed. Pedestrians who run off the sidewalk and into the street are somewhat less in danger of being killed (though still in danger). These are meager benefits indeed.

What about bike traffic? Presumably, reduced danger of being hit by a car would allow more cyclists to ride down Market Street. But in fact, bike traffic on the street is considerably lower than it was pre-pandemic:

A lot of that is the Doom Loop — there are simply fewer stores for cyclists to visit on Market Street, so there’s less reason for them to go there. But much of downtown hasn’t collapsed the way Market Street has, and presumably cyclists could use the street as a way to get to places like the Embarcadero, Chinatown, etc. They’re not doing it. Cyclists are a relatively rare sight on Market these days.

One reason might be that although the city planned to make the car-free stretch of Market more bike-friendly, it never really followed up on those plans. So it’s still pretty dangerous to ride a bike or scooter down the street — you can get caught in the train tracks, and you can get hit by a bus or truck.

In fact, this sloppy implementation is a general pattern with the Market Street closure. Josh Koehn had a great article in 2023 about how the plan degenerated from its initial form:

A $600 million capital project called Better Market Street promised to create a futuristic boulevard that would safely buffer bicycles and scooters on elevated sidewalk lanes, separating the little wheels from rapid bus lines, vintage streetcars and pedestrians…The new vision for Market Street, advocates said, would create a safer, more vibrant multimodal avenue…More than a decade of planning went into alterations of Market Street…

But funds for anything beyond modest improvements along a three-block stretch of Market Street between Fifth and Eighth streets…have evaporated…The cost of Better Market Street, which soared above a billion dollars before being reined in to a still-staggering $604 million, is almost double the amount spent on the tormented Van Ness Avenue redesign…

City officials enraged safe streets advocates when they announced in late 2020 that the elevated bike lanes on sidewalks would be scrapped.

SF’s lack of state capacity had a lot to do with this; constant cost overruns inevitably require ambitious projects to be scaled back. The pandemic also obviously got in the way. But part of what killed the vision for Market Street is simply that the vision itself was never very good.

If you look at Paris, it’s immediately clear how that city’s car-limitation measures were designed to create spaces for pedestrians. In certain areas like the banks of the Seine, Paris didn’t just ban cars; it also banned buses and trucks, so that people could walk safely. Paris also reserved much larger areas for pedestrians on certain days.

But Market Street has no more pedestrian areas than it did in 2019. You can still only walk on the sidewalk. If the entire street were reserved for foot traffic during certain times — like SF does with Valencia Street, for example — then these periodic temporary pedestrianizations could become an event that regularly draws lots of people to the area. This could include farmers’ markets, street concerts, and other fun events. Those would give people a reason to walk around Market Street even before new businesses opened.

Alternatively, if SF permanently closed off some portion of the street to buses and trucks, that stretch of road could become a pedestrian public square, similar to the center of Times Square:

Instead of thinking about how to create spaces that people would actually want to walk around in, the SF government — and the many activist groups and nonprofits that influence its policy — appear to have adhered to the simple rule of “bikes and buses good, cars bad”.

This is a way of thinking centered around modes of transit rather than public space. It implicitly conceives of areas like Market Street as thoroughfares to take people from one place to another, rather than as actual destinations. Market Street’s car closure is all about forcing people to go down Market Street in a different way, rather than about encouraging people to go to Market Street.

There’s something inescapably and depressingly suburban about this way of thinking. In the suburbs, life is lived point-to-point — you go from house to strip-mall to restaurant to office without thinking much about the places you traverse in between. In a suburb, the mode of transportation — how you get from Point A to Point B — is the important question.

Americans are a suburban people; even many of our urban areas look like suburbs in other countries. So perhaps it’s inevitable that the urbanists who closed Market Street off to car traffic would think entirely about modes of transportation and ignore the vibrant city center whose destruction they exacerbated. Instead of Jane Jacobs, they ended up just being the Robert Moses of buses.

Again, careful attention to car limitations in cities like Paris, where people are used to occupying urban places instead of simply whizzing through them, would have proven enlightening. Paris’s Limited Traffic Zone doesn’t ban cars in downtown areas; it merely bans cars from transiting through those areas. People who stay within the area can still drive. The point is to make downtown spaces into places people occupy rather than places people simply go through. What San Francisco did to Market Street was, in many ways, the exact opposite.

In lieu of turning Market Street into a pedestrian paradise, SF’s best move is probably just to allow private cars again. It’s not the optimal way to create more foot traffic to nourish retail businesses, but it’s the quickest and easiest. In fact, Mayor Daniel Lurie has made moves in this direction, allowing certain Uber, Lyft, and Waymo cars to operate on the street. But they might as well simply go all the way. Best to simply bury the era when Market Street was a large empty scar commemorating the decline of San Francisco; if San Francisco can’t be Paris, at least it can return to what it used to be.

Der Untergang

How badly will Trump punish America?

Paul Krugman
Aug 26
 
READ IN APP
 

For all my interviews and more, subscribe on YouTube.

Note: After I recorded this it was reported that Trump officials are threatening to demolish the Kennedy Center if it can’t be renovated to Trump’s taste (and presumably with his name added). Matches my argument exactly.

Der Untergang naht.

Pardon my German pronunciation. I’m going to take a break today from wonky economic analysis and talk about, well, Donald Trump, but in a slightly different way from what I think most people are saying. Not positive, obviously.

Just before recording this, I saw that Trump wants to rename Lake Ontario Lake America. Which is silly, would be funny, except that this guy is the President of the United States. And it’s really kind of troublesome that someone in that position is that out of it, that petty, disconnected from reality.

And look, it’s not news to anybody that Trump is ego-driven, disconnected from reality, and at the same time, somehow commands a level of deference and obedience from the entire machinery of the federal government that no president has ever had before. So this is really quite serious.

What I don’t think people are fully aware of is just how bad it can get, given that Trump is so obviously dissociating, decompensating, that he’s not all there.

Obviously, he was already a very problematic personality, which was doing a great deal of damage to the United States. I don’t think even now people fully appreciate the amount of damage that has been done. Even before the Iran War, Trump’s provocations, insults, his trade wars, really destroyed the world’s trust in America.

America became a country that could not be trusted to honor agreements. It was a country that constantly tried to bully other countries. Our word was worth nothing. Our sanity was not to be taken for granted. And then, of course, along comes Iran, where in addition to showing that we’re not to be trusted, that we’re not going to be relied upon., we also showed that we were far weaker than people imagined.

If there’s one thing people thought it was, well, America has a powerful military. It turns out, well, not as powerful and not nearly as competent as people thought. How much of that is the result of Trump and Hegseth degrading it and how much of it was there to begin with is an interesting question. But anyway, at this point, we are not loved, we are not respected, and we aren’t even feared.

And we’re not getting that back. Even if Trump is succeeded by someone decent —God help us if he isn’t— but even if we have a more or less rational, well-intentioned government that follows, the world now knows that we are capable of putting someone like Trump in a position of unprecedented, almost absolute power and that it can happen again.

And the world also knows that we’re just not as fearsome as we seem to be. That we can be defied much more successfully even by smallish countries than anyone really imagined.

And we’re not getting that back. I anxiously wait for the days when we’re no longer a Trump-ruled country, but this is my country, and what will be left of us, what will be left of our role in the world, even once he’s gone?

Okay, the title I gave, the way that I opened this talk was Der Untergang, which is the German title of the movie Downfall, about the last days of Adolf Hitler. I hope that nobody is going to complain about my using the German, right? We’re long past the point where it’s considered unthinkable and incredibly rude to make Nazi parallels. There’s a lot of people in this administration or close to this administration who are effectively Nazis, in some cases explicitly Nazis. America is not yet Germany under Hitler. But the reason we don’t have a functioning Gestapo in this country is not for lack of desire to have one. It’s because these people, at least so far, don’t have the juice. So all of the stuff, all of the parallels seem appropriate.

And the parallels are there. I mean, the parallels are there even in seemingly small things. Hitler was obsessed with building a gigantic gaudy ballroom. So there’s just a lot of parallels in there.

Now the main message of the movie Der Untergang is that it’s about Hitler in his final days who knew that he was losing. He knew that defeat was looming. He knew that his power was collapsing. And his reaction was, among other things, to take it out on his own country.

Hitler never accepted that he had failed Germany. He felt that Germany had failed him. And so he had a plan, often called the Nero Decree, which was to destroy as much as possible of Germany’s infrastructure. Supposedly to deny it to the victorious allies, but in large part to punish Germany.

Well, Trump knows. He may deny it, he may have his moments when he actually believes that the polls are all fake and all of that, but in many ways he is behaving like somebody who knows that his days of supreme power are about to end. He, of course, is not going to accept that it’s his fault. It’s the fault, obviously, of the Democrats, who are all communists. It’s the fault of the Republicans, who didn’t live up to his leadership. The fault of everybody but him.

What does he do in the position of losing? Probably not committing suicide in the Fuhrerbunker, but still in the position of losing all of his power. Well, what you do in that position, if you are somebody like Trump, who is an empty vessel: there’s nothing in there, the only pleasure he appears to take in life comes from dominating other people.

Well, one thing you do is you try to stick your name everywhere, or leave your imprint everywhere. So Trump, according to reporting by Swan and Haberman, spends most of his time thinking about his construction projects and trying to leave his mark on everything in Washington.

What I don’t think we’re fully appreciating even about those projects is that there isn’t a whole lot of actual construction. There’s a lot of starting of stuff, but so far it’s been mostly destruction, mostly tearing stuff down. We don’t have a triumphal arch, but we have a hole where the ballroom is supposed to be. We have just a lot of damage having been done to our nation’s capital and to the iconic structures that were supposed to define, symbolize who we are as a country. The scale of the destruction is really quite amazing.

So I’m not going to try fancy video editing here. I’m just going to show you a picture of what the environs of the White House look like right now. There you go. That bare area is the South Lawn, ripped up because of Trump’s cage match. You can see in the corner there the hole in the ground, which is where the east wing of the White House used to be. Basically, Trump has left, so far, wreckage in his wake.

Even the things which have not involved tearing stuff down, the gilding of statues, the horrific redecoration of the White House, is surpassingly ugly. That’s partly because Trump has terrible taste, but it’s also, I think, a clear sign of aggression. He’s saying, oh yeah, you’re going to give me a 33% approval rating? Well, I’m going to make the nation’s capital as ugly as I can in this little time as I possibly can.

Now, this is all superficial. This is stuff that can and will be repaired. It’ll cost a lot of money, but OK. So we’ll rebuild the White House. We’ll reseed the South Lawn. We’ll strip the gilding off the statues. We’ll make the White House a dignified place again.

But how much more will be coming? When we talk about Hitler’s last days, as I said, one of his last attempted acts was what’s called the Nero Decree, which was an attempt to destroy as much of Germany’s infrastructure as possible, supposedly to deny it to the victorious allies. But clearly, and even there’s some evidence that he actually he clearly thought this as a way of punishing the German people for failing him.

Now, historiography is a little more complicated than that, as it usually is, but that’s clearly the gist of it. That Hitler’s final acts were to basically try to bring everyone else down with him.

Do you really want to say that that’s not what’s going to happen with Trump? Assuming that he loses much, if not all, of his power to shape events this November, and of course we’re all worried about how he may try to disrupt or overturn the election, but assuming he doesn’t manage to do that, he will find himself much diminished. How much damage will he do basically taking revenge on America?

Because always you want to bear in mind that Trump hates America. He hates the values on which America was built. He hates democracy. He hates rule of law. He hates all of the things that are what we’re supposed to be about as a nation.

But increasingly it looks as if he just plain hates this country because it doesn’t love him. How much damage will he do? How much damage can he do? I don’t want to make a specific prediction, but I’m worried.

And don’t say that he won’t do that or he can’t do that. Those have been famous last words again and again over the past decade. So this is going to be even worse, even uglier, I think than most people imagine.

Have a great rest of your day.

YIMBYs already have a bold vision for solving the housing crisis

Don’t listen to the haters — there’s nothing narrow about this.

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 26
 
READ IN APP
 

YIMBYs, people in the housing abundance movement, do not have a pope or a set of sacred authoritative texts you can consult to find out what we think about things.

But if you asked me what YIMBYism is, I would say our big idea is that if some land is zoned for human development (i.e., not a park or a nature preserve or similar) and the person who owns the land would like to build housing on that land, he or she should be allowed to do so, subject to bona fide regulations related to building safety and environmental externalities.

This is a radical idea.

There is literally nowhere in the United States of America (no, not even Houston) where it works like that.

It’s such a radical idea that, in practice, the vast majority of concrete YIMBY work focuses on incremental steps in that direction. Here we’re rolling back a staircase requirement whose safety rationale is bogus. There we’re legalizing accessory dwelling units as a homeowner-friendly form of land-use reform. Elsewhere, we’re liberalizing the regulations on manufactured housing. YIMBYs somewhere might be pushing for a fourplex bill or parking reform or a corridor or transit-oriented upzoning.

The status quo is so incredibly far from “it should be legal to build safe structures in places where there is market demand for them” that the list of specific reforms YIMBYs advocate for is practically infinite.

Because our analysis of the situation is correct, though, the circle of opponents who explicitly argue against the YIMBY agenda keeps shrinking.

Plenty of people have serious concerns about new housing in their backyard, and no one likes to have their existing veto rights taken away, so the actual politics of working toward housing abundance are difficult. But it’s become increasingly rare to see a writer or intellectual just saying, “There’s no downside to banning new housing in the places where demand is high.”

But there is a deep reluctance, notably among leftist intellectuals, to admit that we are just correct and a radical program of land-use-law reform would largely solve the single biggest economic problem facing the country.

Because if we can solve the single biggest economic problem facing the country with a liberalizing reform, that calls into question the larger project of overthrowing “neo”-liberalism and replacing it with a new post-liberal economic order.

This line of thinking is how you get takes like this one from Christopher Serkin and Daniel Sharfstein who dismiss arguments “about the local regulations governing what and where people can build” as an illustration of “how narrow our imagination has become” and propose instead that we embark on a mass program of federally financed housing construction. But the regulatory reform conversation isn’t narrow at all — it’s exceptionally radical and also a necessary precondition to everything they’re arguing for.

The regulatory landscape was different in the past

The central sleight of hand in the piece (a common one in the anti-abundance literature) is to say that instead of talking about regulatory issues, we should return to the good old days of midcentury progressive politics, when “the federal government responded by treating housing as critical national infrastructure” and “the government directly built housing itself.”

That would be great! But guess what? The post-World War II housing-boom era they’re talking about took place before the modern regulatory landscape came into being.

Los Angeles cut its zoned capacity by 60 percent between 1960 and 1990. New York City did a massive downzoning in 1961 and as recently as Michael Bloomberg’s administration was downzoning on net.

The original Levittown suburbs featured lot sizes of 6,000 square feet. The National Zoning Atlas finds that 56 percent of existing single-family-home land is zoned to require lots of at least 40,000 square feet. Just 4 percent of single-family land is zoned to allow lots of less than 10,000 square feet. A ton of YIMBY activism and leading YIMBY thinkers came out of central cities and “urbanist” thinking, but a lot of what we’ve learned as this policy area has developed is how hostile the contemporary land-use environment has become to traditional suburban development patterns as well.

The United States is, needless to say, a much richer country than it was in the 1950s, so you wouldn’t see the same level of demand for Levittown-scale structures. It’s totally fine if a large share of the population prefers to purchase larger lots and larger homes. But it doesn’t make sense to propose a return to the policy framework that sparked the postwar housing boom as an alternative to regulatory reform.

Zoning was much laxer back then. Fire codes were less strict. NEPA didn’t exist.

In 1976, Harvey Molotch published his groundbreaking article, “The City as a Growth Machine,” observing — and complaining — that municipal politics was dominated by a mix of real estate interests, construction interests, labor interests, and downtown business interests, all of which favored more building, more population growth, more jobs, and more customers. And over the course of the ’70s and ’80s, the pro-growth political coalition Molotch described was repeatedly defeated across the Pacific Coast and the northeastern United States by an explicit “growth control” movement. The Sun Belt, meanwhile, remained more growth-friendly but also embedded low-density presuppositions that generally banned both walkable urbanism and Levittown-scale suburbs.

Calling things “infrastructure” doesn’t solve the problem

In their piece, Serkin and Sharfstein argue that in the good old days, Americans “understood that housing was not just another commodity” but rather treated it like “essential infrastructure for a functioning society.”

This strikes me as much too optimistic about the status quo!

If housing were treated like just another commodity, then obviously you’d be allowed to build extra dwellings on your lot and rent them out. That wouldn’t mean no regulations — there might be rules about what kinds of dwellings are considered safe. And you’d need to pay property taxes, obviously. But while cars are highly regulated across many dimensions, they’re also just another commodity. If you want to buy a car, you can go buy a car. You don’t need to ask your neighbors if they think your car fits with the general vibe of the neighborhood. If your family wants two cars or three or seven, nobody’s going to stop you. It’s a commodity.

Housing is nothing like that.

I’d also note that calling things infrastructure doesn’t speak to the relevant questions here. A garbage dump or a sewage treatment plant is infrastructure. That certainly doesn’t mean it’s easy to get a new garbage dump or sewage treatment plant built.

If anything, housing has been treated too much like infrastructure — treating the mere existence of new homes as a kind of necessary evil that communities need to be protected against. After all, while it’s true that the federal government has gotten out of the business of directly funding public-housing construction, it’s just not the case that all of housing has been privatized and commoditized. The United States has lots of nonprofit affordable-housing developers, a federal tax credit subsidizes these projects, and more progressive states and cities have affordable-housing production funds.

It’s fine to debate spending more on these kinds of programs. But the fact is that America already spends meaningful money on social housing — Americans just also make it illegal to build on most parcels of land.

And is it really true that tweaking the budget to spend more on social housing (instead of on health care or education or national defense or clean energy or child care or any other worthy cause) is a more imaginative solution than revisiting the decision to make it illegal to build housing?

The two big challenges

I’m torn because YIMBYs are stuck confronting two big challenges simultaneously.

I think the main thing we need to do is to reassure normal people who are aware that housing is a big problem but who also mostly like living in the suburbs and are somewhat fearful of change.

Altering the rules so that it’s generally possible to build dense housing where there’s demand for it doesn’t mean that the typical American neighborhood would suddenly look like Manhattan. Even using a high-end estimate of the total scale of the housing shortage in the United States, we’re probably talking about a 10 percent expansion of the national housing stock. A lot of that would be greenfield or brownfield, a lot of it would be infill in places that are already “urban,” and a lot of the suburban infill would be A.D.U.s or smaller lots rather than big buildings.

Spreading the liberalization widely generates a large shift in the housing stock over time without triggering unduly dramatic change in most places.

There are also a lot of non-policy limits to how rapidly the housing stock can expand. If all regulatory barriers were eliminated, there would still be finite amounts of skilled labor and construction equipment. The point of land-use reform is to reach a new, better equilibrium over time, not to suddenly transform the built environment of every single American community.

But then there’s the second challenge.

As the housing abundance movement keeps plugging away, doing the slow boring of hard boards and reassuring and persuading and deal-making, we keep getting stabbed in the back by high-level progressive takesters like Paul Glastris who insist that our ideas are too “meager” in scale to meet the moment.

My main issue with this is that it’s not true.

Housing is, objectively, the largest sector of the economy and the number one source of youth economic pessimism.

Beyond the direct burden on consumers, undue barriers to housing construction are a major blockage of economic growth. Unlocking housing abundance would create new job opportunities for blue-collar men as the economy tried to address the skilled-labor bottleneck that would emerge if zoning restrictions were eased — a topic that’s obsessively discussed in the media. Housing abundance is also a great way to make it easier for people to have kids that does not involve curbing women’s rights or autonomy.

Money and attention matter in politics. If donors and politicians keep hearing that talking about the regulations that underlie the basic structure of where and how everyone lives and works and commutes is “narrow” and boring, then they start spending their time on other, allegedly sexier, topics. And that’s bad.

It’s also a little pointless, because the public-housing enthusiasts genuinely have no conflict with the YIMBYs and land-use reformers.

Our ideas make it easier to execute their ideas. If your main policy goal is to get the federal government to invest more money directly in non-market housing, then the argument you have is with the advocates of spending money on other causes.

But the idea that investing more money directly in non-market housing is a bigger, broader, more exciting concept than rewriting the rules that govern all the residential land in every American community is ridiculous. If you’re looking for a bold, expansive vision of a better world, get on the housing abundance bandwagon, because scarcity is a deliberate policy choice the consequences of which we all now regret.

The “anti-social century” with Derek Thompson

What happens as people spend more and more time alone?

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 27
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Derek Thompson coined the phrase “the anti-social century” to describe an incredible rise over the course of the 21st century in the amount of time that people spend alone. He recently joined Jerusalem and me to talk about it.

This is an issue I’m concerned about. Recent technological progress has been very concentrated in the realm of home entertainment pursuits that have left people spending more time alone and lacking human connection.

Jerusalem is more optimistic — insisting that we distinguish between loneliness and aloneness and that we see much clearer evidence of a rise in the latter than in the former. There’s nothing wrong, she argues, with people being alone as long as it’s not making them lonely and sad. It seems to me, though, that people increasingly are sad and angry even if they don’t say that they are lonely. And people who espouse moderate or liberal politics need some explanation for bad vibes that doesn’t cede the substantive ground to illiberal forces.

Derek brings some data to help draw these distinctions, and we discuss it all.

Next month on the podcast, Jerusalem and I will be reading Friedrich von Hayek’s “The Road to Serfdom.” If you have comments or questions about the book you’d like us to discuss, drop a line in the comments below!

Paid subscribers can watch the ad-free embedded video at the top of this post and read the full transcript below.

WATCH THE EPISODE ON YOUTUBE HERE

New episodes post every Thursday.

Jerusalem Demsas: Hello, everyone. Welcome to The Argument. My name’s Jerusalem Demsas.

Matthew Yglesias: I’m Matthew Yglesias.

Jerusalem Demsas: And this week we have a great friend of the pod on, Derek Thompson. Thanks for coming on.

Derek Thompson: It is wonderful to be here. Thank you so much.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, so we are gonna talk about loneliness today, and, I don’t know, maybe we should start with Derek. Why are you so obsessed with loneliness? What’s going on? Are you OK?

Derek Thompson: I think I’m OK. I mean, you know, like, all research is me-search. So I do think — it’s funny. I wrote this article when I was living in North Carolina, when my wife was finishing up her PhD at UNC. And I met some wonderful people in North Carolina, some people who are still my friends, but I was disconnected from the vast majority of my friends who live in New York or San Francisco or Los Angeles, and many of them live, as you and Matt do, in the non-summer months in Washington, D.C.

And so, to a certain extent, like, yeah, I was kind of lonely in North Carolina. And so, it was not difficult for me to write a 6,000, 7,000, 8,000-word draft on the epidemic of loneliness — of aloneness in America.

Yeah, I do think that there’s a certain way in which, while I love writing and I love podcasting, these are somewhat inherently lonely jobs. Like, it is impossible to write with somebody else. Like, that’s an absolute nightmare. Writing something with someone else is very, very difficult to do.

Matthew Yglesias: Have you ever co-authored a book?

Derek Thompson: Like, co-authoring a book? Yeah, exactly. Fortunately, the nice thing about co-authoring a book is it can be done very asynchronously, right? Like, the Google Doc is there and you can jump into it when Ezra’s out of it. But seeing the EK icon in the upper left-hand corner — upper right-hand corner — while I was writing something. Nightmare. Nightmare.

So, you know, co-writing is, in a synchronous way, is absolutely horrendous. Writing is inherently lonely. Reading is somewhat inherently lonely. Hard to read and also be social at the same time. So I do think that I am particularly — this is a longer answer than you probably bargained for — I think I am particularly sensitive to loneliness, which may have been an inspiration for this article.

Matthew Yglesias: But I also think that, that writers, you know, to generalize a little bit, but I think in part because of what you’re talking about: This is a profession that tends to select for people who are relatively comfortable being alone. You know, that there’s lots of jobs that are much more interpersonal, that are much more interactive. And if that’s something that you really value in life, not to say I— would never, you know, discourage anyone from a career in journalism, which is a thriving field.

Jerusalem Demsas: I think you have done that.

Matthew Yglesias: Growing at all times. My father’s a novelist. You know, this is a guy who, my whole life, like, he would get up in the morning and go to this, like, tiny little office where he worked alone and bang away at his computer all day. And, you know, he’s OK with that. Like, that’s a life that he enjoys.

Derek Thompson: Mm-hmm.

Matthew Yglesias: I’m, like, a little less introverted than he is. And so, I like to at least, like, have a newsroom and participate with people. But still, yeah, when it’s time to work, to put words to the page, it’s like you just, you’re alone, and I like that. And not everybody does.

Derek Thompson: I think you’re already pulling on a major thread of my essay, and a thread that I think a lot of people missed, which is that what you’ll sometimes have is people who have a certain disposition for introversion go into professions — like, say, writing — where they’re often very alone. And, you know, the cliché of the writer, and even the artist, is not one of a worker or profession that’s, like, overwhelmingly happy.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Derek Thompson: In fact, the profession is known for tortured artists and tortured writers, and even, in some cases, writers who hate writing and have a very complicated relationship with the thing that they have, with full volition, chosen to do with their time.

And one of the ideas that I try to get at in my essay is that in some cases — while I believe that introversion exists, and I believe that a spectrum between introversion and extroversion exists, like so many other spectra exist across the human population — I think we over-demand a lot of alone time in the modern world. I think people over-demand alone time when they’re on TikTok, when they’re staying at home watching Netflix, even maybe when they become writers.

You know, maybe the cliché of the writer who is also somewhat miserable is not so much the phenomenon of writing itself being misery — although of course all of us having written know that writing can be misery. It’s also the fact that we’ve chosen a profession which sometimes disconnects us from the kind of social connection that often provides support when people in other jobs feel a certain kind of ennui in their work. And so, I think this is an important ball to keep in the air, which is that, sometimes, we demand a certain amount of aloneness that isn’t particularly good for us, even if the name that we give to that kind of sickly feeling isn’t loneliness.

Jerusalem Demsas: So, I’m a data respecter, and so I want us to get into the weeds here about what you’re actually finding about increased rates of — aloneness. Because, I mean, again, like, maybe this is just ’cause I’m a writer or whatever, you know, you don’t want to overlean on your own personal experiences.

I agree that I am alone a lot, whether I’m writing or maybe when you’re commuting home, whatever it is. I do not feel bad about this. It feels, like, totally fine to me. And I think we’ll get into this a little bit more. I know you make this distinction between aloneness and loneliness, but let’s just — what are the facts? Like, are people alone more? Where are they alone more? Why? What’s going on?

Derek Thompson: Yeah, so I think you’re already beginning to break this down into two really important questions. One is what’s going on? And two is why is it bad, right? Because maybe people are spending more time alone, and that’s actually fantastic. Like, maybe we should spend way more time alone than we already are.

So, first off, you know, Robert Putnam published this book in the year 2000 called Bowling Alone, and it was about the fact that there was declining social capital and people were spending more time amongst themselves. And a lot of sociologists and academics laughed at him. And they were like, “This is crazy. Like, in the 21st century, you’re obviously going to see people snap back to socializing.”

So what have we seen? Well, the American Time Use Survey thankfully asks Americans how much time they spend socializing in person. And between 2003 and 2024, 2025, in-person socializing declined by about 20, 25%. According to follow-up surveys that have been done by economists at the Federal Reserve, Americans spend more time alone than in any period for which we have good data.

Some other numbers that I remember calculating — I spent, like, so much time in the American Time Use Survey databases, of course, entirely by myself. So Derek alone, researching all the ways that aloneness can be bad for us.

And just some of the facts I thought were incredible were, one, men who watch television now spend seven hours in front of the TV for every one hour that they spend hanging out with somebody outside of their house. This one was really controversial: The typical female pet owner now spends more time actively engaged with her pet than she spends in face-to-face contact with friends of her own species. And since the early 2000s, the amount of time that Americans say they spend helping or caring for people outside their nuclear family has also declined by more than 30%.

So, in many cases, I think this is chosen solitude. I think this is people choosing to be alone. And there’s many, many reasons for this, but maybe the most important reason is one that Matt has written about all the time, or certainly tweeted about all the time, which is just that aloneness is way easier and better in many ways than it used to be. It’s certainly more entertaining. It’s just so easy to stay alone at home on your couch watching Netflix, looking at TikTok. That is free, or at least no additional charge on a per-hour basis entertainment.

And indeed, Patrick Sharkey, a sociologist at Princeton, has found that the amount of time that we spend in our houses has increased significantly this century. So people are choosing over and over again to spend more time alone in their homes rather than socializing with other people.

Matthew Yglesias: And, you know, I think about — I’m, you know, older than you and older than Jerusalem,

Jerusalem Demsas: Certainly older than me.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, and so, I mean, I remember vividly being a young adult in a moment when the technology of home entertainment was quite different from how it is today.

And so, when I lived in a house with five roommates, which was not that long ago in the grand — I guess there were five of us in the house, so me and four roommates — and we had mobile phones, but our phones did not have streaming video apps on them. Like, I couldn’t watch a movie on my phone.

We had a television, one television that sat in the living room, and it was connected to a cable box or to a TiVo that had a cable card in it. And so if you wanted to watch TV, there was this one room, and you would typically find yourself watching TV with other people. And the downside of that is that it meant you weren’t always watching the thing you wanted to watch.

Like, I watched a lot of Felicity reruns because two of my roommates were into that. And my probably most pro-Felicity roommate also found herself watching a lot of Star Trek: The Next Generation reruns. You know, and there’s, like, a swing man who liked both of those shows.

And it’s like, would I say that Felicity is one of my favorite television shows of all time? No. I wouldn’t choose to watch it in my alone time. I would never put it on. But are some of my good memories of life watching Felicity with other people? Like, yes, right?

And that, to me, is the yin and the yang of it. Like, it’s just — it’s unquestionably better to be able to watch the show that you want to watch, rather than the show that your roommates want to watch. It’s better to be able to relax alone than to come back home from a stressful day of work and be like, “Ugh, I just kind of have to stay on.”

But also, I obtained value from those experiences of doing things I didn’t necessarily want to do with other people that endure. Whereas I can’t be like, “Oh, six years ago, when I rewatched The Sopranos for the second time, I really appreciated the artistry of this…” Like I did. I love that show. It’s great. I love to rewatch old Sopranos episodes, but it’s like, you’re not building social capital.

Jerusalem Demsas: But I think there’s an implicit thing going on here that I want to make a little bit more explicit. That thee charge here from people who are concerned about all this time we’re spending alone is that we are opting in to the things that we think in that moment will make us most happy, whether that’s hanging out with your dog rather than going to an uncomfortable happy hour where you have to maybe, like, mingle with people you don’t know and it’s awkward.

It’s choosing to watch Star Trek rather than Felicity. And so, no one else wants to watch with you because no one else is a nerd and a weirdo. And so they’re watching cool shows. Or — and that — these kinds of, the options that we now have to match us to the exact thing that we want to do isolate us because everyone you know around you is different from you.

And then, the implicit thing there is that what makes you happy in the short run is actually not what’s going to make you fulfilled or happy or whatever in the long run, which kind of raises my next question, which is, are we seeing that people themselves are unhappy with the situation they find themselves in?

And I ask this — we just released a new poll here at The Argument, which is mostly about elites. But one question I tacked on at the end was asking people whether they would describe themselves as a lonely person. And only 7% of people said that they would definitely describe themselves as a lonely person. Thirty-eight percent said no, not at all. In the middle, you had 23% saying yes, to some extent and another 30% saying no, not really. So, vast majority of people are saying no — like, 70%, roughly, are saying no, not at all. Or not really, “I’m a lonely person.”

You can look more at these gradients a bit, which are interesting, which indicate that younger people are slightly more likely to feel this way. So, you have 3% of 65-plus saying they’re definitely a lonely person, and 13% of 18-to-29-year-olds saying that they’re definitely a lonely person. So there’s some story here, obviously, that you could say, but I’m just curious: In general, when you’re looking at this data, Derek, do you find that people are really unhappy with the choices they’re making?

Derek Thompson: Yeah. So there’s three really interesting pieces that you guys have put on the table in your last two comments and questions, and I just want to make sure that my answer does my best to tack off all three.

First, Jerusalem, so on the point of a small minority of Americans say that they’re lonely — that’s a really, really important and I think under-remarked-on fact. That it’s very, very difficult if you’re trying to be scientific about this to prove that loneliness itself is rising. It’s much easier to prove two other things. Number one, that alone time is rising, and number two, that Americans, especially the Americans that are spending — that are seeing the largest declines in socialization — are less happy than they used to be.

So, loneliness is, I mean, sociologically or psychologically, like, a very specific thing. It’s a felt disconnection between your experienced social connection and your desired social connection. So people, you know, I can be at home, you know, reading Freedom from Fear by David M. Kennedy and, like, just having the best time learning about the New Deal and not feel lonely at all, even though there’s no one around me.

I can also — and everyone’s had this experience, I think — like, go to a party and be surrounded by, like, 50 people and feel heartbreakingly alone because there’s no one there to talk to or someone’s just hurt my feelings, right? So, you can be very lonely around other people. You can be not lonely all by yourself. Loneliness is the feeling of this disconnect between what you’re experiencing and what you want.

And I think basically what’s happened is that a lot of technology, in particular a lot of convenience, has made it harder for us to feel that ancient biological cue to feel lonely. And, as a result, we’re not getting off the couch. We’re not spending time, you know, watching the equivalent, experiencing the equivalent of a Felicity rerun with friends: We might not really want to do [it], but actually, doing it is gonna create a memory that’s gonna be valuable for us and create friendships that will serve us in the long run.

So, I am much more concerned not about the fact that expressed loneliness is increasing, but I’m concerned about the fact that it’s not increasing. And that tells me that as loneliness — sorry, as aloneness increases and as unhappiness increases, we’re not feeling that cue to fix the unhappiness by reducing our aloneness. Like, that’s, that’s the main problem here.

Matt’s observation also pulls at this theme that I think I’m, like, constantly wrestling with around my work, which is that the most interesting things to write about in society are when human values are pitted against each other. So I’ve, I write a lot about the costs of optimization culture in health. Like, I’m very interested in that right now.

Because, on the one hand, of course we should want to be healthy. It’s, like, very weird to hope that you get unhealthy, to want to die earlier. But there are absolutely ways in which if all you want to do is optimize for, like, HRV and resting heart rate in the minute before you go to bed, well, in that case, you would never see anybody or have any social experience after, like, 8 p.m. or 9 p.m. You would certainly never drink. You would never go to a party.

In fact, according to the Oura data, nothing correlates more negatively…
