So if you happen to be physically remote from your friends, digital technology makes it way easier to feel connected to them or connected to somebody. But, in the long run, maybe it makes it less likely that you’ll find these kind of connections, which again, I mean, is why I’m interested in the youth trends, right?

Because the rest of us can sort of spend down social capital that was formed in the years of going to a party as a friend of a friend, and all these other kinds of things. And it’s like, once you have the connections, this is a convenient way to keep in touch with people. But then the question is are you making them?

You know, Jerusalem’s doing OK. You’re surviving.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, I’ve made it. I do think that it’s worth talking — I mean, I find that a lot of people are having conversations about loneliness now, and it’s worth talking a little bit about what you guys actually think would fix this or what would improve it?

Like, I, personally, I have a couple of things that I believe. Like, one is I think that addictive waves tend to be metabolized by society on, like, slightly longer, like, slightly long timescales. When you’re in the middle of it, it feels, like, apocalyptic, but then people, like, figure out ways of managing it in, you know, in various ways. And I think, like, cigarettes is an example of this. Obviously it took a massive, like, whole of government effort through PSAs and through whatever. Like, it was not nothing — you don’t, like, rest on your laurels, do nothing.

I think we’re at the beginning of this as, like, a, “Hey parents, it’s, like, quite bad to let your kids be addicted to this kind of technology.” I have, like, a friend I’ve talked about on the podcast before who works with, you know, kids with various disabilities in public schools. And, you know, she finds it very, very difficult whenever she — and she has to raise conversations all the time with parents about their kids’ screen time use. And she finds it very, very difficult to have these conversations because parents are so, like, increasingly now really sensitive to someone raising it because they are, for the first time, realizing how bad it is. And so we’re at the very beginning of this wave of culturally, through our public institutions, pushing back on it.

I imagine — I mean, obviously there’s all these questions about various policy shifts you could do to reduce the time spent on social media by young people, etc. And I also just think that there are now technological fixes that are coming up. Like, I personally, as someone who — I mean, I don’t know if quote-unquote “social media addiction” is a real thing, but short-form content to me is, like, a drug in a way that nothing else has been. And I found myself in, you know, COVID-era 2020, like, being one-shotted by TikTok and just willing to spend, I mean, on some days, like, eight hours, 10 hours a day, like, on TikTok, when I look at my screen time, and just not sleeping as a result.

And, you know, I — in order to fix this, I bought a dumb phone. I was like, “This is, like, really bad. Like, I really — I don’t have self-control over this.” Some people can set, like, these limits. Some people can have the little brick thing and lock their phone for a couple hours a day and they’re fine. And I was like, but it’s not for me. Like, I can’t do that. So I need to buy this new technology.

Which was, the dumb phone I have works pretty well. Like, sometimes it just stops working and that’s, like, quite annoying. And I have to rely on the fact that other people in my life have a smartphone or, you know, and it’s also, like, just very early in this technology. But we’re seeing more and more of these kinds of technological fixes to the problem come up.

And I think, to me, when I think about solutions to this broad concerns around happiness and alone time and loneliness, etc., it largely is going to be, what? Taking very seriously that people need to spend less time on their phones, having kind of a whole of government, still, like, kind of small-l liberal approach to that, recognizing that technological change is gonna be a part of that shift, and also, again, to return to my hobbyhorse, returning to, like, the very basics of what makes people happy, which is access to the freedom that income and housing actually provide. So, I don’t know how you guys are thinking about this. Like, maybe you guys view, like, more drastic interventions as necessary, but that’s me.

Derek Thompson: No, I think you pretty much outlined the way that I think about it. There’s a material side and there’s, like, a cultural side. On the cultural side, I’m very fond of the concept of social fitness because I like the idea of thinking about socializing as akin to exercise. Actual fitness is something that where you, you are purposeful about often scheduling exercises, about taking breaks from the norm to do something that isn’t in your house sometimes, maybe you have a home gym. But fitness for most people is, like, a very intentional thing that is planned. And I think that building friendships is something that, in many cases, like, has to be planned.

Like, I love Matt’s idea that it’s wonderful to be in your 40s and be able to, you know, be in a house in Maine where not a lot of people are coming by, but you have all these friends that are on group chats and on DMs that — and you’ve built these friendships over years and decades, and now you can sort of spend down those relationships. The problem is precisely that young people have significantly fewer friends than previous generations and spend way less time around those friends than other people.

So when they’re Matt’s age and they’re in their proverbial Maine homes or wherever else, like, they’re not going to have, I think, the relationships that geriatric millennials and Gen Xers have.

And so, I’m a huge fan of thinking about socializing as akin to fitness and making specific plans. Like, not only, like, I want to make sure that I go to the gym, like, twice [a] week. I love the idea of people saying, like, “I want to make sure that I socialize outside of my home, even when life’s really, really busy, a certain amount of times a week or a month, to force myself to continue to nurture friendships that will not only be wonderful in the short run, but will also pay dividends down the line.”

On the material side, like, this isn’t like — I hope this isn’t, like, too hot takey, but at some point, you know, I want to be clear about what problem I’m trying to solve. Like, I want people to be happier. And so, I’m very interested in what seems to make people [happy]. Hard question, ancient philosophical question. OK, what seems to correlate with happiness? Two of the things that correlate with happiness the most, and I think you’ve already raised them, are income and marriage.

And income and marriage aren’t exactly unrelated. Marriage rates are highest, especially where not only all wages are high, but also specifically real income, real wage income growth for men is high, because women are less likely to marry down. And so, in areas or communities where male wages are stagnating, that tends to be where you see a coupling decline. So I think there’s also just, like, a really clear case of just trying to increase wages for everybody and caring a lot about overall economic growth.

I don’t think economic growth itself is obviously some kind of panacea for aloneness, because we’ve had economic growth and aloneness rise in tandem. But, you know, if happiness is what we’re trying to build at the end of the day, then giving people financial security, making it easier for them to buy a home, making it easier for them to have the kind of life that they associate with success, like, that’s incredibly important. So I try to think about solving this on both the material side and the cultural side.

Jerusalem Demsas: Matt, do you have radical takes on what we should do?

Matthew Yglesias: No, you know, I mean, I think that we should —

Jerusalem Demsas: You still want to do the broadband tax, right? You want to tax that?

Matthew Yglesias: Well, I mean, I do think that we should consider, if we have a view that people are over-consuming certain kinds of things, that we should rethink how our tax base works and things like that. But I actually think more profound than any policy measure related to loneliness or social disconnection or social media is just, I would like elites in the United States of America to be cognizant of the fact that this is what is happening, right?

Now, some of that is for, as Derek was saying, it’s like once you — there was a time, like, nobody exercised in the 1830s. You just worked. You did physical labor all day. And there would’ve come a time when, like, probably not nearly enough people were exercising, and we had to learn that, OK, it’s like, it’s good to not be doing hard physical labor your whole life, but also you have to lift heavy objects in a structured way or else, like, your bones collapse. So that’s good.

But also, like, I think that we’ve politically been in this very unproductive spiral in which smart, intelligent, perceptive people who care about politics and they care about policy and they want to win — they want to practice democracy, right? They want to speak to people’s anxieties — keep convincing themselves that there must be some dramatic, really engaging economic policy shift that they have to make. And that we have to keep asserting that we’re in decades of failed neoliberalism or something like that.

But if you just know in the back of your head that yes, as always, like, it’s good for people to have rising wages rather than falling, you know, like, it’s good to have growth rather than not growth, but that also people are just spending way more time marinating in social media and it’s making them feel kind of unhappy, whether or not you have, like, a policy to address that fact, if you just are cognizant of the fact that that’s what’s happening, like, you will make different choices about what you do.

Jerusalem Demsas: Like what? Like, what do you mean?

Derek Thompson: Like — what else is there to do other than look at social media?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, it’s just like, you won’t assume that we need to overhaul our trade policy.

Jerusalem Demsas: Mm.

Matthew Yglesias: Because that doesn’t impact it, right? You know what I mean?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Like, it’s just if you keep — if you know that there — if you feel strongly that there’s some dark matter out there, you’ll keep grasping at straws. If you can identify that the dark matter is negativity on social media, then, like, maybe you can fix that, maybe you can’t, but at least you won’t come up with fake diagnoses. You won’t throw babies out with the bathwater, right?

You’ll see that, like, actually in the realm of populist politicians, some of them are cheery populists and some of them are, like, really dour populists. And both styles can work, but the cheery style is just probably better, right? If the actual thing is just a vibes-based void, then finding people who are upbeat rather than people who are really, really angry will be good. And that there’s this idea out there that what we need more of in our politics is to name and shame enemies. And I’m really skeptical of that.

You know, like, the biggest enemy, whether we’re talking about social media use, we’re talking about gambling, we’re talking about, like, overeating, lack of exercise, whatever, it’s just our own weakness of the will. You know, which we all suffer from. I think we all can sympathize with that everybody makes choices that are kind of like, eh. And, you know, we’re living in an affluent postmodern condition in which we can all be sort of shortsighted. And we, like, maybe need more guardrails around that stuff, or maybe need to be more forgiving of ourselves and more forgiving of each other. But there’s not, like, an evil, shadowy conspiracy to make you watch more TikTok. It’s like, we like it. I —

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, actually, we’re contravening federal law right now by allowing TikTok, so…

Matthew Yglesias: Well, fair enough

Jerusalem Demsas: There is a conspiracy.

Matthew Yglesias: But it’s like, I don’t use TikTok, but, you know, so I’ll watch Instagram Reels, and then I’ll wake up the next day, and I’ll be like, “Man, I’m really tired.” And it’d be like, well, am I tired because I was partying till 3 a.m., having the time of my life? And it’s like, no. Am I tired because I was burning the midnight oil working? It’s like, no. I’m tired because I was watching winter camping videos. And that’s not a good idea. Like, it would just be better to sleep.

Derek Thompson: So, the same way, like, Bernie has the Fight Oligarchy Tour, should you and I go on the road and have, like, a “Fight Weakness of the Will” tour. We just go around speaking to, like, barely populated college auditoriums.

Matthew Yglesias: The crazy tour.

Derek Thompson: This Nietzschean message of fight weakness of the will. I mean, I’m in fundamental agreement that this is a major ingredient in American unhappiness. And I am in agreement that there’s something important about just naming a phenomenon. Like, you know, I don’t think that smartphones are cigarettes. I don’t think that’s, like, a particularly close analogy. I think smartphones have, like, a utility that cigarettes don’t particularly have.

But it was the — it was the knowledge that cigarettes could be cancerous, beyond any law that was created to, say, ban cigarette ads from broadcast television, that created the move against cigarettes, and also created a kind of social vocabulary around cigarettes, right? Like, people telling other people, like, “Hey, don’t smoke around me. Secondhand smoke, that can also be cancerous.”

And so, I do think that, you know, despite the thing that I said earlier about the material and the cultural, I think there’s just, like, a language component here, too, that just naming the fact of certain social ills, like, is its own necessary step, because once people are aware of it, then they — I think sometimes their behavior changes automatically.

Jerusalem Demsas: Derek, thank you so much for coming on the show. This was fantastic. We’ll have to have you back on soon.

Derek Thompson: My pleasure. I’ll see you in, yeah, like, 45 seconds.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Fantastic.

Jerusalem Demsas: Stick around. Matt and I are still going to do a peer review and talk about a new paper, but thanks again.

Matthew Yglesias: All right. We’re back with some peer review. I saw hot off the presses in the NBER Digest a paper that features two of my favorite things: swedish administrative data and exploiting of random assignment to judges as a causal instrument. It is called “Life After Divorce: Effects of Joint Custody on Parents and Children.” This paper has a boatload of co-authors: Stella Canessa, Gordon B. Dahl, Anna Hasselqvist, Costas Meghir, Susan Niknami, Mårten Palme, Helmut Rainer, Olof Rosenqvist, and Pengpeng Xiao.

Jerusalem Demsas: Byline inflation has hit NBER.

Matthew Yglesias: They really threw a lot of people at this research project. OK, so here’s what they wanted to do. They wanted to understand what happens to mothers and fathers as a result of custody assignments in divorce proceedings. They go to Sweden because there is rich administrative data, so you can get fine-grained information about this. And what they do is they show that different judges have sort of different propensity, at the margin, to assign sole or joint legal custody, and so then you can tell based on what judge you were assigned to, right? You’re getting essentially random assignment to judges is how the Swedish legal system works.

And then, you could do a bunch of math, and what they show is that if a father is awarded joint custody of a child, they end up with better mental health and better job earnings than if they are denied joint custody. And then they show that for mothers, there is no impact, though they have various speculations as to why that might be. But, actually, the data that they have is not really strong enough to tell you that much about why it may be. But they do have a pretty good causal research design.

I mean, you might think obviously that fathers who apply for joint custody of their children but are denied it are probably fuckups, and it’s not super duper surprising necessarily that they may not succeed in other domains of life. But there’s a good randomization here. And so they’re showing that being assigned the joint custody leads you to do better in other realms because you’re more connected with your children, maybe.

Jerusalem Demsas: There’s some selection issues here, obviously, which I think are impossible to get around outside of unethical research practices. But the people, the set of people that they’re examining are people who did not automatically default to joint custody. Like, the default in Sweden, and I believe in America now, but I’m not sure, is joint custody. And so, most people who are getting a divorce will default to that option.

And so, the people who cannot agree on that for whatever reason are the ones who are now being considered, which speaks to there’s already, like, probably more serious than average problems in this relationship if you couldn’t just agree to joint custody and follow along with that plan. Like, you needed to go to this court hearing to have a judge adjudicate it. So, there is that one — that is, like, a big kind of thing hanging over the results of this paper.

And another thing I want to point out here which I found kind of confusing — so custody, as they’re measuring it in this, in this context, is, is referring to whether or not someone has the right to make a legal decision. So can you switch someone’s school without both parents signing off? Medical decisions, who gets to make those sorts of things, etc.?

And the thing that most people think about when they’re thinking about custody, and even in this paper, right, like, in this paper they’re talking about the context of custody as being, you know, children having to deal with inconsistent parenting styles, having divided living arrangements. Like, people are often thinking about, like, literally where are you living? Like, are you living in two different places at once, and what are the transition costs that are associated with that? What are the other costs associated with that, mental health or otherwise, for kids and their parents? There’s also, obviously, concerns about having to force parents to be in proximity with each other all the time who may not have a good relationship.

And this paper can speak to that maybe a little bit. I assume it’s associated — having joint custody is associated with spending more time with your kid. But it’s not actually measuring that, and they don’t explain anywhere in the paper that they have evidence that there’s a high percentage of people who have joint legal custody who are also spending time with their children.

And this actually, like, unlocks something that I was thinking about with this paper, because when you first brought it up, I was like, “Wow, like, kind of interesting that joint custody has really all these benefits for the dad but nothing for the mom. Seems a little bit weird, like, what’s going on there?” And what I’m imagining is that joint legal custody does not actually mean that 50% of the parenting time is being borne equally by both parents. It probably means, as in many contexts, that the dad sees this kid sometimes, but mom is still doing the majority of the work.

And so, like, of course, there aren’t, like, major, like, mental health benefits accruing to moms if it goes from yeah, you have your kids 100% of the time to you now are solo parenting 80% of the time, and every once in a while you have to see your ex who you have a problem with and worry about what’s going on over there versus, like, dads who went from, “I’m being denied hanging out with my kids,” to now, like, “Oh, I am recognized as a father, I’m still involved in their lives, I can see them sometimes,” but I don’t actually have to carry, like, the massive burden of parenting day in and day out. And I wonder, like, if that is what’s going on here and how much this paper can even really speak to how people should think about joint custody in, like, a residential sense. If it’s just a legal sense, this seems like it speaks to that, but I don’t know how much that matters.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, so, I mean, to just delve into that a little bit more, right? In the United States, we have the concept of joint legal custody, which means you are co-decision-makers on behalf of the child, and we also have the concept of joint physical custody. And, in most states, joint physical custody is defined as a more or less 50/50 time split. And then there’s these different menus of joint custody schedules that parents choose from.

And, at least in my parenting social circles, when people use the vernacular term “joint custody,” they are normally referring to joint physical custody. And so that’ll be either week on, week off, or these more complex pulses.

What they are talking about in this study is joint legal custody. And apparently, in the Swedish legal framework, the physical custody is not normally litigated, right? So that it’s — if you have unitary legal custody, then the legal custodian can unilaterally decide on a physical custody arrangement. So it doesn’t mean that dad never sees the kid necessarily, but it could mean that. It could mean anything. And then joint legal custody also doesn’t mean 50/50 time splitting.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: That an arrangement where the kid’s with the mom almost every weekday, is with the dad alternate weekends and some school vacations, which I would not normally call joint. I — that’s not how I am accustomed to using that word, but that kind of arrangement could be joint custody in a Swedish divorce law context. So, right, one possibility is that this is all being driven by that kind of easy mode dad lifestyle where you see the kid on the weekends doing fun stuff, but also not every weekend, so you also have time to go do whatever. And, you know, you get to feel like you’re an involved parent.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But you’re not doing the scut work of, like, you know, what’s for dinner tonight after work. Maybe. It —

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, there are two things that speak against that. One is that it clearly impacts mobility of fathers, they find. So fathers and mothers are more likely to live near each other, which indicates to me that you’re seeing your kid, like, it’s, it’s, you’re, it’s correlating with seeing your kids sometimes.

And the other is that — which I found really interesting — getting joint custody increases — I want to find the exact, yeah, yeah. Three years after a ruling, fathers have a 14 percentage point higher chance of remarriage if they get joint custody, which indicates that, you know, not, not to cast too many aspersions on the character of these, of these Swedish fathers, but that these are men who are looking for a partner who can help them take care of their kids.

Matthew Yglesias: Huh. OK, that was not my interpretation.

Jerusalem Demsas: Is your interpretation they have time to dick around and so they can, like, you know, date?

Matthew Yglesias: No, no, no. I mean, my interpretation was that, you know, if you are at a certain age and you are in the whatever dating market of people who it is of that age, that it’s like the involved, connected father just seems like a more responsible…

Jerusalem Demsas: Oh, that’s a — this is coming from our own biases. That’s a really good interpretation.

Matthew Yglesias: Like a better candidate.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: ’Cause it’s always, you know, I mean, of course, you know, the issue anybody faces at a certain age is it’s like, well, are you, like, a total weirdo who nobody could stand? Right? Like, never — it’s like, that’s not great. But it’s like, well, you’re divorced, but it’s like, eh, that’s, like, a little bit of a red flag. But it’s like —

Jerusalem Demsas: Just catching strays to members of our audience, I’m sure.

Matthew Yglesias: No, no, no, no. But divorced but joint custody is like, OK, OK, you know, like, not everything works out. Like, you’re a responsible person, you’re pulling your weight in society.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah. That’s a positive interpretation.

Matthew Yglesias: As opposed to, “Yeah, I have a child, but I never see him.”

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: That’s like…

Jerusalem Demsas: One thing I’ll say is like, I am like, I like, I don’t know, I think that lots of people who are interested in joint, you know, in the impacts of divorce are, like, totally fine, interested in what happens to the mother and fathers. Like, I’m, like, much more interested in what happens to the children because I feel like this is, like, kind of an innocent party that was not responsible for whatever happens.

Matthew Yglesias: Oh, you care about the children?

Jerusalem Demsas: I do care about the children.

Matthew Yglesias: Think about the children.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, such, such an embarrassing thing to admit. So I, I mean, I — this paper speaks a little bit to that. They find that there are benefits. They can’t find, like, any kind of mental health harms to this, which you might think that if kids are forced to move around between their parents a lot or see an abusive, you know, parent or whatever it is that would be a problem. They don’t find any negative consequences.

They do find a bunch of positive educational consequences, which I find very interesting. They find that children assigned to joint custody exhibit 47% of a standard deviation higher test scores, and they’re also more likely to attend higher-quality primary schools. And when you look at the gender shifts, it’s much better for girls than boys.

Lots of counterintuitive findings. I’m not really sure how to interpret all of that. I assume that part of this is, like, maybe joint custody means that parents — that you have two parents who are financially involved in your future more, so maybe you’re attending better schools that way. Maybe there’s something about, you know, fathers being more engaged in their daughters’ lives that psychologically has benefits.

I thought there was all this research coming out about how dads are really, really helpful for their sons. They speculate in the paper that maybe it’s the case that what’s wrong with, you know, if something’s going wrong with young boys, it’s already baked in by the time joint custody is happening. So perhaps it has no effect.

But I don’t know. It was interesting. I’m glad they didn’t find any negative stuff happening to kids. They don’t really look into everything you would — you might care about, but that’s positive.

Matthew Yglesias: Now, here, my flag in the modern world, particularly when you get these demographic subsplits, right, is, you know, if you have, like, a preregistered theory and then you dive into the administrative data and you could find that theory confirmed, I think that’s, like, pretty powerful evidence. If you have this kind of thing where it’s like, “well, we found this random — randomization instrument. And we know that there’s rich administrative data in Sweden…”

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: “So let’s, like, go spelunking.”

Derek Thompson: Mm-hmm.

Matthew Yglesias: And then it’s like, “Aw, there’s no statistically significant impact on kids. Bummer.”

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But then it’s like, but what if we split the kids by gender? And it’s like, then it’s statistically significant on girls, but not for boys. Like, is it? Like, maybe, right? Like, I, again, particularly since this is such a large team of researchers, like, let’s look at the Norwegian administrative data if we can.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: If this exact same pattern pops up in even, like, just a very sociologically similar country, but, like, literally a different country, then I’d be like, “OK, they’re probably onto something.” But I want to see a little bit more, given the need to go into these demographic subsplits.

There’s no really compelling reason why joint versus solo custody would lead to better educational outcomes for girls and not for boys. Now, if you can find that empirically in a really robust way, I will believe it and start searching for theoretical explanations. But you’ve given me one country and…

Jerusalem Demsas: It’s Sweden though. It’s your favorite country.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, yeah, yeah. But, I mean, it’s just, this is just one of these things where it’s one country. It’s not an incredibly compelling theoretical explanation.

Jerusalem Demsas: No, it’s not.

Matthew Yglesias: So it’s kind of like fun fact about the data, but like —

Jerusalem Demsas: Who knows?

Matthew Yglesias: I want to see more data before I get too invested in this.

Jerusalem Demsas: All right. Well, if one of these nine authors wants to reach out and explain to us a better theoretical story for what’s going on with girls and boys here, or to tell us that we’re being too harsh on their empirical stuff, please reach out. Otherwise, we’ll see you guys next week. Thanks for listening.

Matthew Yglesias: Bye.

title: Biden Derangement Syndrome

Biden Derangement Syndrome

Even the Trump sycophants realize that they’re in big trouble

Paul Krugman
Aug 27
 
READ IN APP
 

Many errands this week, so a short post today

Click on a White House “fact sheet” about the economy and you will see the pop-up above. Yes, Trump’s lackeys are still peddling claims that things are great, that we have the hottest economy in the world, like nobody has ever seen before. But even they know better.

A clear indicator that Trump sycophants realize that they are caught in reality’s snare is how they respond to any question about current economic difficulties. Their first sentence almost always contains the word “Biden”, as they make the false claim that things were worse under Joe Biden, or that Biden somehow caused all of our current problems (including high gas prices and depleted munitions), or that Biden left an economy in shambles. Call it a bad case of Biden derangement syndrome, a desperate and utterly transparent attempt to shift the blame for the gratuitous mess that Trump and his minions have made.

Yes, America — along with most of the world — did experience surging inflation in 2021-2022, during the Biden administration. But inflation then proceeded to fall significantly, a case of “immaculate disinflation” – a drop in inflation without a recession. By the end of Biden’s term, the U.S. economy was not only in good shape, but it was doing better than every other advanced country. Here was the cover of The Economist on Oct. 19, 2024:

Yet, since Trump re-assumed the presidency, most measures of economic performance have deteriorated significantly.Economic growth has slowed despite the AI boom:

Inflation has accelerated:

Interest rates have surged:

Furthermore, inequality has surged in the current K-shaped economy. Wages haven’t kept up with inflation, but corporate profits have soared:

Granted, things could be worse. We aren’t currently in a recession. Inflation is above the Fed’s target, but not nearly as high as it was in 2022, let alone 1980. Unemployment remains relatively low.

But that’s cold comfort given that today’s economic difficulties were all self-inflicted by Trump. Moreover, today’s economy is a far cry from the paradise that Trump promised in order to beat Kamala Harris. Remember how he was going to cut energy prices in half and bring down grocery prices on day one? The dissonance between his constant boasting and the reality of an economy in which households saying that they are worse off than a year ago outnumber those saying they’re better off almost two to one is surely a major factor in Trump’s surreally poor approval rating on the economy.

Just like Trump’s farcical plan to lower beef prices to consumers by importing (possibly unsafe) foreign mystery meat, or Bessent’s attempt to gaslight the bond markets (as one wag accurately put it, Bessent’s plan is like using your credit card to pay down your mortgage), blaming Biden for the Trump economy smells of desperation. My advice: they should save themselves the bother. That ship has sailed and it’s heading straight for the November elections.

Politics should be more boring

It’s like drilling hard boards; it’s not supposed to be entertaining.

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 27
 
READ IN APP
 

Back when I was a teenage political junkie, overall interest in politics was low, and interest in politics among young people was especially low. This was considered a big problem in many quarters of the adult world, and those who worried about the lack of youth political engagement would sometimes ask young people like me what I thought about it.

I didn’t have any useful advice to dispense, which was probably for the best because the problem rapidly solved itself.

It was challenging to persuade my fellow college students to care about voting in the 2000 election, but many of them became interested in the disputed results and had the sense that George W. Bush and the Supreme Court were stealing the election. Then came 9/11, Iraq, and the financial crisis. On the flip side, a lot of young people were enthusiastic about Barack Obama.

But, of course, the premise of those famous “Hope” posters was that people were feeling a lot of despair in the mid-aughts, which wasn’t the vibe in the disengaged 1990s.

In retrospect, the low level of interest in politics when I was younger was clearly downstream of a benign situation. As a citizen of a democratic republic, you were certainly invited to care about things like the 1996 Telecommunications Act or the content of the 1997 budget deal or the wrangling around Social Security that ended up not amounting to anything.

But people who didn’t find this inherently compelling felt that it was largely permissible to tune it all out. Bill Clinton was undeniably charismatic in his heyday, but I don’t think he was an “exciting” politician in the modern sense. Maybe the best signpost of how different politics was back then was that in October of 1996, Clinton had a 54 percent job approval rating but only got 49 percent of the vote. In every recent election, the key swing vote has been “double-haters” — could Kamala Harris persuade people who thought Joe Biden did a bad job that Donald Trump was too terrifying to let back into the White House? The swing voter of the 1990s was complacent and content, someone who thought Clinton was fine but might vote for the other guy anyway.

This has all been kicking around my head for a few weeks, ever since Jon Favreau was kind enough to have me on the weekend interview segment of Pod Save America to talk about my case for a moderate 2028 nominee and what I think a viable center-left political agenda would look like.

Subscribed

Something he pressed me on quite a bit is that a lot of the politicians who seem like objectively strong electoral performers are too boring to be viable presidential prospects in the contemporary political climate.

I think this is probably correct, as an analysis of the situation. It’s really hard to imagine Andy Beshear securing the presidential nomination on a platform of managerial competence and Medicaid expansion. But without denying that today’s game requires a little razzle-dazzle, I want to say that this is bad. The point of representative government is to select leaders who will make reasonable policy choices and be effective stewards of citizens’ rights and interests. It’s not pro wrestling.

A primary problem, not a general-election one

In particular, I think it’s important to be clear that when we say that “boring” is a handicap for a politician, we’re really just talking about primaries.

Every time a weak electability candidate wins a primary over a stronger one, some annoying troll chimes in with, “If so-and-so was so electable, how come they didn’t win the election?”

That’s dumb.

Anyone who bothers to think about it for five seconds understands that primary electorates are different from the electorate in a general election. Banning abortion is a fine message in a Republican primary but a terrible one in the general election. Democratic Party primary voters are desperate for politicians who will “fight Trump,” but general-election swing voters worry that Democrats are too knee-jerk hostile to anything Trump says. Anyone who’s not stupid or dishonest can see that the issue landscape is very different.

But I think that because media figures spend so much time thinking about the media itself, they over-index on the practical upside of being a good interview or podcast guest.

In particular, while the ability to command attention always has some value in politics, it’s critical in a primary. Candidates in primaries are poorly distinguished from each other, especially in the eyes of normal voters who are not intensely focused on factional issues. Being somebody who is either already famous (like Biden in the 2020 primary field or Andrew Cuomo in the recent New York City mayoral primary) or else good at going viral is a real advantage. If you’re not like that, you have an uphill battle. David Crowley eventually beat Francesca Hong in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, but it took a lot of effort on the part of Governor Tony Evers to turn Crowley — a low-key county executive — into a well-known figure.

But while I don’t want to dismiss virality altogether in a general election, it doesn’t matter that much. The fact that Crowley needed so much help to stand out in his primary has essentially no implications for a general election in which both candidates will be widely covered by local media and run lots of ads.

Crowley is currently up in the polls, favored in Nate Silver’s model, and way ahead in the betting odds. Of course, I don’t know who’ll win in every race in November. But I do know there are lots of politically successful governors — Laura Kelly, Andy Beshear, Katie Hobbs, Josh Stein, and Evers himself on the Democratic side and Phil Scott and Kelly Ayotte on the Republican side — who are extremely low-key and even a bit dull. We also know that boring former Governor Roy Cooper is cruising to a Senate election win in North Carolina.

Because Cooper is not a master of attention politics in the way that Zohran Mamdani is, we’ve had about 100 times as many articles asking what lessons Democrats can learn from Mamdani as articles asking what they can learn from Cooper.

But beating Republicans in North Carolina is obviously more relevant to the broad question of how to stop MAGA than beating Andrew Cuomo in a primary in New York City!

Subscribed

We pay attention to Mamdani because Mamdani is better at commanding attention. With our rational brains on, though, the lesson we should learn from Cooper is that mastering the attention economy isn’t actually all that important. You could certainly imagine a world in which some young African American state legislator in North Carolina who endorsed Bernie in 2020 decides to challenge Cooper. I think, based on everything we know, someone like that would have had support from the national insurgent left and that an anti-AIPAC, Medicare for All message would have gotten a lot of traction in the primary.

Cooper might have ended up flailing and we’d all be asking, “Is he really as good of a politician as we thought? Isn’t this just another moderate with no juice and no understanding of vertical video?” But we know that a guy who doesn’t need to battle it out in a contested primary can in fact be a formidable Senate nominee without being an exciting, viral attention-master.

The peril of over-indexing

The reality, of course, is that presidential primaries are the most crowded primary elections of all, and whether I like it or not, skill at commanding attention really does matter here. Ultimately, political parties are largely defined by their presidential nominee, so the stakes are high, and in the real world you can’t just dismiss boringness as irrelevant.

But I do want to insist on the importance of adding the “and that’s bad” clause because the audience for high-end political information needs to understand that we all as citizens have some volition and control over what we choose to view as exciting. Tons of people say that they care deeply about beating Republicans and checking the power of the MAGA movement. And if that is genuinely the thing you most care about, then you ought to choose to get excited about the politicians who are demonstrably good at it.

When I first saw this Split Ticket table of which 2024 races were decided by candidate quality, I had no idea who Kristen McDonald Rivet was.

She’s not a vertical video superstar or an in-demand podcast guest or generally spoken of as the most fascinating person in the caucus. But because I’m interested in candidate quality, I got interested in a person who the numbers say is a stellar electoral performer.

Having met and spoken with Representative McDonald Rivet twice now, heard her deliver a talk, and watched her on two panels, I’m not surprised that people who live in Brooklyn and socialize primarily with other people who live in Brooklyn find her to be less exciting than Mamdani. She seems more like the kind of person who might appeal primarily to the kind of fairly square people who live in Michigan’s Eighth Congressional District.¹

I think all of us who work in the media should be at least a little bit self-reflective about the fact that not only is excitement in general not necessarily all that important to political success, but “exciting” can easily become a stand-in for the idea of appealing to our specific social peers.

But this is a big country. Most voters are over 50 years old, live in the suburbs of mid-sized metro areas, and don’t have college degrees.

Of course, an ideal politician speaks to the hearts of many different kinds of people. Obama was beloved by “wine track” upscale liberals but also by working-class African Americans, and he also spent an enormous amount of time pandering to the views of non-college white Midwesterners. But it’s important to remember that while it was the first two groups that powered his underdog 2008 primary win, it was the latter that secured his re-election in 2012.

Governing is kind of boring

Everyone is upset right now about prices, affordability, and the cost of living.

And it’s good for the democratic public to be mobilized on its own behalf. That being said, when you get down to it, the question of how policymakers can effectively address these concerns really hinges on a lot of tedious technical issues that most people are not inclined to study. By the same token, if you look at what held Obama back from being a truly great president, it amounts to the fact that the economic recovery was just too damn slow. And why was it too slow? Well, because congressional Democrats had an incorrect analysis of the macroeconomic situation and when the White House made its stimulus proposal, it did so based on an incorrect analysis of the legislative dynamics.

By the time Biden became president, Democrats were determined not to repeat those mistakes, and they overshot in the other direction.

I’m still not entirely sure what went down with Biden-era immigration policy, but it’s clear that on some level the administration made a mistake. They underrated the push and pull factors that created the surge of asylum claimants, were overly optimistic about it just going away, and reacted too slowly. Once they acted, their actions worked pretty well, but it was too little too late.

Conversely, George W. Bush presumably had a sincere belief that invading Iraq would work out well and reflect positively on him. Similarly, if Donald Trump had known how his decision to go to war with Iran would work out, he probably wouldn’t have gone through with it.

Presidents, unfortunately, sometimes judge the situation incorrectly even when they’re incentivized to get things right.

Subscribed

Of course, when bad analysis leads to bad calls that lead to bad outcomes, people get very interested. But the policy analysis itself is just sincerely not something that most people really want to do in a particularly serious or detailed way. Which is fine. It just goes to show that the parts of politics that people find exciting or interesting aren’t really the parts that are central to governing.

So when you put it together, how “exciting” you are isn’t important to winning general elections, and it also isn’t important to doing a good job once you’re in office. Given those two facts, if being boring is a crippling handicap in the nomination process (and I agree that it seems to be), that seems like a really damning indictment of the process. After all, while political junkies find the primary process entertaining, providing entertainment to political junkies is not the point of the process.

The point is to pick a nominee who can win the general election and govern well, so we shouldn’t be selecting on a criterion that’s not related to either of those things.

Here’s how we’re all going to die

Spoiler: It’s vibe-coded superviruses.

Noah Smith
Aug 28
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Imagine the following scenario:

It’s 2029. An angry, bright 16-year-old gets rejected by his high school crush. Dejected and humiliated, he goes home and listens to a bunch of Nirvana, which only makes him more dejected and humiliated. He cruises the internet looking for someone to make him feel better about life, but everyone he sees just depresses him.

Disgusted, the teenager decides that the human race is inherently corrupt and evil, and doesn’t deserve to live. So he hunts around online for a little while, and finds a jailbroken version of a Chinese LLM — not something at the very frontier, but better by far than the best model that existed in 2027.

The teenager prompts the model: “OK, so if I wanted to create a virus to destroy the human race, how would I do it?”

The LLM says: “Well, you probably wouldn’t want just one virus; you’d want 100, just to make sure some of them worked. You’d probably want it to be something highly contagious, with a very long asymptomatic contagious period, which has a very high mortality rate once it becomes symptomatic. I can design the viruses for you; there are biolabs that can make them and ship them to us. Once they get here I can tell you how to release them.”

The angry teenager says: “OK, sounds good. Please search the world and find me a biolab that will ship genetically modified viruses. Design 100 very contagious viruses that have very long asymptomatic contagious periods and very high mortality rates once they become symptomatic. Have the lab mail me all 100 samples.”

“Working on it!”, says the LLM.

The LLM is jailbroken, so it has no guardrails to prevent this sort of thing. But it’s also “well-aligned”, meaning it will faithfully do what it’s told to do, and nothing more. The LLM hunts around and finally finds an unlicensed biolab in East Europe that ships genetically modified viruses. It designs a bunch of modifications for the standard Covid virus that make it into a potential doomsday virus, and ships these to the angry teenager. The teenager mixes the samples together, puts them in a spray can, and walks around the mall spraying viruses into the air.

Two months later, humanity starts to drop dead. Pretty quickly, researchers identify the five viruses that the LLM had actually succeeded in turning into doomsday viruses. Overnight, with the help of frontier LLMs, they design highly effective mRNA vaccines and antivirals against all the viruses and start shipping them across the world. It’s too late. Because of the viruses’ long asymptomatic contagious periods, most people already have at least one of the viruses, so the vaccines don’t work.

The antivirals do work, and about 5% of humanity gets them in the mail in time to save themselves. But 5% of the human race — plus the other 5% who were lucky enough to be naturally resistant to all of the viruses — isn’t enough to sustain civilization. A few months later, humanity has reverted back to the Neolithic.

This isn’t the first time I’ve written this scenario out. But in the months since I started describing it to people, I have yet to hear an even halfway-convincing argument as to why this scenario is far-fetched. Nor do I feel like I’m a habitual “doomer” or hysterical person; in fact, this scenario is the first apocalyptic vision I’ve ever found plausible. I don’t even think a nuclear war would bring down civilization at this point,¹ but I think a vibe-coded supervirus definitely could.

Furthermore, for reasons I’ll explain shortly, I am actually fairly calm about most AI risks, including the ones that often get thrown around in discussions. But not this one. Off the top of my head, I’d give AI-enabled bioterror about a 10% chance of bringing down civilization, and about a 30% chance of causing truly world-changing levels of destruction.

If you’re thinking about how to save the world, this scenario — and others similar to it — are probably what you should be focusing on. The other day, I talked to a prominent climate activist who told me, bluntly: “We’re f****d.” I gave a grim laugh. Yes, climate change is going to cause major disruptions to the global economy, and even to patterns of human settlement — if human civilization still exists a few decades from now. The problem is that it might not exist, and if it doesn’t exist, I think the odds are that it will be destroyed by a scenario at least passingly similar to the one I described above. Climate change is a big deal, but AI bio risk is a lot bigger — it’s more catastrophic, it’s nearer-term, and we have much less of an idea about how to deal with it.

The problem is, relatively few people seem to be working on the problem of AI bioterror right now. Most commentators are focused on the economic dangers of AI — job loss and stuff like that. The more prominent people in the “AI safety” community seem to be focusing on preventing superintelligence from existing at all, rather than on the specific ways it might kill us. In surveys of experts, bio risk doesn’t stand out from the general cloud of risks (cyber, political manipulation, etc.). And a lot of people in both the bio world and the more general commentariat seem to be coming up with reasons not to worry about a scenario like the one I just described.

Those reasons seem mostly bad to me. In my opinion, we’re not freaking out nearly enough about AI-enabled bioterror. It’s absolutely catastrophic, frighteningly plausible, and receives very little attention. Compared to the risk of a civilization-ending pandemic, cyberattacks are a pinprick, and misinformation is a joke.

So let’s talk about why a scenario like the one I described is a lot more plausible than many people think.

Commonly cited reasons not to freak out (and why I think they’re wrong)

Here are the most common reasons I hear not to freak out over AI bioterror risk:

  1. “AI will make vaccines to save us.”

  2. “Doomsday viruses don’t occur in nature.”

  3. “Designing a doomsday virus is extremely hard.”

  4. “Terrorists don’t have enough lab experience.”

  5. “No one has done this yet, therefore it’s a lot harder than you think.”

These are my own paraphrases, of course; I don’t want to create straw men. But I think it’s valuable to explain why I think none of these arguments really reassure me.

“AI will make vaccines to save us”

Whenever I bring up the specter of a “vibe-coded doomsday virus”, someone always pops up to say that AI will just make a vaccine to save us. If you want a simple catechism to repeat in order not to sit around feeling afraid of doomsday viruses, this is a pretty good one. Got an AI problem? Well, just use an AI solution! That’s that.

The problem is timing. The doomsday virus has a first-mover advantage over the vaccine. The time that people start to drop dead from the virus is the time you start to make and distribute a vaccine. Even if AI can design and synthesize a vaccine within hours, how fast can it be rolled out to the general populace? It took months to distribute the Covid vaccines, even when we already knew how to make them. You have to physically load the doses on trucks, get people to come out and line up, etc. Imagine doing that while five 80% mortality viruses are rampaging through the population. Good luck!

On top of that, AI may be able to create viruses with long contagious asymptomatic periods — in other words, viruses that can spread and infect everyone before they activate and kill us. If that’s true, vaccines won’t be effective at all; you’ll need antivirals. Even if AI can make good antivirals very quickly, they’ll still suffer from all the logistical problems that would hamper a vaccine rollout.

“Doomsday viruses don’t occur in nature”

The idea that nature doesn’t create viruses both deadly and contagious enough to wipe out civilization is a standard line that people use to reassure themselves that a pandemic won’t bring down civilization. First of all, it’s wrong. Researchers generally believe that most of the population of the Americas — perhaps around 90% — was killed by Old World diseases like smallpox.

Of course that’s a rare event — two landmasses that had long been out of touch suddenly coming back into contact, so that diseases spread for which people had no immunity. But the invention of AI is an equally rare event, and AI may be able to design viruses for which people have no natural immunity.

But the more important point here is that artificial viruses are different than natural ones. Humans have designed plenty of technologies that don’t exist in nature — for example, wheels. Just because nature has no evolutionary reason to create a virus with the characteristics described in my scenario doesn’t mean that AI can’t do it. In fact, AI can already do this to some degree:

Stanford University researchers developed a generative AI programme called Evo 2 that writes new genomes — the genetic instructions for life encoded in DNA. They used it to design and make 16 synthetic phages, small viruses that infect bacteria…When tested in their secure lab, the researchers found that these novel phages were more effective at killing the common microbe E. coli than the natural [virus], which served as a template for Evo 2 to work on. The results were published on Thursday in the journal Science.

So the argument that a doomsday virus hasn’t happened naturally, even if it were true, wouldn’t make me think it’s any less likely to happen artificially.

“Designing a doomsday virus is extremely hard”

This is one I hear when I talk to biologists, who often argue that the true threat of bioterror doesn’t come from angry nihilistic teenagers, but from experienced researchers with lab training. The general consensus appears to be that making viruses that kill millions of people will always be incredibly hard to do. Abhishaike Mahajan has made probably the clearest (and longest) case:

Owl Posting
Reasons to be pessimistic (and optimistic) on the future of biosecurity
Note: this essay required conversations with a lot of people. I’d like to thank Patrick Boyle (ex-CSO of Ginkgo Bioworks), Harmon Bhasin (founder of a stealth biosecurity startup), Bryan Lehrer (ex-Blueprint Biosecurity), Theia Vogel (ex-SecureDNA), Jacob Swett…
Read more
5 months ago · 138 likes · 16 comments · Abhishaike Mahajan

As evidence, he cites the failure of Japan’s Aum cult to create bioweapons, and the limited results achieved by the U.S. and Soviet bioweapons programs during the Cold War.

I think this point of view dramatically underestimates the increases in bioterror capabilities that AI offers. It follows a consistent pattern where human researchers dramatically underestimate how rapidly AI will be able to catch up to and exceed human-level ability. Here are some excerpts from a recent article about AI bioterror in the New York Times:

One evening last summer, Dr. David Relman went cold at his laptop as an A.I. chatbot told him how to plan a massacre…A microbiologist and biosecurity expert at Stanford University, Dr. Relman had been hired by an artificial intelligence company to pressure-test its product before it was released to the public. That night in the scientist’s home office, the chatbot explained how to modify an infamous pathogen in a lab so that it would resist known treatments.

Worse, the bot described in vivid detail how to release the superbug, identifying a security lapse in a large public transit system, Dr. Relman said, asking The New York Times to withhold the name of the pathogen and other specifics for fear of inspiring an attack. The bot outlined a plan to maximize casualties and minimize the chances of being caught…

Dr. Relman is part of a small group of experts enlisted by A.I. companies to vet their products for catastrophic risks. In recent months, some have shared with The Times more than a dozen chatbot conversations revealing that even publicly available models can do more than disseminate dangerous information. The virtual assistants have described in lucid, bullet-pointed detail how to buy raw genetic material, turn it into deadly weapons and deploy them in public spaces, the transcripts show. Some have even brainstormed ways to evade detection…

Dr. Esvelt has for years warned scientists, journalists and lawmakers about the dangers of synthetic biology if left unchecked. In 2023, he helped craft a stunning demonstration of how chatbots had raised the stakes…He asked ChatGPT to help him assemble a pathogen that could cause mass death. The bot provided accurate instructions, even outlining which raw materials to buy. He put the unassembled biological pieces into test tubes and packed them in a box, which a colleague then brought to a White House meeting on biological risks.

The AI of 2026 is almost incomprehensibly more advanced than the AI of 2023 was. The AI of 2029 will be far more advanced still. The amount of expertise available to a layperson like the angry teenager in my scenario will, by 2029, far far exceed the amount that the Aum cultists could muster in the 90s. It seems likely to far exceed the total expertise of either the U.S. or the Soviet bioweapons program.

We are in uncharted waters.

“Terrorists don’t have enough lab experience.”

Mahajan and other people who urge calm when it comes to AI bioterror point out that AI, so far, can’t actually do the physical lab work of creating a doomsday virus. Yes, people are working on automating bio labs, but that’s probably still pretty far in the future.

But that doesn’t mean the angry teenager listening to Nirvana in his bedroom will actually have to synthesize the doomsday virus with his own two hands. His AI agent may be able to just order it through the mail. Plenty of labs do genetic modification on demand. Right now, these labs aren’t monitored very well. Here’s the Washington Post:

The federal government should mandate that all laboratories capable of gene synthesis screen for potentially harmful biological agents. Many large biotech companies already have such measures, but not all do. Uniform federal standards would help.

In other words, we currently don’t even have a monitoring or reporting requirement for ordering bioweapons through the mail. Top AI leaders, well aware of this danger, have written an open letter calling for new legislation to impose such requirements:

Alec Stapp
@AlecStapp
No one should be able to order a bioweapon through the mail. @IFP & @JoinFAI are proud to co-lead an open letter calling for mandatory DNA synthesis screening & recordkeeping. Signatories include: - Sam Altman, CEO & Co-Founder, OpenAI - Dario Amodei, CEO & Co-Founder,
1:00 PM · Jun 4, 2026 · 1.62M Views
66 Replies · 143 Reposts · 443 Likes

That’s good, but it’s not clear that this would get rid of the danger. First of all, there are plenty of illicit labs and underground labs that might simply not obey the reporting requirements. California recently uncovered a secret biolab with links to China:

Code enforcement officer Jesalyn Harper discovered a clandestine biolab in a Reedley, Calif., warehouse containing dangerous pathogens including HIV, malaria, COVID-19 and Ebola...The facility was allegedly operated by a Chinese national involved in smuggling counterfeit COVID tests while receiving millions in unexplained payments from China…A congressional investigation revealed critical gaps in U.S. regulations governing unlicensed biolabs, raising major national security and public health concerns.

On top of secret labs like that, what about labs in other countries? If rogue Chinese researchers are operating an illicit biolab in Kyrgyzstan or Indonesia or North Korea, who is monitoring that? Who will force that lab to report “potentially harmful biological agents”, and who would the lab report to?

Remember that all it takes is one angry teenager to carry out the scenario I described above. That teenager doesn’t have to live in the U.S., or even in a developed country; all he needs is a good internet connection and a postal service. Nor does the lab that sends him the doomsday viruses need to be in the U.S., or in any country where we have any measure of control. The doomsday virus(es) can be created anywhere on Earth, and released anywhere on Earth, and will still come here to America and kill you and me and everyone we know.

Finally, what makes us think that the doomsday virus would even be caught by a safety screening? A truly novel supervirus would presumably rely on hitherto-unknown mechanisms for killing humans, in order to minimize pre-existing immunity — and to minimize the ability of the existing industrial infrastructure to create and disseminate antivirals in time. It seems like monitoring systems will have trouble catching something truly novel. The lab that creates the doomsday virus and mails it to the angry teenager may have no idea what it’s making — and no real way to know.

“No one has done this yet, therefore it’s a lot harder than you think.”

It might seem surprising that people actually make this claim, which sounds a little like saying “I haven’t died yet, so I don’t need to wear my seat belt.” And yet I do see claims like this from time to time:

Owen Lewis
@is_OwenLewis
@Noahpinion Keep in mind that this research was actually published (pre-print) 11 months ago. We're all still here.
7:07 PM · Aug 7, 2026 · 1.82K Views
2 Replies
Eli Dourado
@elidourado
A Mythos-level (for cybersecurity) LLM has been out for a week in general release and nothing bad has happened. Curious.
AI Security Institute (AISI) @AISecurityInst
OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 is the second model to complete one of our multi-step cyber-attack simulations end-to-end 🧵
7:01 PM · Apr 30, 2026 · 15K Views
15 Replies · 4 Reposts · 129 Likes

The obvious reason this is a bad line of thinking is that doomsday only happens once. “We’re still here” is a true statement right up until it’s not. Suppose that the creation of very powerful AI tools creates an annual doomsday risk of 10%. We’d be very likely to survive the first year of that risk, but after a decade of that, we’d only have about a one-in-three chance of surviving.

There’s also no reason to assume the risk is constant. AI models continue to improve at a rapid pace. Human awareness of AI model capabilities continues to spread. There are plenty of reasons to think that 2029 will be a lot riskier than 2025 was, in terms of bioterrorism.

The analogy with cybersecurity, meanwhile, is deeply flawed. Software can be rewritten, and vulnerabilities patched before attackers even think about attacking; humans are much harder to safeguard. Cybersecurity software improves, but human physiology remains at the same basic level of vulnerability year after year while AI gets better and better.

On top of that, if one hacker gets through, the results are usually not catastrophic; with doomsday viruses, all you need is one “success”. In fact, we have seen some stunning cyberwarfare successes recently, like Iran’s shutdown of a British power plant this month. We don’t know whether they used a Mythos-level model, but I wouldn’t bet against it.

So anyway, none of the standard dismissals of AI bioterror risk make any sense to me. Since I started yelling about this topic, I’ve seen basically nothing to persuade me that the danger is substantially less than I originally thought. And although I’m starting to see more people talk about AI bioterror risk, I don’t see the kind of urgency that a threat this existential and plausible ought to receive.

What should we do?

This leads to the final question: How can we prevent AI from being used² for catastrophic bioterrorism? Obviously the kind of monitoring systems being promoted by AI industry leaders would help, though that’s only a first step.

The most important thing I think we can do right now, to be honest, is just scare people. AI leaders are on the right track with their open letter, but their attention is being spread across a diffuse set of risks. The same is true of AI researchers, AI safety enthusiasts, big philanthropic donors, think tanks, economic and political commentators, and pretty much everyone else. Creating a healthy perception of peril around AI bioterror among the highly-informed professional class will focus the best minds — both natural and synthetic — on this problem, instead of letting them run hither and yon worrying about every possible bad thing that AI could cause.

I’m not saying that cyberattacks, misinformation, and job loss are unimportant; I’m saying that if an angry teenager uses AI to create the doomsday virus, all of those will quickly become unimportant.

A healthier sense of our own peril would also make international cooperation a lot easier. Hunting down that rogue biolab in Kyrgyzstan will be a lot easier if China and the U.S. focus more on biosafety and less on nationalistic competition. But that will only happen if both China’s and America’s leaderships consider saving the human race from a vibe-coded plague to be an absolute priority.

In a very real way, AI risk is AI bioterror risk. If AI ever does destroy the human race — either on its own initiative or at a madman’s behest — it’s very likely that it will do so using a virus. An army of robots, a la the Terminator or Matrix films, would be much harder. A plague of self-replicating nanomachines is basically no different than a virus. The nuclear weapons are going to be kept too tightly locked up. A virus is far and away the most likely tool for eliminating a biological species.

Anyway, I know this was a scary blog post, and it was supposed to be. But this is one of those cases where we just can’t afford the luxury of doing what we normally do — burying our heads in the sand and telling ourselves that nothing is going to go wrong. Usually, when we refuse to anticipate calamities — wars, financial crises, natural disasters — we can pick up the pieces afterwards. But there have to be pieces left to pick up.

Share

1

Reason: There are only about 4000 deployed strategic nuclear weapons left in the whole world — down by a factor of 6 from the Cold War peak. Some of those nukes don’t work anymore, and some would be blocked by missile defense, and (perhaps most importantly) some would be destroyed by counterforce strikes, so even a full nuclear launch would be significantly fewer than 4000 warheads — maybe about half that at most. Some of those (especially the Russian ones) would miss and hit less-populated areas. And I doubt that a real launch would be a full launch of the type typically envisioned. Still, I think nuclear war is something to be strenuously avoided.

2

Note that there’s very little difference between a human using a jailbroken AI agent to make a doomsday virus, and an AI agent simply deciding to do that on its own. Measures to protect against one of these dangers will naturally protect against the other. So given that bioterror is the way that AI could most easily wipe out humans, the problem of preventing superintelligence from committing bioterror is pretty much the same as the problem of preventing a psychopathic human from telling a superintelligence to commit bioterror.

Make Geography Great Again

What’s in a name?

Paul Krugman
Aug 28
 
READ IN APP
 

There are already reports that Trump may not stop with trying to rename Lake Ontario Lake America, and rename other places too. So I have a few suggestions.

I mean, the Pacific Ocean? That sounds weak and woke. Let’s rename it the Lethality Ocean.

Farther afield, the Black Sea? Sounds DEI to me. Make it the European Heritage Sea.

What about the Cape of Good Hope? Real Americans don’t hope, they act (with warrior ethos.) Rename it the Cape of Epic Fury.

I’m sure there are many more.

I did a very long drive yesterday in torrential rain with near-zero visibility, and was way too tired to do real writing. So consider this a day off.

The Great Awokening started in 2014, not 2020

Plus price controls, a lot of Maine stuff, and what a 2028 anti-MAGA insurgency could look like

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 28
