Why you won’t get a flying car

A review of “Where is My Flying Car?”, by J. Storrs Hall, and some other thoughts on the future of technology.

Noah Smith
Sep 3
 
READ IN APP
 

Stripe Press was kind enough to send me several books it had published, and one of these was J. Storrs Hall’s Where Is My Flying Car?. I had been meaning to read this book for a while, especially after Tyler Cowen recommended it and Jason Crawford gave it a glowing review, so I was glad Stripe gave me a copy. I promptly stuck it on my shelf, paid for the audiobook, and listened to it while walking around San Francisco. That’s called ordinary abundance, folks!

In 2011, Peter Thiel famously said: “We wanted flying cars, instead we got 140 characters.” When I first saw that quote, I chuckled, because for my entire life, we’ve had flying buses. And again and again, as I sit on a flying bus and marvel at the thrill of takeoff, and reflect on how amazing it is that man has conquered the air, I look around and see my fellow passengers with their window shades drawn, their noses buried in a book or staring at a phone.

If we had flying cars, we’d enjoy the thrill for a few weeks, and then we’d be back to tweeting on our phones and wondering when the trip would be over.

I’ve noticed a loose collection of beliefs and attitudes that I’ve decided to call “engineerism”, because I see it most often among engineers. I coined the term when I was in college, when I noticed that the engineering majors in my physics classes tended to think differently about the world than the physics majors like myself did. Later, I recognized “engineerism” in various sci-fi novels — Lucifer’s Hammer and Footfall by Larry Niven and Jerry Pournelle, The Peace War by Vernor Vinge, and so on.¹

When I say “engineerism”, I am not talking about Friedrich Hayek’s “engineering mentality” — the belief that society can be designed and optimized like a machine.² Nor am I referring to Evgeny Morozov’s “technological solutionism”, which is the idea that social problems can be fixed with technology. If I had to define what I call “engineerism” in succinct, simple terms, it would be something like: “The idea that if a technology can be built, we ought to build it.” Simply put, engineers like to engineer things, and they become disgruntled when society does not give them the resources to do this.

Of course, engineerism is not quite so simple in the real world. It involves a lot of thinking habits that come in handy in engineering — linear approximation, back-of-the-envelope calculations, and so on. And in America, it also involves a set of beliefs that have sort of accreted over the years — for example, a belief in the importance of nuclear power.

I’ve had the concept of engineerism kicking around in my mind for many years, but in Where Is My Flying Car? I have found its perfect encapsulation — you might even say its Bible. Nowhere are both the value and the limitations of engineerism more perfectly on display than in this book.

Where Is My Flying Car? occupies an interesting middle space between genres. Futurism is about predicting the future. Science fiction is about (among other things) speculating on possible futures. And history of technology explains the past. Where Is My Flying Car? has bits of all three of these, but fundamentally it’s a book of retrofuturism — it’s about the technologies we thought we would get but didn’t, and why we didn’t, and how we could get them now.

The main technology Hall talks about is, unsurprisingly, flying cars. The other three are cold fusion, nanotechnology (Hall’s own area of research), and nuclear (fission) power. Hall argues that a combination of overregulation, scientific groupthink, bad funding mechanisms, and cultural aversion prevented us from achieving all four of these.

The Galileo Fallacy

Wait…cold fusion? Is that even real?? Well, not as far as we know, no. In 1989, two top chemists reported that they had managed to get much more heat out of a nuclear experiment than chemistry would be able to produce. The chemists thought that they had discovered a way to produce nuclear fusion without injecting huge amounts of energy — smashing ions together at insanely high speed, blasting them with a laser, etc. If it worked, cold fusion would be an incredible energy source.

So naturally, a lot of people tried to follow up on cold fusion. A wave of initial replication efforts mostly failed (though some people claimed to find the effect). But there have been plenty more efforts, including:

  • A Japanese government project in the 1990s, with funding of around $20 million

  • A project by Toyota in the 1990s, with around $18 million in funding

  • A project by the Electric Power Research Institute in the 2000s, with around $10 million in funding

  • A project by Google in the 2010s, with $10 million of funding

None of these efforts have reliably reproduced the effect that the two chemists claimed in 1989. A few of the researchers found some strange anomalies and possible new physical effects, but nothing even remotely similar to the kind of energy source that cold fusion would represent — and no consistent evidence that fusion is causing the occasional anomalies.³ Some other scientists have found ways to enhance fusion using chemical techniques vaguely reminiscent of the methods in the 1989 experiments, but nothing remotely close to the scale of what “cold fusion” would require. There’s interesting nuclear physics going on in solid-state chemistry, but the original burst of excitement around the 1989 experiment looks like it was misplaced.

That’s not the way Hall tells it, though. He claims that cold fusion is a promising area of research, and that what he terms the “Machiavelli Effect” — basically, vested interests trying to shut down research that would supersede their own research programs — strangled the promising field of cold fusion in its cradle by stigmatizing it and depriving it of funding.

That story just doesn’t pass the smell test. Multiple optimistic, good-faith research efforts, from various countries, from both the public and private sectors, have each thrown tens of millions of dollars at the idea, despite repeated lack of success. That is just not what a marginalized area of science looks like. Yes, lots of people regarded (and regard) the idea of cold fusion as kooky, but plenty of others didn’t and don’t — including the people who headed the many multimillion-dollar research efforts.

Hall knew about all of those efforts, and their outcomes, when he published the 2021 version of his book. But although he mentions some of them, he continues to insist that cold fusion research was mainly stifled by malign social influences. And in his projections of the possibilities of the future, cold fusion figures prominently.

This suggests one weakness of engineerism — the stubborn, contrarian belief that if someone tells you something is impossible, it must be possible. Yes, people sneered unfairly at cold fusion back in the 90s, but that doesn’t mean it must actually work. Not everyone who gets persecuted by the Church is Galileo.

Hall’s stubborn love for the idea of cold fusion also has the unfortunate effect of reducing the credibility of other parts of his book. I am no expert in nanotech, and Hall is an expert. But when he relies on the magical effects of atom-sized nanotech to support key parts of his future visions, I’m skeptical of how much of that is based on careful homework and how much is based on pure optimism. When Hall tells us that nanotech should eventually be able to rebuild the U.S.’ entire existing infrastructure in a few hours, I naturally wonder if the back-of-the-envelope calculations that support that conclusion were the only ones he needed to do.⁴ If Hall hadn’t gone all-in on cold fusion, I would have probably been less instinctively skeptical of the nanotech sections.

To the stars! (But why?)

One of Hall’s main points in Where Is My Flying Car? — and the book’s best point, in my opinion — is that physical technology began to stagnate when energy use began to stagnate. In fact, I wrote a post about this a decade ago, before the first edition of Hall’s book even came out! Here’s what I wrote:

Why did mid-20th-century sci fi whiff so badly? Why didn't we get the Star Trek future, or the Jetsons future, or the Asimov future?…[W]e ran out of energy…In the industrial age, we got better at carrying energy around with us. And then, at the dawn of the nuclear age, it looked like we were about to get MUCH better at carrying energy around with us. One kilogram of uranium has almost two million times as much energy in it as a kilogram of gasoline.

I didn’t know it at the time, but I was talking about the Henry Adams Curve. This is a curve of energy use per capita in the U.S., which was rising smoothly but suddenly leveled off in the 1970s:

In fact, the curve is too simplistic, but the basic point is solid. We failed to transition to energy sources better than fossil fuels.

It’s a simple truth that if you want your economy to escape poverty, you need lots of energy consumption:

But that doesn’t mean wealth is always inherently tied to energy. U.S. primary energy use per person stagnated after 1970 and has been falling since the turn of the century:

And yet since the turn of the century, even as energy use has fallen, U.S. per capita GDP has grown by 40%!

This is the magic of dematerialization, and it’s the reason economic growth doesn’t inevitably exhaust the planet’s resources. Not only have humans in rich countries figured out how to produce the same physical stuff with far less energy use, but we’ve found lots of other stuff we like that isn’t physical. Around 1970, Americans started spending more on services than on goods, and the gap has only grown wider since then:

Interestingly, something similar is even happening in China — the country that fetishizes manufacturing the most, and whose autocratic state has moved heaven and earth to provide cheap energy, steamroll the environmental movement, and maintain manufacturing primacy:

It’s possible that this is just a fundamental feature of human nature. Perhaps eventually, once we all have plenty of food, big houses filled with gadgets and nice furniture, and cheap enough transportation to go out to eat twice a week, our desires just naturally turn toward things like health care, entertainment, and spa visits for our dogs.

Nor is it clear that there’s any limit to dematerialization. It might be possible to immerse humans in totally realistic virtual reality environments — allowing us to live in any sort of world we wanted — for only a modest amount of energy. We could conceivably explore virtual galaxies, create virtual ecosystems, live as dinosaurs or sentient spaceships, experience hundreds of lives, all for the low price of an AI to run the whole simulation.

Hall doesn’t really talk about alternative future visions like this. His triumphant futures always revolve around the conquest of the physical — real spaceships, real weather control, real flying cars. And yet he never really explains why we should expend such massive amounts of energy and resources conquering the physical world — it’s simply presented as a triumphant, “Wouldn’t this be awesome?” kind of vision.

But it’s very rare for humans to undertake grandiose endeavors if similar or greater enjoyment can be had closer to home. We’re not going to conquer the stars just because engineers think it’s cool. This is a second limitation of engineerism — the conviction that difficult feats of engineering are desirable in and of themselves.

Of course, there are a few individuals who do think that conquering the physical universe is just really damn awesome, and occasionally they command enough resources to make it happen. But even then, it’s questionable whether they truly derive more value from the physical world or the virtual. Elon Musk has done far more to conquer space than any other human in the last half century, but he personally has never even been to orbit. He has spent a lot of time tweeting, though.

Maybe in the end, 140 characters is just what humanity wants the most?

The wrong energy revolution

Of course, I do think the United States needs more abundant energy. We excel in the production of services, but J. Storrs Hall is exactly right when he says that our failure to harness cheaper sources of energy has limited our ability to produce physical goods — and to undertake the kind of engineering feats that we might want to undertake if we had enough energy.

Hall blames America’s energy stagnation on culture — on “ergophobia” (fear of energy), and on an environmental movement that has become more of a religion than a scientifically guided enterprise. I think Hall is generally on the right track here, but I think he gets the specifics a bit wrong. Americans aren’t afraid of energy, they’re afraid of land use; the 70s saw the anti-growth movement impose restrictions not just on power plants, but on housing, factories, infrastructure, and every other kind of physical development.

And it was this more parochial environmentalism — the desire to preserve “open space” near people’s suburban houses — that paralyzed America’s physical economy far more than the climate movement. Endangered species law was often abused to block development, but the underlying motivation was almost always NIMBYism rather than green religion.

Where I think Hall goes even more wrong, though, is in his predictions about what kind of energy technology can break our long stagnation. Hall puts his faith in nuclear fission power, first and foremost. Only the coming of a “second atomic age”, he predicts, will make energy too cheap to meter. And like many, he blames misguided safety regulations for robbing us of this nuclear future.

On one hand, I think Hall is pretty much right about the past. Nuclear power has its risks, of course, but I agree that we significantly overstated the risks and overregulated nuclear power as a result. We obviously could have chosen a different path, because France actually did choose a different path. Most of France’s electricity comes from nuclear power, and has since the 1980s. That could have been us, too, if we hadn’t been so spooked by Three Mile Island.

But the idea that embracing nuclear would have led to cheap, plentiful energy is…well, pretty suspect. France has plenty of nuclear power, but its electricity costs 28 cents per kWh, compared to 18 cents in America. France’s electricity is much cleaner — nuclear power has allowed it to reduce its carbon emissions enormously. But nuclear has not made energy abundant in France.

Perhaps this is also because of regulation? Maybe France allows nuclear, but simply makes it too expensive. Other countries that encourage nuclear construction can bend the cost curve down, and harness scaling effects to make nuclear cheaper and cheaper…right?

Well…maybe. China has probably done the best job of bending the nuclear cost curve downward, and even there, reactor costs aren’t lower than they were in 2010:

But at the same time, there has been another energy revolution that has nothing to do with nuclear. Solar power has become cheaper at absolutely stupendous rates:

You’d think Hall would love the solar revolution, but he doesn’t even recognize that it exists. As far as I can tell, he only mentions solar once, and it’s to dismiss the whole thing with an airy hand-wave:

The currently fashionable “renewables,” such as wind and solar power, have largely escaped the attacks. Battery-powered electric cars are the darlings of the Greens. But this is because they are simply not capable of providing anywhere near the energy or range that civilization depends on at a price it can afford.

This belief — that nuclear power is for real and solar, wind, and electric cars are B.S. — seems to be part of American engineerism. I don’t see why it should be. Getting electricity from sunlight and trapping it in batteries is an inherently very cool engineering task. And yet if you talk to American engineers about energy, nine times out of ten it’s just nuclear, nuclear, nuclear.

Chinese engineers, on the other hand, are embracing the electric revolution with gusto. They’ve created electric cars so cheap and high-quality that they’re conquering the global auto market. And despite the fact that China has kept nuclear costs down, and is perfectly willing to build nuclear, it’s building a lot more solar:

J. Storrs Hall barely even mentions China in his book, and this is one of its biggest failings. We don’t have to think very hard about the hypothetical technological details of nuclear vs. solar; we can just watch what China does. China is ruthlessly focused on growing its economy, its manufacturing industries, and its geopolitical power; it is not swayed by hippie environmentalists. When coal was the cheapest power source, China burned as much as it could.

And yet now, China is building solar far faster than it’s building nuclear. Why? Because solar has, broadly speaking, won the technological race. Intermittency was the last big problem, and batteries have gotten good and cheap enough to make solar reliable. If this were not the case, China would not be transitioning its economy to solar power as rapidly as possible.

Why does American engineerism long for nuclear even after it’s clear it’s been surpassed (for most applications) by something even cheaper and better? My best guess is that this is a historical grudge. In the 70s and 80s, environmentalists told engineers they weren’t allowed to build nuclear power. A lot of engineers still chafe at being told what not to build, and some probably resent solar and batteries for being the things environmentalists told them to go build instead.

But this has resulted in a bunch of American engineers becoming trapped in a retrofuturistic daydream, unable to take advantage of the very real revolution in electric technology.

Why don’t we have flying cars?

Which brings me, at last, to flying cars. Hall spends a lot of the book explaining why flying cars are technologically feasible, going through details like the difficulty of flying a plane, prospects for a future air traffic control system to control high volumes of flying cars, and so on.

My guess is that human-piloted flying cars were always going to be a bridge too far, for safety reasons alone — teenagers probably can’t be trusted to fly aircraft over populated areas, to say nothing of potential terrorists. But in the age of AI, we probably don’t need human pilots; we can just automate everything. Here’s a video of EHang’s pilotless VTOL craft giving someone a ride:

The EHang vehicle can’t move along roads, so it isn’t a true, classic flying car. But…close enough, right?

EHang may take off, but for right now it’s a niche type of transportation, authorized at only a few select locations. China has built the world’s most extensive network of high-speed trains, but seems in no hurry to roll out flying cars to the masses. Why?

The obvious answer is that demand for flying cars is limited. Where are you going to go in a flying car? For short distances you already have ground cars, which go slower but are probably a lot cheaper to drive and easier to park. For long distances — international travel, business travel to other cities, etc. — you have airplanes, which are really just flying buses.

There’s an intermediate distance — maybe about 150 to 500 miles — where flying cars might be able to beat both airplanes and ground cars. I had GPT calculate travel times for ground cars, flying cars of the type described in J. Storrs Hall’s book, and airplanes:

Flying cars do OK over short distances, but over intermediate distances they’re the clear winner. (Incidentally, this is also the distance range over which high-speed rail is usually thought to compete effectively with cars and airplanes.)

The real question is what there is within 150 to 500 miles that you’d A) want to visit often enough to justify owning a flying car, and B) be willing to travel 1-3 hours to get to. You certainly don’t need to go that far to shop for groceries or go to the gym. You’re probably not going to go to that many restaurants that require you to travel 1-3 hours each way.

That basically leaves commuting and vacations.

A 1-hour commute is fairly punishing; a 2-hour commute is absolutely brutal; a 3-hour commute is impossible. For shorter commutes, cars (or trains, if they exist near you) work just fine. Even with flying cars, most people aren’t going to want to live 200 miles from their place of work.

As for vacations, these are rare. When people do take trips, they tend to take luggage (which is a lot more expensive to move through the air than along the ground). Planes work perfectly well for most trips, which leaves flying cars to handle short-range vacations. If you’re in San Francisco, that could mean a weekend in Tahoe or Yosemite, or a beach trip to Santa Barbara. Those trips are nice, I’m sure, but probably don’t come close to justifying the expense of flying cars.

In his book, J. Storrs Hall addresses this issue by arguing that if lots of people had flying cars, new destinations would spring up at the requisite distances. First of all, this completely ignores the cold start problem. Without enough flying cars, the new destinations can’t spring up; without enough destinations, owning a flying car is an unattractive proposition.

But even if tourist resorts and awesome restaurants and cool stores sprang up to blanket the American countryside in order to take advantage of swarms of flying cars, their business would have to be diverted from existing destinations closer to where people live. America is a very built-up country with lots of shops, restaurants, and entertainment spots. If you flew your flying car to go eat at a restaurant 100 miles away, you’d be spending almost an hour in transit each way, instead of driving 15 minutes to a restaurant nearby. Sure, you’ll go to the more distant restaurant sometimes, because it’s probably a lot more famous and high-quality than whatever happens to be in your local neighborhood. But will you go often enough to justify owning a flying car?

We should also consider changes in communication technology, which can substitute for some percentage of physical travel; we can now text or video chat with friends, colleagues, or even potential lovers some of the time instead of always driving to see them. Or we can simply amuse ourselves watching TikTok or reading Substacks instead of motoring around the countryside like in 1925 or cruising the strip like in 1960.

In Where Is My Flying Car?, Hall acknowledges this substitutability, but waves it away, saying it would be a shame if communication technology outpaced transportation technology. And yet that may be exactly what’s happening. Young Americans traveled fewer than half as many miles per day in 2022 as they did two decades earlier:

This is just another example of dematerialization of economic output. The internet is substituting for cars. And if the internet is substituting for regular cars, why are people going to rush out and buy flying cars?

In other words, the answer to the question in the title of this post is that you won’t get a flying car — at least, not anytime soon — because you don’t really want one.

This leads me, at last, to the biggest pitfall of engineerism: It focuses too much on supply and not enough on demand. To many engineers, the most important question is “Can we build this?”, not “Why would anyone want this?”. This is a common pitfall for startups, but it applies equally well to futurists (and retrofuturists).

Engineers can grouse all they want, but the blunt fact is that in the long run, technology gets built because human consumers want it. Sometimes, those consumers are governments, who want weapons for war and monuments to prove their greatness. That can sometimes look like building things just for the coolness factor, but in the end, monument-builders tire of making pyramids. And in capitalist, individualist, democratic societies — the kind Americans (roughly speaking) still live in today — the consumers are regular people who mostly just want to get to work on time, watch some funny stuff online, sleep in a comfy bed, and enjoy a nice night out or a vacation once in a while.

Engineers often fail to understand this. Building things is their passion; they want to build, build, build, because it’s awesome. But society will only give them the resources to build the truly big stuff — space elevators and Mars colonies and fleets of flying cars — if they can justify it with a broad-based value proposition. “Hey, let’s embrace our destiny and conquer the stars” makes for a fun rallying cry, but the actual future of technology will be driven by parents shopping for diapers.

Is there a liberal center? Should there be?

A conversation with Nate Silver and Jeremiah Johnson

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 3
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Back in July, Nate Silver asked “12 questions for the center-left,” raising a bunch of tactical, strategic, and even moral questions about the political faction he (and I) most closely identify with. Soon after, I offered a very narrowly tactical reply about the kind of center-left 2028 presidential primary campaign that I believe can persuade the Democratic Party base and win a general election handily. But in a sense that response ducked the larger questions Silver was raising.

This week on the pod, Nate and Jeremiah Johnson from “The New Liberal Podcast” joined Jerusalem and me to think about the big picture.

One of the core divides you’ll hear us discuss is the relationship between moderation as a political brand and liberalism as a philosophy. We can all agree, I think, that these are distinct things. But the nature of the relationship is harder to parse. Jerusalem is strongly critical of flattening the distinction, arguing for liberalism as an ideology with moderate implications on some issues and radical ones on others.

I see this as largely accurate as an account of liberalism’s history. But 2026 is not 1826, and core liberal views about electoral democracy, equal rights, and the rule of law are not radical notions in the contemporary context. Instead, contemporary liberalism finds itself stuck with the dreary task of largely defending established institutions that reflect liberal ideas and liberal influence, and that in practice means fighting for the idea of the liberal center of American politics.

Nate makes the observation that in multiparty European systems, liberal parties tend to be located near the center of the ideological spectrum, but they are also relatively small — in that context, there is a difference between a “moderate” ideological orientation (which signifies willingness to work with either left-wing or right-wing parties depending on the circumstances) and the idea of majoritarian politics, where you’re trying to be broadly popular all the time.

We dive into all of this and more over the course of an in-depth conversation that I hope you’ll enjoy.

Later this month on the pod, Jerusalem and I will be reading Friedrich von Hayek’s “The Road to Serfdom.” If you have thoughts or questions about the book you’d like us to discuss, drop a line in the comments below!

Paid subscribers can watch the ad-free embedded video at the top of this post and read the full transcript below.

WATCH THE EPISODE ON YOUTUBE HERE

New episodes post every Thursday.

Jerusalem Demsas: All right. Hello, everyone. Welcome to The Argument. My name is Jerusalem Demsas, and today we have something a little bit different for you. We have my normal co-host, Matt Yglesias, with us today, but we also have two guests. One is Jeremiah Johnson, who you know as a staff writer from The Argument, but also from his podcast, The New Liberal Podcast, to which we will also be cross-posting this. I think everyone who listens to our podcast would love Jeremiah’s, and I will speak for him and say vice versa as well.

But all three of us got together, and we independently were really excited to talk to Nate Silver because he wrote something really great on his Substack, Silver Bulletin, which you should all subscribe to if you are not already subscribed. Nate, welcome to the show.

Nate Silver: Thank you. Happy to be on. Happy to make this happen.

Jerusalem Demsas: For sure. So, we have four people who like to talk a lot, so we will all attempt to constrain ourselves and fail. And so I’m sure we’ll set some records for longest ever podcast today. But you wrote a piece called “12 Questions for the Center-Left.” And before we get into these questions: Like, why did you write this piece? What was the point?

Nate Silver: One of the little sub-beats that Silver Bulletin has, I think, is to kind of do anthropology on the Democratic Party, or maybe the broader kind of center and left coalition. I have critiqued establishment liberals in different ways. I have critiqued Bluesky liberals in different ways. I’ve written pieces about how liberal and left — and we’ll probably not be strict with this over the podcast — but how liberal and left are not synonyms in quite important ways. But I hadn’t really kind of hit the target on the group that I guess I’m most identified with, or self-identified with, which is kind of the center-left.

And I guess — I mean, Matt writes about this a lot — the frustrations over the electability debate and things like that. But I guess the premise is kind of, maybe the center-leftists are right on the merits a lot about a lot of this stuff, but they seem like they’re kind of losing the argument in a lot of ways. You know, the argument over whether Kamala Harris was a centrist or a left-wing progressive… I mean, I think she’s neither exactly, but much closer to a left progressive candidate than a centrist.

And the fact that the establishment — which is very unpopular and that, you know, I critique a lot on Silver Bulletin — has been smushed together with the center-left, I think is problematic potentially. It seems like Democrats were once very concerned about electability, and there’s still a lot of bounds on that. The fact that El-Sayed won in Michigan, but Francesca Hong didn’t win in Wisconsin, that’s an interesting differentiator. They’re both pretty far left. I would say El-Sayed has some appealing qualities if you look at — I think he’s an articulate, accomplished, smart guy who’s a good politician, whereas Hong was a very awkward fit for anything involving electoral politics.

But yeah, we’re going to be hearing these debates over and over again. I mean, the 2028 primary will start on November 4th, the day after the midterm. And so I want to kind of probe at things that I think were a bit contradictory maybe, in part because what the center-left is, is not all that easy to define either.

Jerusalem Demsas: Are the vibes — OK, Matt, Jeremiah, do you guys think the vibes are bad with center-left? It sounds like Nate feels like vibes are quite bad.

Matthew Yglesias: My vibes are excellent. They’re doing amazing.

No, I mean, look, I think that they’re — and this is running through sort of Nate’s commentary, right? But clearly, a number of establishment Democratic figures have been losing to this sort of insurgent left forces. And I think one question that my readers, the people who agree with me, affiliate with Slow Boring, etc., have to ask themselves is, how sad are we about a Diana DeGette losing a primary to a Melat Kiros? Because DeGette herself is really left-wing, and much more left-wing than I am, or than I would advocate the Democrats become.

And yet it is true that I see my factional enemies being thrilled on Twitter, and I feel depressed. And then I have to be like, well, but is that actually what I think? Or am I excited about Bobby Pulido running in Texas 15 — up in polls, I think reflecting, like, my idea of how politics should be practiced?

And when I’m in that mindset, I’m like, you know what? Like, there’s a number of races where candidates who I really like seem to be doing well, who I think themselves are breaking from the establishment, and I wish I could get some more attention to them. And the problem is, is like they don’t represent New York City, right? And everything that happens in New York is amplified 100x, but there’s no real reason electorally that, like… New York shouldn’t have young charismatic leftists. Like, it’s just a very left-wing city.

But then it’s like, well, why is the discourse so dominated by that? Like, does it matter? Like, who has backbench House seats from Brooklyn? You know, looms very large in the minds of people, like writers who live in Brooklyn, but doesn’t seem actually important to the future of the country. And that’s how I talk myself into a better vibe. But then we have the 2028 primary looming, and, you know, these things are always, like, really high stakes, and I don’t feel like it’s going that well for people who — ideas that I agree with.

Jeremiah Johnson: Yeah, I would say it depends just where you look. Look, like if you are defining the center-left by their foreign policy views, and, you know, the obvious Israel-Gaza debate has, you know, gone very strongly in one direction, pro-Israel Democrats are really going through it right now. And so can humans still retain some kind of value in that kind of arrangement? Seems important. But even if it is the case that, right, that the AI technology is able to direct exactly where investigations should go, that doesn’t actually take the human out of the equation at all still. And I know that you’re not, you know — maybe you are saying that, but I don’t know if you’re actually saying that. But I do think the case that in cases like CPS, I really do think people are gonna want, like, human interaction involved in CPS investigations. Like, a robot sending you a digital message, or even like a robot physically showing up at your house to do an investigation by itself — I think it’s just not gonna be the vibe.

Matthew Yglesias: Probably. I mean, you know, like robot cops seems — I guess I don’t know. Well, but I mean, I think we already have these questions around automation and policing and algorithms, right? And there’s a big —

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, they won’t even let us do the fucking cameras. We can’t even do fit cameras, you know?

Matthew Yglesias: Well, I mean, and it’s — I have always thought it was very interesting that, you know, there’s a lot of left skepticism of surveillance cameras as a law enforcement tactic, as part of a kind of a comprehensive left view that you shouldn’t punish crime, but that, like —

Jerusalem Demsas: Or concerns about privacy, you know?

Matthew Yglesias: Well, but conservatives specifically seem much more worried about cameras than about human police officers. And to be uncharitable, I always thought one of my favorite pieces of journalism ever was this piece Dara Lind did for us at Vox, I think probably over 10 years ago now. But she was pointing out that in experimental settings, when you told people that the criminal justice system is racially biased, that this causes African Americans to become more skeptical, but white people to become more enthusiastic.

And so on net, you’re increasing support for law enforcement, because if people think that there’s a trade-off between privacy and security, but then you’re guaranteeing them that all of the downside of that trade-off will be concentrated on people who belong to an ethnic group that they don’t belong to, and they also get the security benefits, then they’re like, that’s great, right? And if you come up with something that’s more neutral, like just traffic cameras, then you actually get more civil libertarian instincts from white people. Civil libertarian instincts that I do not share personally, but depending on how you look at it, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Are you not more concerned? I used to be very, like, much less concerned about privacy in general. But with the surprising rise of AI capabilities, and coupled with seeming like the potential for, you know, we’re just removing almost all liberal procedural constraints as fast as possible — like, it seems like quite bad to give government the power that this level of surveillance would give them.

Matthew Yglesias: No, I don’t agree. I mean, this is a different podcast, but I think that, like, you know, the world that we have now where we’ve, like, surrendered all of our privacy to commercial entities but continue to make, like, like blind the state is, like, quite bad. And, like, very — like, it’s very annoying to me how challenging it is to prove to D.C. Public Schools rules that I live where I live, when on some level, A, Google knows where I live, Apple knows where I live, Amazon knows where I live, and also other government agencies, they deliver the mail to my house, but the government is not allowed to communicate with the government about where it is that people live.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, I mean, I agree that state capacity, is that something that we should all care about? And making it easier for government agencies to talk to each other and share information is good. Like, that’s also, like, you know, like how fascist states end up enacting terrible policies. You know what I mean? It’s, like, pretty easy to target people.

Matthew Yglesias: This is like — I remember I was in Germany and I was having lunch with this guy.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And I was like, “Google — “ I was telling him, I was like, “I tried to check this place out and I couldn’t see it on Google Street View.” And he’s like, “Well, we don’t have Google Street View here.” And I was like, “Why?” He’s like, “Well, if you understood the history of this country, you know, you would know.” And I was like, I don’t think actually that Hitler needed Google Street View. Like, I’m pretty sure that wasn’t — I’m pretty sure that’s not the history of your country at all.

Jerusalem Demsas: OK, that is what we call a straw man in action, Matthew.

Matthew Yglesias: I stand by it. Like, thinking back to the CPS thing, it’s just like providing a richer set of information allowed the algorithms to judge people less on these crude racial heuristics.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, also why —

Matthew Yglesias: And generated a better outcome.

Jerusalem Demsas: The algorithm wasn’t —

Matthew Yglesias: I don’t understand what was going on with the Latino families.

Jerusalem Demsas: I don’t know. I think it might’ve been an income thing, but it was income and Hispanic. It was significantly more Hispanic and SNAP recipient low-income children than human workers would’ve. And those extra investigations were not accompanied by better health outcomes for those groups. So the disparity is not warranted.

Matthew Yglesias: No, no. I mean, I understand, but this was just really one where it’s like, I want to understand more what is causing it to have that view of Hispanic families in particular. Because I mean, you could — I mean, I don’t know. Also, why can’t you just fix it? Why can’t you just tell it —

Nate Silver: I mean, I’m sure —

Matthew Yglesias: Put +7 for Latino families. And how — I mean —

Jerusalem Demsas: We need to bring an actual ML engineer in here to explain to us how any of this function.

Matthew Yglesias: OK, let me pause it. Oftentimes if you hear about the income level of a given family, you draw certain inferences of what it’s like. But then actually, if it turns out that that family are first-generation immigrants, you have to readjust your sense of what’s going on, because obviously people who don’t speak English face, like, labor market disadvantages, that among native English speakers, poor labor market outcomes are associated with all kinds of other cognitive attributes. Whereas, like, if your problem is just that you don’t speak English, like, that’s going to make you poorer than you otherwise might be without having any of the other kind of deficits, right? Because whenever somebody’s low income, like, there’s like, some reason why.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And those reasons correlate with other things. And understanding it correctly in a socially sophisticated way leads you to have a better understanding of what’s actually going on. I mean, I don’t know.

Jerusalem Demsas: I don’t know if it’s — I mean, my limited understanding about how you train machine learning models is that doing very crude plus 7s, as you put it, is like, is actually like can mess up a lot of stuff. Like, the whole, like, there’s a whole world reinforcement — yeah, reinforcement learning from human feedback. And the whole point is that that after you’ve trained the model on a, you know, all the corpus of text that exists in all of humanity, you then have feedback from human training, often, like, from Nigeria and India or whatever, that are then giving you, like, yes, no, yes, no, you did this right, you did this wrong, etc.

And I think they’re, like — again, I don’t understand this, and probably we shouldn’t just posit, like, randomly on this podcast about it, but, like — my thing is like, if they were just, like, yeah, don’t be biased to Black people, and you could just do that without fucking up the entire model, I’m sure they would.

Matthew Yglesias: No, right. But I mean, that is why I ultimately think that the algorithm will supersede the team, because you should be able to do this reinforcement learning where right now humans are providing an important corrective to the algorithmic decision-making. But at least a good machine learning algorithm will learn from those corrections.

Jerusalem Demsas: I don’t know. I think there are biases, even really good frontier models right now. I see biases pop up in these models all the time. I wouldn’t call — I don’t see, like, you know, I’m not seeing racial biases all the time, but like, you know, right now the current Claude model is really irritating to me because it, like, really defaults to finding flaws in things that there aren’t flaws in. So if you send it something that’s, like, very simple, it’ll go like, “Well, have you — “ “Did you know this?” And it’s like — and I’m like, I don’t think that’s wrong. It’s like, you’re right, I was just looking for something to be wrong.

And I’m like, you know, I just think, like, it’s a mind, just like — I mean, it’s super intelligent and it’s, like, much smarter and faster than me and has a lot more information. It’s not the exact same thing as a person, but I would expect that no matter how good these minds get, there will still be biases to correct for.

Matthew Yglesias: I think it’s worth saying, right, at least as I understand it, this is not actually using frontier artificial intelligence, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: No.

Matthew Yglesias: This was some kind of simpler algorithmic decision-making.

Nate Silver: Yes, yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: So the sort of thesis of this paper, which I do think is important, is that we should probably be incorporating some more algorithmic work into our evaluations. I think this is probably really important in sentencing and parole, which are two areas where we right now have, like, very consequential decisions being made with a lot of human discretion — and a big kind of around who are the humans exercising that discretion? Like, who is checking whether they’re exercising that discretion well?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: What are the incentives and biases that are kind of facing them? Like, it’s a real kind, like, you know, dark matter of the American criminal justice system.

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, CPS is, like, super unpopular in all directions. It’s like they’re either over-enforcing or under-enforcing. And, like, I mean, I, at some level, you feel bad for them, because it’s an agency where you really can’t do it right. Like, if you are over-investigating someone, you’re really violating someone’s home. Like, it’s an extremely traumatic thing to go through a real CPS investigation and feel like your family’s under a microscope.

I mean, Pete Buttigieg had this recently happen where they separated him from his children because of a — I mean, what was clearly a swatting type thing where someone had, you know, called in a false report. And that’s, like, horrible, right, to have that happen to you. But then if something goes wrong in a family and CPS wasn’t, you know, as intensive as they could have been, that also creates huge problems. And so you would hope that algorithms would help out here, but I actually don’t think you can solve this problem with just algorithms unless you get a level of data from people that I would find extremely concerning for the government to have.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, I also, I think it’s not well understood how widespread CPS investigations are. They say the numbers is like 37% of children at some point come under CPS surveillance, not necessarily intervention.

Jerusalem Demsas: And more than 50% of Black children. It’s crazy.

Matthew Yglesias: Right. Because, I mean, I don’t know, put it — anytime something goes horribly wrong, you look back and you’re like, man, somebody should have said something.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? And so then we create these new mandatory reporter classes so people are raising these red flags. But you have this kind of, you know, like Bayes’ Law sort of issue, right? Where instances of suboptimal parenting are, I’m sure, quite widespread.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But instances of parenting that is so bad that it would actually be better to yank a child out of the parent’s home is quite, quite rare.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: So when you focus on those cases where in retrospect you wish there had been an intervention, you find, sure, there’s all kinds of red flags, but how red are those flags actually, right? They’re often — I would say a lot of these flags are pretty pink or very — it’s just…

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, it’s really hard. Like, there are a lot of parenting failures where they — I could view them as horrible and even abusive, but it still is not the best thing for someone to be taken out of the home. Like, separating a kid from their house and from their parents to go into a foster care situation where they also may not be in a good situation — like, you have to be, like, really certain that it’s the worst possible case for that kid to remain there.

Matthew Yglesias: But then that becomes like a tough —

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: You know, if you’re like, something gets me, flagged by a mandatory reporter. And then you look into it and you’re like, ugh, this is like a 20th-percentile home environment.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But to then just be like, OK, but would it be constructive to actually intervene?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Like, maybe not.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, this began as something where I was really happy and uplifted, and it ended on a very sad and difficult note. So I think that that’s a great place for us to close out. I think this is our longest ever podcast, but we had four people talking in the first bit, so I think we should feel good about that.

We are reading The Road to Serfdom for our book club, so that’ll be our next episode. If you want to pick it up, if you have some questions you want us to interact with — this is our, I think our first right-wing book that we’re reading on this podcast. The others have been mostly on the left. So read along with us, and we’ll see you next week. Bye.

Matthew Yglesias: Bye.

Stop making up reasons to be mad at your adversaries

A harmless old A.E.S. tweet, a paranoid anti-A.E.S. conspiracy theory, and the case for a mind of winter

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 3
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Abdul El-Sayed is in hot water in certain corners of the internet over a tweet from five years ago in which he said that on 9/11 itself he would mourn the victims of the terrorist attack but that the next day he would mourn the tragic ways in which the American response went awry.

Eyal Yakoby
@EYakoby
Abdul El-Seyed deleted this post. It would be a shame if it went viral.
8:45 PM · Aug 31, 2026 · 439K Views
201 Replies · 5.08K Reposts · 12.7K Likes

My sincere advice to anyone considering a run for elected office at any point in their life would be to never, under any circumstances, try to say anything thoughtful or provocative around a national day of mourning.

That said, as someone in the line of work where you are supposed to be thoughtful and provocative, this statement seems completely reasonable.

The view that the American military response to 9/11 ended up being unproductive is very widely held. Many innocent people died as a result of the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. An enormous amount of money was spent, money which could’ve been used in many other, better ways. Lots of American soldiers died or were injured. I used to be on the same workout schedule as a guy who lost his left foot to an I.E.D. in Iraq. I respect his service and the service of others I know who fought in those wars, but unlike my grandfather who fought the Nazis, I can’t really say that their sacrifices were worth it.

It’s a pretty fucked up situation, and El-Sayed is right about that.

Unless, of course, he’s actually a hardcore anti-American Islamo-leftist who hates this country and is leaping at the opportunity to besmirch its name on a sacred day of mourning.

But is he?

There’s certainly no evidence within the text of that tweet that he is. It’s true that if you want to look at the most outré things Hasan Piker has ever said and then assert both that those things reflect Piker’s true feelings about the world and that El-Sayed’s association with Piker during the Michigan Senate primary campaign reflects his uncritical endorsement of that version of Piker’s worldview, you can read the tweet that way. But that’s a fully circular argument. If El-Sayed had never tweeted about 9/11, you could still be mad about the other stuff. Being mad about the tweet doesn’t add anything.

And he has specifically disavowed Piker’s remarks about 9/11. What’s more, El-Sayed supports Western aid to Ukraine — he is not part of the campist anti-American left, while Piker seems to be.

Not to do a whole take about 9/11, and I don’t want to get started on Piker, but this is an illustration of a problematic internet trend where you decide first that someone is your enemy, then read everything he says through the presumption that he’s a bad guy, and then treat this purely circular reasoning as if it’s new evidence of new wrongdoing.

I thought both El-Sayed and Haley Stevens had kind of bad takes on Israel and that all things considered, El-Sayed was a riskier electability choice who creates unnecessary complications for Democrats’ effort to take the Senate. But he is, in fact, the Democratic nominee, and there’s no need to make that into something bigger than it is.

A mind of winter

My favorite poem is Wallace Stevens’s “The Snow Man” from 1921.

Stevens is obsessed with the relationships between sense and perception. In another of his poems, the longer and less snappy “The Man With the Blue Guitar,” the titular man is challenged by an unknown audience who complain “You have a blue guitar / You do not play things as they are.” The guitarist retorts that “Things as they are / Are changed upon the blue guitar.”

“The Snow Man” is about the blue guitar of our minds.

It’s tempting to look upon the bleak emptiness of a snowy New England field in January and read it as a kind of metaphor. And it’s true that a writer setting a story against the backdrop of a bleak New England winter who took the time to dwell on this imagery would be making some kind of metaphorical or thematic point. The ice storm in the 1997 Ang Lee movie is a point about the weather, but it’s also symbolism.

Like the characters in the movie, Stevens is a guy who lived in Connecticut. And if you live in Connecticut, you sometimes get bleak January weather. That’s just a thing that happens; it’s genuinely what the weather is like. It doesn’t actually mean anything. The short daylight in the New England winter can make you feel sad. The decline in the pace of social activity can make you feel sad. But it’s not the case that God has chosen the weather to symbolize something or make you feel a certain way.

Stevens calls on us to reject the fog of metaphor and to “have a mind of winter,” which will allow us to see “nothing that is not there and the nothing that is.”

This is, of course, a terrible engagement strategy. If you want to gain clout and clicks on social media, you have to imbue everything and everyone your audience already dislikes with secret meaning and nefarious portent.

People who don’t like El-Sayed frequently do this, and it’s a big vibe in general on Islamophobic Twitter. But when you see a headline like “Hochul wears hijab at N.Y.C. Islamic center ahead of 9/11 anniversary, sparking backlash,” you have to ask yourself what kind of sense this makes. It’s totally normal to dress in line with religious norms when you’re visiting a place that’s not of your faith, and why shouldn’t she go there two weeks before the 9/11 commemoration?

The negative responses are clearly people who don’t like Kathy Hochul looking for stuff to get mad at. And stuff like this is totally endemic to contemporary internet culture.

Hypothetical anger

You see this on all sides, of course.

Abdul El-Sayed’s primary victory doesn’t change the fact that pro-Israel Democrats disagree with him about Israel, some of them quite strongly. This is categorically different from leftists who might be disappointed about being asked to support Mary Peltola, even though she’s moderate. Moderate as she may be, Peltola is still more progressive than Dan Sullivan. Pro-Israel Democrats in Michigan, on the other hand, are being asked to vote for El-Sayed, even if they’re closer to Mike Rogers’ views on the issue. It’s a real ask.

Still, Chuck Schumer and Gretchen Whitmer — who both pulled out all the stops for Haley Stevens — have endorsed El-Sayed. So did Elissa Slotkin. So did Stevens herself. That’s normal politics! But it’s become dogma on the left to seize on every bit of friction as evidence not of policy disagreements but of a secret plan to sabotage his election.

Cenk Uygur
@cenkuygur
I've never seen anything like this Michigan race. The Democratic Party is attacking its own candidate! In an absolutely pivotal race! I've seen more Democrats on TV attacking @AbdulElSayed than I've seen Democrats taking on GOP. Dems are attacking him more than Republicans are!
1:18 AM · Sep 1, 2026 · 311K Views
1.75K Replies · 2.01K Reposts · 15.4K Likes

There is just zero evidence of this. In fact, while Schumer has endorsed El-Sayed, El-Sayed says he doesn’t support Schumer for majority leader. Under the circumstances, they are getting along pretty well!

David Sirota is making stuff up here, though.

Or, rather, based on his longstanding dislike of the bogeyman “corporate Democrats” he has decided that it’s clearly the case that in a purely hypothetical situation in which those Democrats could be assured of a Senate majority while El-Sayed loses, they would sabotage him. From that he infers that in the actual, non-hypothetical situation these unnamed corporate Dems are “willing to risk losing Congress to try to get what they want.”

I would say that in the completely non-hypothetical context of the Michigan primary, left-wing Democrats were willing to risk losing Congress by backing the weaker electability choice to try to get what they want. But they did get what they want, and while I think El-Sayed will almost certainly underperform the fundamentals, he’ll probably win. And everyone is endorsing him.

It’s not helpful for the pro-Israel faction to make up things about him beyond the scope of that disagreement, and it’s equally unhelpful for his fans to invent conspiracies.

Choosing to be angry

I think one of the real tells of this rhetorical style is its obsession with hypothetical scenarios. Earlier this week, a woman carrying knives stabbed multiple people in Times Square before being killed by police officers. Because crime is a lot lower in New York City than it used to be and because events in Times Square are inherently noteworthy, this was the subject of a high-profile press conference featuring the mayor and the police commissioner, during which the mayor commended the officers for their swift action in saving lives.

A number of people got upset not at what Zohran Mamdani said or did but at the idea that had this same set of facts played out at an earlier time in Mamdani’s career, he would have had a different reaction.

Lee Kuan Yimby
@LeeKuanYimby
Zohran literally would have started a protest in this woman's name 3 years ago and called to abolish the NYPD.
Fox News @FoxNews
BREAKING: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani addresses the deadly Times Square stabbing, saying a woman carrying multiple knives stabbed two people before responding NYPD officers deployed a Taser and opened fire. "I want to thank the NYPD officers who stepped in and prevented a
3:49 AM · Sep 1, 2026 · 133K Views
17 Replies · 47 Reposts · 1.15K Likes

As a fan of counterfactual histories, I find this speculation plausible but … so what?

I’m glad that Mamdani has come closer to my views on these issues, and I’m glad that many of his supporters acknowledge the wisdom of his new approach, and I hope it brings us all toward a more sensible view of crime and law enforcement.

Now, again, if you just know deep in your heart that Mamdani is secretly burning with rage at the N.Y.P.D. and itching at the chance to go totally soft on crime, I guess you can find random splotches of data to “confirm” that.

But everything he’s actually saying and doing suggests that he understands the political imperative of low crime and that he broadly believes deference to the expert judgment of the existing set of police officials is a good way to secure that. And crime is, in fact, continuing to fall under this policy mix. Take the win!

Some of this is, obviously, opportunism:

  • If you don’t agree with Mamdani’s overall approach to being mayor, it’s objectively inconvenient for you that he’s done a good job of handling crime issues. So it might be better to just pretend he hasn’t.

  • If you want El-Sayed to lose, and you know his views on Israel are probably something the voters are reasonably comfortable with, it’s convenient to attribute to him a much farther-reaching anti-American view of foreign policy that he hasn’t actually articulated.

  • If you’re worried that El-Sayed running much weaker than Michigan gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson debunks your larger thesis about the electorate’s hunger for leftist candidates, it’s convenient to explain this away with a conspiracy theory.

But I also think a lot of people are just addicted to a kind of internet rage.

Hyper-negative coverage of the Mamdani administration clearly sells copies of the New York Post. If your whole brand is selling people an anti-establishment insurgency, you can’t really say “the primary is over, we didn’t get all our guys but we got some of them and now it’s time to shift into cooperative mode.” Negativity does well on the internet, in general.

It would be boring for people who disagree with El-Sayed’s actual positions to just say that again every day; it’s more engaging to make stuff up and pretend this old 9/11 tweet said something it didn’t say. But beyond the immorality of the opportunism, there’s something soul-deadening and misery-inducing about behaving this way. Do you really want yourself and your audience to be sad and angry all the time? It’s a lot better to try to keep a calm head and not read maximum nefariousness into everything you see.

title: Ingots We No Longer Trust

Ingots We No Longer Trust

America’s word is as good as gold — that is, unreliable

Paul Krugman
Sep 4
 
READ IN APP
 

In the Yap islands of Micronesia, rai stones carved out of crystalline limestone, with a hole in the center, are considered objects of great value, sometimes described as a form of money. However, they are often large — sometimes as big as 12 feet in diameter — and they rarely literally change hands, given how difficult they are to move. So they stay wherever they are. Their ownership is established by oral history, with changes in ownership established by appending transfers to that shared oral history. This is, by the way, a sort of preliterate version of the blockchain!

For the most part, monetary gold — gold held as reserves by national central banks — is a lot like the stones of Yap. Central banks own trillions of dollars’ worth of gold, which they sometimes sell to each other to settle international payments. But these transfers rarely involve physically moving gold across borders. A large fraction of the world’s gold reserves actually sits in a vault underneath the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, although the New York Fed does move ingots between compartments when transfers take place.

And why not? The sanctity of nations’ ownership of gold stored in New York is guaranteed by the word of the U.S. government — a government that is utterly reliable, because it honors the role of law.

Or anyway, that’s the country we used to be.

“Rule of law” is not a phrase often applied to the Trump administration. And the administration has special contempt for international law. Many of Trump’s tariffs have been ruled illegal under U.S. law, but more or less all of those tariffs were and are in clear violation of past agreements solemnly signed by previous U.S. presidents, including Trump himself.

So the idea that the U.S. government might devise some excuse to seize gold held in the Fed’s vault is no longer far-fetched. And nations are taking precautions. Earlier this week the Dutch central bank announced that it was shifting about $12 billion in gold from the vault in New York to the Bank of England’s vault in London. This follows a move by the French central bank to shift an even larger sum from New York to Paris. Other countries are considering similar moves.

The direct economic or financial impact of these actions will be minimal. There won’t even be large trans-Atlantic gold shipments: foreign central banks will sell their New York gold to private buyers in America and replenish it with purchases from private sellers in Europe.

But the symbolism is chilling. America is no longer trusted. Foreign governments can no longer count on us to obey the most basic rules, like the commandment that thou shalt not steal other people’s gold.

And even when Trump is gone, it will take many years of honest, responsible U.S. government to restore that lost trust.

Still extremely busy. So that’s all for today.

You can’t blame housing shortages for literally everything

Plus alternate Reconstructions, saving D.C. real estate, and the truth about Tupac

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 4
∙

READ IN APP
 

Join us on Wednesday for a Slow Boring D.C. happy hour! We’ll be downtown on September 9 at 6 p.m. Details available for paid subscribers at the end of this post.

Subscribed

Before diving into this week’s Mailbag, let’s talk television. Against my better judgment, I’ve become a fan of the new HBO Max show “Lanterns,” and it’s reminding me why I kind of hate TV. Is the show good? It seems good to me. At least, the three episodes that have aired are good. At least, they seem good. But are they actually good? The truth is that I have no idea. When you read a novel or watch a movie and you decide that it’s good, part of the goodness of the scenes or chapters that come at the beginning is how they relate to the overall story. And more to the point, if someone else tells you that “Moby Dick” is great, then when you come across something in the beginning that seems intriguing, you have reason to believe that the intriguing vibe isn’t just a vibe.

Other people who have actually read the end of the book say that it’s good.

But it’s not just that I haven’t seen the end of “Lanterns” and you haven’t seen it and none of the critics or podcasters talking about it have seen it — there literally is no end for anyone to see. An ending hasn’t been filmed. It hasn’t been written. It doesn’t exist. All this intrigue and vibes and setup and flashback could mean nothing. I was really happy to sit out watching “The Americans” while a lot of people I knew were singing its praises, then fire up the first episode after the final one aired and people were still saying it was great. And it is indeed great! I can tell you that because I know how it ends and it really all hangs together.

Michael Tolhurst: I am sort of curious. Have you investigated the housing stock and regulatory framework for housing in the Austro Hungarian Empire? Could the challenges of the Empire been solved by more market rate housing in growing industrial urban zones for national minorities to improve their economic standing and have more commitment to a joint polity? (Or, another way to put it, does the housing theory of everything really generalize *to everything*?) Is there an exciting alternate history genre waiting to be launched based on counterfactual housing policy?

I am only slightly knowledgeable about this, but I have looked into it a little because there is an obsession throughout the worldwide left with the successful public housing program that was inaugurated in the “Red Vienna” days of the 1920s and continues today in Austria. I think there are a lot of problems with the way this is usually invoked, and part of that involves dropping the historical context.

Obviously Vienna in 1910 was the capital of a large empire while by 1920 it was the capital of a rather small country that was ravaged by war and whose whole economy was in tatters. This is not really a situation that has much in common with any contemporary city, and it meant there were a lot of weird dynamics in place.

If you flip back to the prewar years, though, Vienna was growing very rapidly. I don’t know exactly what their land use policies were, but this is similar to what we see in the industrializing boomtowns of the American Midwest. It’s a reminder that zoning-induced housing scarcity is, broadly speaking, a postwar phenomenon. All across the Western world we used to know how to let housing supply grow with demand.

In 1850, the municipal boundaries of Vienna were expanded to include suburban districts beyond what’s today known as the “inner city” that was bounded by the old city walls. Soon after, the walls and adjacent fortifications were torn down to make space for new buildings and the construction of what today is the Ringstrasse. By the 1890s, the precursor to what today is the Vienna S-Bahn was in operation. So, contrary to the presumption of this question, I don’t think we can attribute anything in particular to housing issues when we’re looking at the problems of the late-phase Habsburg Empire. They seemed to have a pretty reasonable housing situation.

Beyond Vienna, as far as I know other Habsburg cities were also growing. The 1910 census, for example, apparently showed that 43 percent of the residents of Trieste were born outside the municipality. Of those about a quarter were immigrants from Italy (Trieste was a majority Italian-speaking city), and the rest were from elsewhere in the empire.

Share

Several years ago, when I made the case that the collapse of the Habsburg Empire was far from inevitable and the polyglot polity could have survived indefinitely if not for defeat in World War I, this internal migration was key to my argument. Austria was a relatively late industrializer compared with the leading countries of Western Europe, but by the 1910s the Industrial Revolution was beginning to take off. There were, however, marked regional differences inside the empire with the western parts considerably more advanced and prosperous than the eastern parts. In practice, this meant there was a lot of concrete economic value in the way that membership in the empire meant that people who spoke Romanian or Ruthenian or Slovene or Croatian or Polish had the ability to migrate to richer cities like Vienna and Prague. For much of the 19th century, lots of people were moving from Central Europe to the United States of America. But right around when World War I broke out, America was moving in the direction of restricting immigration, so the right to internal migration would have become more valuable.

Conversely, the aforementioned Trieste went into a spiral of decline when it switched from being the main port of the Austro-Hungarian Empire to one of dozens of mid-sized Italian coastal cities.

There would have been, in other words, pretty strong countervailing reasons for members of minority national groups to not want the empire to break up. But that internal migration would have, of course, also created tensions of its own. Big influxes of non-Germans into Vienna would have generated NIMBYism and what you can’t quite call “anti-immigration” sentiment but something politically similar. Again, though, this simply points to the need for the imperial government to act as an honest broker rather than as an instrument of German oppression, helping to manage a multi-lingual entity in a way that would facilitate peace and prosperity for everyone — just as today’s European Union has a lot of problems and controversies but is also broadly recognized as offering a lot of concrete advantages.

Matthew: Alternate history question of the week! Two American Civil War scenarios to consider:

1) The First Battle of Bull Run ends in a decisive Confederate defeat, destroying the Confederate army in northern Virginia and opening the road to Richmond. Is there an outcome where the American Civil War ends up being a few months of political violence followed by some kind of negotiated settlement for the Confederate states to return to the Union (with slavery likely intact)?

2) Rather than surrender and go home, Confederate forces in 1865 disperse into the hills and maintain a guerrilla war against Union forces. What does a prolonged campaign of insurgency/counterinsurgency in the South look like for post-war American politics? Would a violent Confederate insurgency result in a better outcome for the African-American population in the South, with U.S. Government forces reliant on them as valuable local allies (rather than as a victimized group that needed protecting and could ultimately be politically bargained away, as in actual Reconstruction)?

On (2), in terms of the perennial debates about what the war was really about, the fact that guerrilla fighting didn’t happen is very telling. Letting the Union take the cities and the railroad lines and fighting an endless insurgency from the countryside would, after all, be the normal way for a war of national liberation to proceed. But if you head to the hills to fight as a guerrilla, you can’t hang on to your estates and your slaves. And the goal of the war was to hang on to the estates and the slaves. Once it became impossible to win, the Southern elite surrendered on terms that would let them keep their estates even if they had to give up the slaves.

So I think the big difference in an insurgent war scenario is really that you would have ended up with land reform: rebel estates seized and allocated to freedmen (the fabled “40 acres and a mule”) or white collaborators.

For roughly the same reasons that the Democrats eventually won power and abandoned Reconstruction, I think northern whites would have lost patience with an endless guerrilla war in the South and backed down eventually. But as you suggest, it would have probably led to the creation of a more entrenched class of armed African American small farmers who would have been harder to displace than in the historical Redemption process where Southern whites regained political control of their states and disenfranchised African American voters. This is kind of wild speculation, but it’s possible that the ultimate political settlement of this longer-running and more violent version of the conflict would have been population transfers and a kind of de facto partition of the South.

In the 1880 census, considered a lot more reliable than the 1870 one, three Southern states — South Carolina, Mississippi, and Louisiana — had a Black majority and Georgia and Alabama were both at 47 percent. What if four or five of the 11 Confederate states had been Reconstructed permanently and the other six or seven Redeemed with population migrations between the two blocs? One could try to spin this out.

Separately, the Bull Run question is interesting. It seems like, yeah, the Confederacy might have collapsed fast. Then it would have turned out that when Southern senators resumed their seats in Washington, the Republicans would only have 31 seats out of 68. So it’s not just that moderate Republicans like Abraham Lincoln would have promised not to end slavery in the existing states; it’s not clear how the Republicans would have actually been able to enact any of their ideas about halting the spread of slavery into the territories. The whole secession concept was a panicky overreach that actually brought about the Radical Republican legislative hegemony that Southern whites were afraid of.

Share

lwdlyndale: Do you have a Tupac take?

If I told the world what I know, I’m afraid they’d kill me to keep me quiet.

Eric H: Do you lean more towards buying books or getting them from the library? Reading physical books, or reading on an e-reader, or listening to audio books? Does any of this vary based on genre, topic, or reason for reading?

I’m a Kindle guy — I love the portability and convenience. That’s not to say that print is bad, since I’ve read many books in print and where I have space I do like to have a shelf full of books that I admire. But on a practical level, I prefer to read on my Kindle.

Dan Diamond: Do you see a realistic path to revitalizing downtown DC and local real estate markets to the city’s pre-covid, pre-DOGE days?

One thing is that I sincerely think that while every other place on earth zigs against data centers we in D.C. ought to zag. The District of Columbia is unusual in not offering a sales and use tax exemption for people buying computer equipment to put in a data center, and we ought to consider changing course on that and clarifying our industrial zoning to facilitate data center construction. Our property tax base is seriously ailing at the moment, and it seems like an opportune time to grab some investment that will create jobs short term during a localized recession in construction and that will support the tax base over the longer term.

Beyond that, what we have right now is a central business district where the office space is like 20 percent empty and as a result the ground-floor-retail ecology in the central business district is also ailing.

The medium-term solution for this is for the office district to shrink geographically. Right now, there are non-trivial numbers of office buildings in the West End, Navy Yard, and NoMa, and those buildings should mostly close and be replaced by apartments and condos. Then the current office tenants in those neighborhoods could relocate to downtown proper, at which point the vacancy rate would normalize and the ground-floor-retail situation downtown would normalize as well.

A big problem that the city is having at the moment is that not only is the general DOGE shock to the local economy hurting demand for residential real estate, but the D.C. Council and the court system have also done a bunch of stuff to make us less attractive as a place to build and invest. The new mayor is committed to zoning reform and secured the support of most of the city’s local YIMBY activists. Allowing accessory dwelling units and rowhouses in the most exclusionary neighborhoods should do something to juice construction, but unfortunately with current demand conditions and capital competition I don’t think zoning changes are really going to get new multifamily builds. Smaller projects might be financially viable because they are subject to lower regulatory burdens, but if the mayor wants to make her YIMBY dreams come true, she needs to look at the broader regulatory system. Some of that is eviction rules and some of it is inclusionary zoning (which, remember, is a tax on housing), but some of it honestly is just rhetoric and openness.

Investors have gotten spooked over the past several years by the political direction of the city and that’s shut investment down. Electing a democratic socialist mayor doesn’t help.

On the other hand, to some extent it just means the thing investors feared would happen did happen. If the worst-case-scenario mayor showed up before taking office with some business-friendly regulatory reforms and then started taking meetings and speaking publicly about how she understands the need to attract private capital, that could really turn sentiment around.

The point of all of this is that despite the currently sagging market, the absolute price of housing in D.C. remains high. With a sensible, pro-growth regulatory structure, new multifamily housing should make sense financially. In fact, new multifamily housing is getting built in Virginia as we speak, despite it being exposed to the same regional economy. If there is demand for new multifamily housing, then the office district could shrink but become more vibrant and there would be plenty of demand for the city’s stores and restaurants. But if investors remain spooked, things will just sit partially empty instead of being repurposed.
