Liberalism needs a new philosophy of immigration

We need to make a principled stand instead of a tactical retreat.

Noah Smith
Sep 9
 
READ IN APP
 

So, Germany’s far-right party, the AfD, just won a huge landslide election victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. This doesn’t mean AfD is taking over Germany — the far right is much more popular in the post-communist east than in the more populated western regions. Germany is also a parliamentary democracy, and almost everyone else hates and fears the AfD. But the statewide victory is a warning shot, and everyone in Germany — and in Europe — is taking it seriously.

AfD’s surge means two things. First, it means that the rise of far-right parties was not simply a reaction to the pandemic. Back in 2024-25, a number of pundits I respect argued that voters in the U.S. and Europe were backing rightist leaders out of anger at incumbents over Covid. That thesis now looks dead.

Second, it means that something is making many German voters so angry that they’re finally willing to overlook all of the AfD’s catastrophic flaws — its obvious ties to Vladimir Putin, the fact that the party is filled with crooks, its extreme rhetoric, its lack of governing experience, and so on.

What is that “something”? A number of socialist types have tried to claim that AfD’s new voters are responding to economic despair, and can be won back with more socialism. But more sober voices agree that the “something” is immigration. Adam Tooze, who strongly leans to the left, tries to be gentle as he explains that there’s no getting around the immigration issue:

If you ask AfD voters what they worry about, along with their xenophobic concerns about “too many foreigners”, they will mention the cost of living and their concerns for their standard of living. They also mention climate change and the threat of external war…But if you ask them what they think about the AfD and why they voted for it, economic issues are barely mentioned. What comes first is security, foreigners, woke politics, remoteness etc…

If you are hard up and working-class it would after all be nothing short of bizarre to vote for the AfD in the hope of improved social protection…Voting for the AfD in the current landscape, whatever your economic issues, in short, is not a vote to have your economic issues addressed by social democracy, or welfare or government intervention. It is a vote to crackdown on foreigners[.] [emphasis mine]

Robin Brooks is more blunt:

There’s lots going on in Germany at the moment, but - when it comes to the surge in AfD popularity - you don’t need to overthink it. The AfD is relentlessly campaigning on immigration, which tells you that this is what resonates most with voters…A key driver of the recent surge in AfD popularity is that the CDU - SPD grand coalition is proving itself incapable of confronting immigration with the urgency many voters want.

In fact, anger over immigration is probably the main reason that the right is surging everywhere in Europe. Here are Konstantinou and Roumanias (2024) with some data:

We use regional data spanning over 4500 electoral outcomes…between 2000 and 2017 to assess the impact of immigration on Western European Far-Right voting. To deal with potential reverse causation, we use immigration in neighboring countries as an instrument for domestic immigration. The estimated effects of immigration are positive, significant and larger compared to those obtained by simple OLS and fixed effects regressions. Depending on the measure of immigration used, we find that a 1% increase in immigration stocks leads to a between 1.78% and 2.97% in Far-Right voting…Our estimated effects explain a large part of the observed rise in Far-Right in Western European countries that experienced high levels of immigration during the span of our sample.

2026 is hardly the beginning of the trend. Here’s Brookings in 2024:

In the European Union (EU), one election after another has demonstrated the centrality of irregular migration and border security in public discussions and forced mainstream parties to take more restrictive approaches…The results of the European Parliament election, France’s snap election, three German state elections, and the Austrian election all showed a strong rightward drift and signaled voters’ distrust in their national governments, confirming the notable shift in tone on migration in Europe toward a more securitized, hardline approach, even among mainstream parties.

Trump’s election in 2024 was also partially about immigration. Trump voters rated it as one of their top issues, along with inflation. It was the issue where Trump had the strongest lead over Kamala Harris in polls. American voters clearly soured on immigration in 2023-24.

Progressives in America and socialists in Europe still desperately claim that what angry working-class voters really want is more economic support. They keep offering more and more lavish promises of welfare supports and price controls, while staunchly opposing restrictions on immigration. The approach keeps failing, and the far right keeps rising.

Center-right and center-left politicians, on the other hand, realize the source of their voters’ anger very clearly, and are taking steps to reduce immigration. Germany’s center-right CDU has already stanched the flow with restrictive policies:

And Chancellor Friedrich Merz is responding to AfD’s gains by making it harder to get citizenship. Meanwhile, France and Italy are tightening border controls. France is making it harder to become a citizen. The EU is toughening up its asylum rules. Sweden is offering migrants large sums of money to leave the country. European countries are streamlining their infrastructure for kicking out large numbers of failed asylum-seekers. Japan is tightening its own immigration policies after a period of liberalization.

Even Canada, one of the most immigration-friendly and progressive countries on Earth, has scrambled to reduce immigration, cutting targets for permanent residents, reducing student visas, and slashing the number of temporary workers. Immigration levels are still high, but are falling quickly — all under the center-left government of Mark Carney.

And yet I’m worried that voters around the world will see these measures as superficial — tactical pauses to let populist anger simmer down before resuming the same permissive immigration policies that made voters mad in the first place. This certainly seemed to be the case in Europe, where the government stopped admitting asylum seekers from the Middle East in the late 2010s after a popular outcry, only to resume taking them in en masse in the 2020s:

And it also seems to be true in the U.S.; Biden mostly closed the border to asylum-seekers in 2024 after he saw how mad it was making Americans, but many Democrats are now calling for the abolition of ICE. This is a somewhat popular position right now, thanks to the agency’s abuses under Trump. But if Democrats actually try to abolish federal immigration enforcement instead of just reshuffling and renaming the agencies, I predict it will take just a couple of years for Americans to realize that the difference between “open borders” and “immigration laws with no one to enforce them” is largely semantic.

What’s needed, I believe, is not just a tactical, temporary retreat. We need to stop and think why a maximal pro-immigration policy is something that we need to retreat from in the first place. We need a new concept of what a sustainable liberal immigration policy looks like.

Since I started writing, I’ve been an advocate of more immigration to the United States. This does not mean I ever favored unrestrained immigration or open borders. I’ve consistently argued that favoring skilled immigration will bring more economic benefits to native-born Americans, and be more politically palatable as well. And while I don’t hate illegal immigrants for trying to better their lot in life, I favor strong border controls, because nations have the right to decide, democratically, who gets in and out. It’s understandable when people get mad at seeing their decisions flouted.

On top of that, I’ve always remained agnostic on immigration to other countries; although I find much to admire in Canada’s points-based system, for example, I don’t think that qualifies me to decide whether more immigration is good for Canada overall. If the people of a country decide that immigration is diluting their local culture unacceptably, for instance, I think they have every right to cut it off. That’s just Westphalian sovereignty — not a perfect system, but the best system we’ve ever found for organizing humanity into geographic units. As an American, I don’t view it as my place to tell Japan, or the UK, or any other country that immigration is the right choice for them.

Despite those reservations, I’ve always thought that immigration to the U.S. is a basically good thing, and should be expanded. The economic benefits are pretty undeniable — higher tax revenue to shore up our dangerously depleted government finances, dominance in high-tech industries and innovation, and so on. And while some of the economic costs are real — local housing shortages and strains on local government finances being the two biggest ones — many of the fears are overblown. In particular, the bulk of the evidence concludes that immigrants don’t reduce wages or job opportunities for native-born Americans.

And importantly, lots of Americans share my overall positive view of immigration. If you ask Americans whether they think immigration is good or bad, most will say “good”:

And if you ask Americans whether the annual rate of immigration should be increased, decreased, or kept the same, you get a pretty even split:

So I’ve never really felt like I was going out on a limb or advocating an unpopular position when it came to this issue. Sure, rightists will direct online vitriol toward anyone who supports any immigration at all, but their energy and savagery shouldn’t be mistaken for majority support.

And yet there will always be some amount of immigration — and some types of immigration — that will arouse even the most open and welcoming people to ire and make them think about shutting the doors. We saw this in the U.S. in 2023-24, when anti-immigration sentiment spiked in response to Biden’s permissive asylum policies. Yes, that sentiment crashed again when Trump took power and started committing abuses. But if liberals don’t change how we approach immigration, the sentiment will simply rise again and again, as it has so many times throughout our history. And the Donald Trump and Stephen Miller types will be right back in power — and our country will be worse off for it.

Liberals need an immigration approach that can be sustained for long periods of time — i.e., one that doesn’t enrage the public every time it manages to get in power. What would that look like?

The first thing liberals (and progressives, and Democrats, and European lefties, etc.) need to admit is that migration is not a human right. We live in a world of sovereign nation-states, and unless we find some better way of dividing up and administering the world, we will continue to live in a world of sovereign nation-states. And nations are, necessarily, exclusive clubs; they have the right to restrict immigration for any reason whatsoever.

Liberals must therefore not view borders and citizenship as annoying obstacles to be tactically circumvented or overcome; instead, we must view them as fundamental parts of the social compact that allows nations, including liberal nations, to exist in the first place. Nation-states and their laws and their police and their courts and their armies are the fundamental guarantors of the human rights that define liberalism. And for better or for worse, the ability to decide who gets in and who has to keep out is a necessary precondition for nation-states to exist.

That means we need to recognize that immigration law is legitimate and needs to be upheld. Some progressives have tried to advance the notion that being undocumented is a marginalized identity that needs to be protected and supported by the state. But this is absurd; it’s like if progressives decided that people who drive over the speed limit are a minority group.

Illegal immigrants chose to break U.S. law when they came to this country. Our democratically elected leaders made those laws, and they should be honored. We should treat illegal immigrants humanely, of course, and we should not tear local communities apart just to hunt down a few people. But there has to be some way of enforcing the law, because a law without enforcement is no law at all.

A third principle that liberals should embrace is that the purpose of immigration is to benefit the people who already live in the country that is receiving the immigrants. Immigration to America must be for the benefit of Americans. We must flatly reject any concept of immigration that sees it as a necessary sacrifice on the part of American citizens.

For example, the book This Land is Our Land, by Suketu Mehta, argues that immigration is a form of reparations for colonialism — a sacrifice that Western nations owe to other nations, even at their own expense. This idea has found some purchase in progressive circles, but liberals must reject it as wholly illegitimate.

Instead, liberals need to promote immigration because of the benefits it brings to the American citizenry. This includes economic benefits — the tax revenue, the investment, the eldercare, the innovation, the entrepreneurship, the expanded market size. But it also includes cultural benefits — the constant reinvigoration of this nation of immigrants by new waves of people with the gumption and bravery to pick up and move across the world in search of opportunity and freedom.

America has always been the country of the frontier; in order to maintain that ethos in the modern age, we need people for whom America itself is the frontier. And our founding ideals — which are very liberal ideals, of liberty and opportunity and the rights of the individual — are strengthened by people who make the conscious choice to move to a country that represents those ideals.

These are the kinds of arguments liberals made in the past. We can — we should — make them again.

And if this requires us to be selective about which immigrants we bring in, then so be it. Skilled immigrants bring far more economic benefits per capita than others — so by all means, let us tilt our system toward them, as American voters of both parties want. Immigrants who don’t love and embrace American culture will probably invigorate our nation less — so by all means, let us bar immigrants who have been part of groups that see America as evil, using the law with which we once banned immigration by members of communist parties.

These are the kinds of decisions that nation-states, including liberal nation-states, are inherently entitled to make. And we should expect Europe to make different decisions than America makes. That’s perfectly OK. Because immigration is fundamentally the decision of each sovereign nation-state, it’s inevitable that we’ll make different decisions. JD Vance wants us to think that France’s immigration policy, or Germany’s, is inextricably tied to America’s. But it’s not, and we shouldn’t let him get away with conflating the two.

A liberal immigration program based on these three principles could defuse the anti-immigration sentiment now sweeping the developed world — not just now, but permanently. But it will only do so if liberal leaders explicitly articulate and avow these principles. That’s what’s required in order to convince the electorate that liberals are trustworthy on immigration — that embracing the kind of immigration policies Americans demand represents a principled stand rather than a tactical retreat from a hidden agenda of open borders.

For America, the kind of immigration agenda I’ve sketched out — which all the polls show Americans favor by substantial margins — would not be a “far right” policy, even though some progressives and leftists will inevitably try to label it as such. In fact, it would allow in far more immigration than the policies of Franklin D. Roosevelt or Harry Truman. It won’t satisfy progressives who dream of a borderless world, or leftists who salivate over the chance to make the West pay for colonialism. But I believe it will preserve America as the kind of liberal nation-state that we knew it as in the days before Trump.

As for the rest of the world, countries like Germany and Canada and Japan have to make their own decisions. I can’t tell them what kind of nation to build; I can only try to promise that as an American, I’ll respect their decision. If they want to shut their doors in order to slow the pace of cultural change, it’s not my job to lecture them otherwise. All I can say is that I hope they do what they need to do in order to avoid getting taken over by parties that take their marching orders from the Kremlin.

But speaking only for my own country, I believe that if America gives up immigration, it will lose one of the key things that has made it great. With the GOP in the hands of a xenophobic rightist movement that sees immigration as an invasion, it’s up to the Democrats to craft a system that can be preserved for the long term.

Adding Injury to Insult, Canada Edition

This idiotic trade war will hurt more than people realize

Paul Krugman
Sep 9
 
READ IN APP
 

Posted by Trump on Truth Social

There have been many trade conflicts in history, some of them more destructive than the US-Canada fight. But I don’t think there has ever been a dispute this stupid.

Bear in mind that this crisis is entirely gratuitous. Canada has done nothing wrong. Even if one buys into Trumpian nonsense about how every nation that sells us more than it buys is ripping us off, Canada isn’t a villain. Last year Canada did run a modest trade surplus with the United States in goods, but more than half of this imbalance was offset by a U.S. surplus in services. Overall trade between our nations was almost balanced.

So what is this about? Clearly, we’re looking at a symptom of deranged Trump syndrome. As Trump’s failures, from soaring fuel prices to plunging approval, multiply, he is doubling down on his disrespect for and attempted bullying of our northern neighbor and former ally. That is, you should think of this conflict not as something reflecting U.S. national interests, but as a form of self-medication from a sundowning president.

And the derangement isn’t coming solely from Donald Trump. Yes, he — or more likely Natalie Harp — has been posting puerile insults and images on social media. But we also have Scott Bessent, the Treasury Secretary, comparing our northern neighbor to a “little yippy dog.” This is a bigger deal than it might seem. Part of the job of being a finance minister involves projecting a certain gravitas, so that he or she will have credibility in a crisis. When he sounds like an immature thirteen-year-old instead, that does real damage.

It’s all deeply humiliating — for us, not the Canadians. But beyond the embarrassment, it’s also important to realize that an escalating trade war with Canada will do real damage to the U.S. economy.

Trump and his economic officials don’t appear to understand this (although Bessent may just be pretending to be ignorant.) Their expressed view is that Canada’s economy is too small — a “little yippy dog” — for a disruption of cross-border trade to matter. But this complacency is foolish.

The essential thing to understand about U.S.-Canada trade is that our two economies have been closely integrated for a very long time. We’ve had free trade in autos and automotive products since 1965. We signed an overall free trade agreement in 1988, six years before the creation of NAFTA, which included Mexico. And all those decades of free trade have encouraged a great deal of specialization.

That is, the Canadian economy isn’t a miniature version of the U.S. economy, producing the same mix of stuff on a smaller scale. Instead, Canada concentrates on producing a limited range of goods. In some cases Canada produces goods like lumber or aluminum that take advantage of Canada’s natural resources — vast forests and abundant hydropower, which generates the electricity used to smelt aluminum. In other cases, like autos, Canada achieves economies of scale by manufacturing a limited range of goods, exporting most of what it produces to the United States while importing the auto models and components it doesn’t produce.

The flip side of this Canadian specialization is that while the U.S. economy is roughly a dozen times larger than Canada’s, Canada supplies a surprisingly large share of many crucial goods. Canada provides 70 percent of the oil refined in the U.S. Midwest. Canada supplies about 60 percent of US aluminum. Canada supplies almost all of America’s spruce-pine-fir lumber — preferred for framing in residential construction.

If the tit-for-tat with Canada were to escalate into all-out trade war, could the U.S. economy manage? Yes — but it would be expensive and take a great deal of time.

In short, if Trump, Bessent and company think that trade conflict with Canada is a trivial issue, one that Americans will barely notice, they’re in for a rude awakening.

Now, I haven’t talked about the damage a trade war would do to Canada, but it would clearly be immense — possibly bigger in dollar terms than the damage here, although that’s unclear. What is clear is that because Canada’s economy is far smaller than ours, Canada would suffer much more damage from a trade war as a percentage of GDP than we would.

But Canadians understand why they are being asked to suffer this pain: They are defending their sovereignty and their national identity. Will Americans be willing to suffer economically to soothe Trump’s bruised ego?

Improve flawed programs — don’t destroy them.

Trump’s terrible plan to break skilled immigration

Improve flawed programs — don’t destroy them.

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 9
 
READ IN APP
 

Reminder: Paid subscribers are invited to join us this evening for our fall happy hour in downtown D.C. Full details here!

Fifteen years ago, the H-1B visa program that provides temporary employment opportunities for workers with technical skills was relatively uncontroversial.

Or, rather, the controversy was over how to respond to the fact that this one aspect of the immigration system had broad political support. Republicans wanted to expand skilled-worker visa programs, but only by cutting other visa programs; Democrats wanted to expand skilled-worker visa programs, but only as part of a broader immigration-reform package. And a minority in both parties thought that if we all agree on expanding employment visas for skilled workers, maybe we should just do that.

The wheel of history has turned, though, and H-1B discourse has increasingly focused on the program’s flaws.

Most notably, while many incredibly high-achieving people came to the United States on H-1B visas, the program is very much not optimized to attract the “best and the brightest” from all around the world. A large fraction of H-1B recipients are serving as the U.S.-based staff of companies whose main line of work is outsourcing I.T. work, usually to India, rather than helping American software companies grow.

I find this backlash a little bit misguided.

Pointing out flaws is good. Putting forward ideas for improvement is good. But the general tenor of the discourse around outsourcing, H-1B abuse, and “body shops” (basically high-tech temping firms that rent their workers out to other companies) has created the impression that this program people used to say was good is in fact bad.

But actually it’s good! Adam Ozimek and Sarah Eckhardt show that the median H-1B worker earns $130,075 per year (the 91st percentile nationally), meaning that the average H-1B household makes a net federal fiscal contribution that’s 2.6 times as much as the typical American household’s. This is a big win for the federal budget and for state and local governments and also means customers for the large majority of working Americans who provide locally facing services.

Immigration of full-time workers always generates a positive impact on the economy. When these are low-wage workers, though, there are concerns about the impact on inequality and on the fiscal balance. But the actually existing flawed H-1B program raises neither of those concerns. Even if you don’t want to believe the most optimistic research findings about positive innovation spillovers and agglomeration benefits, it’s just straightforwardly a good thing to have these high-earning workers in the country. If you took the program exactly as it existed pre-Trump, made zero reforms, fixed zero problems, and just made it bigger, that would be good.

Of course, an even better idea would be to improve the program. And if you improved it, the case for expanding would be even stronger.

The Trump administration, though, is basically just shrinking America’s skilled immigration programs under the guise of addressing legitimate concerns about them. That’s in part through a misguided effort to impose a six-figure fee on H-1B visas, which they are then exacerbating with a plan to kill off work opportunities for foreign-born graduates of American colleges and universities.

Subscribed

Donald Trump wants a big tax on skilled workers

From a policy-design standpoint, the H-1B visa program has two big design flaws.

One is that it relies heavily on a lottery mechanism. Applicants need to hit certain thresholds to be eligible (which is why the average earnings of recipients are so high), but the decision is ultimately made by a lottery. So while the average earnings are high, there is a lot of variation, and the government is being stingy with the visas but only slightly selective about who gets them.

The other design flaw is that while there are a bunch of wage requirements associated with the program, it’s all sort of based around a desire to avoid undercutting occupation-specific earnings. Instead of asking whether an applicant is highly paid relative to the entire wage spectrum of the United States, it asks about the salary relative to the occupational category, assuming it’s an eligible occupation in the first place.

Again, I do want to emphasize that despite this flawed design, on average the H-1B visas are in fact going to highly paid workers who generate positive fiscal effects and meaningful G.D.P. gains. But the program design is pretty flawed.

The Trump administration has proposed two changes here: 1) shifting to a wage-weighted lottery and 2) imposing a $100,000 fee on employers who get H-1B visas for people filing from abroad (many H-1Bs go to people who are already here on another visa).

The fee idea was struck down in court on the grounds that a presidential proclamation can’t create a large new tax. The administration is now trying to accomplish essentially the same thing as a regulation rather than a proclamation. I am not nearly lawyer-brained enough to tell you whether this new process will pass muster. Notably, though, the administration is also trying to impose a similar $100,000 fee on foreign students who want to work through the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program after they graduate. Even skilled people in highly paid occupations tend not to earn very high salaries in literally their first job. If you make a company pay a special $100,000 tax on hiring a foreign-born person for an entry-level job, that basically kills the OPT program entirely.

Setting that aside for a minute, the virtue of the $100,000 fee for H-1Bs is that it should eliminate the use of these visas for low-paid workers.

This makes sense as a policy goal, but think about the numbers here. The median H-1B worker is earning $130,075, which is a top decile wage in the United States. But a $100,000 fee per visa kills off not just the bottom 20-30 percent of current H-1B uses — it kills off the typical H-1B job. This isn’t taking a flawed program and improving it here. It’s shrinking the program dramatically.

Share

Counterproductive program-design elements

Worse, as Sam Peak and Jiaxin He wrote in an August policy brief, the move to kill off OPT actually shifts H-1B further in the direction of being a visa program for outsourcing firms like Infosys and Tata.

The reason is that American companies normally prefer to hire foreign-born workers who’ve already lived in the United States, speak English, and have other “soft skills” that make them good colleagues. Companies that are not large outsourcers normally use H-1Bs to hire foreigners who had student visas and did OPT before getting their H-1B.

But if we kill OPT, that whole pipeline collapses, and what’s left is a visa program for outsourcing companies.

It’s true that the $100,000 fee will also kill off a lot of current outsourcing practices. But this is not reallocating visas to higher-value uses. It’s just squeezing the balloon from multiple directions simultaneously.

Incorporating wage-weighting into the lottery system, meanwhile, sounds like a good idea, but the actual implementation doubles down on the flaws of the program rather than fixing them.

The problem is that the weight is determined not by the actual wage being offered but by the Wage Level, a four-part classification scheme that compares a given job’s wages to the wages paid to other people doing a similar occupation in any given labor market. You can look wage levels up using this tool. It shows that, for example, an accountant in Birmingham, Ala., earning $85,000 would be at Wage Level Three. By contrast, a chemical engineer in Atlanta earning $95,000 would be at Wage Level Two.

Now, I’m not an accountant, but I can tell you that $95,000 > $85,000. If you’re talking about fiscal contribution or impact on the national income distribution, it’s the actual salary that counts. I don’t want to be a total utopian about the efficiency of labor markets and say that salary offers precisely correspond to the economic value of the work done. But roughly speaking, if you want to weight the odds in favor of higher-value immigrants, you should just give more weight to higher-paid jobs, not do this Wage Level rigamarole.

A better way forward

A wiser path forward on skilled immigration would start with an intuition previously offered by Donald Trump: when foreigners come here to study, we should facilitate them staying after they graduate.

Donald J. Trump
@realDonaldTrump
When foreigners attend our great colleges & want to stay in the U.S., they should not be thrown out of our country.
5:42 PM · Aug 18, 2015
2.56K Replies · 12.1K Reposts · 23.8K Likes

Back in 2015, I might have agreed with Trump’s proposal exactly as stated there. From the vantage point of 2026, though, we know that it’s a bit more complicated than this. The precedent from Boris Johnson’s unfortunate tenure as prime minister of the United Kingdom reminds us that if you turn an educational institution into an automatic pathway to a work visa, that incentivizes the creation/expansion of diploma mills as loopholes in the immigration system.

We need to have standards for allowing a former student to remain in the country, based either on the academic caliber of the student (minimum SAT/GRE score or something), the salary of the job, or both. Erecting some guardrails will let us select for bright people with good career prospects, but then we should welcome them, not drive them out with a $100,000 tax.

We should give recent graduates who meet those standards a year or two or three to work in the United States and prove themselves and perhaps switch to a new visa category.

For H-1Bs, trying to further improve the wage profile of the people who get these visas makes perfect sense. But the way to achieve that isn’t with a $100,000 tax or further monkeying around with the Wage Level. Just allocate the visas preferentially to jobs that pay more!

Right now the program does, in effect, select for highly paid workers, but we could better optimize for this and make the fiscal and economic benefits of the program even larger. I would say that since the current program is already good and the country would benefit from expanding it, we would benefit even more from expansion if we made the program even better. If it were up to me, we would make both changes simultaneously — double or triple the number of H-1B visas and allocate them by salary rather than by lottery.

But stepwise reform works, too. If you allocate the visas by salary, then the marginal candidate who just misses out on getting one would still be a very highly paid worker and the political argument for expansion to let more people in would be very compelling. It’ll be good for growth, good for the fiscal balance, and ultimately good for America.

The 9/11 attacks and the crisis of global liberalism

Cosmopolitan Humanism 1 was crazy.

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 10
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

“The 9/11 terrorist attacks were a really big deal” is perhaps not the hottest take in the world. But as time has passed and a larger and larger share of the population was either not yet born or else — like my Co-Host Jerusalem — not an adult at the time, I think the sheer extent to which history really pivoted on that day can get lost. Younger people who know all about the ways in which the American foreign-policy response went wrong don’t necessarily have the full context for understanding what the prior trajectory of the country was and how things changed.

The episode starts with a review of the literal facts of what happened.

As Jerusalem observes, “Every time you read about almost any major event in U.S. history or in world history or whatever, the contingencies are really shocking.” The plot itself was by no means foreordained to succeed. One prospective hijacker was even arrested before the attack, but the F.B.I. failed to crack the case in part because the legal standard at the time made it difficult for them to get a warrant to search his laptop. Two hijackers had been positively identified as al-Qaeda associates by the C.I.A. and were nonetheless able to enter the country with lawful visas. If the attack had been foiled, that would still have merited a response. But the emotional and political impact would have been dramatically reduced and the national-security response completely different. It also seems likely that if the attack had occurred under an Al Gore administration, the immediate political aftermath would have gone more to questions of the failure to prevent the attack rather than toward a hawkish politics of national unity.

But we got the attack and we got the response that we got.

Looking back from a generation later, liberals tend to appreciate the effort that George W. Bush made to express solidarity with American Muslims and direct public anger away from hate crimes, even as they of course bemoan the fact that the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan ended up costing many more lives than the attack itself. An argument I make on the podcast is that these really are in some sense two faces of the same coin — just as it’s no coincidence that many of the leading “neocon” foreign-policy hawks of that era went on to become prominent dissenters from the later MAGA turn in the Republican Party. The grandiose vision of democratizing the world at gunpoint, however deeply misguided, was in a very real sense an expression of liberal ideals about democracy and human rights and universal values. The failure of those wars is, in an important way, one of the major origin points of the contemporary crisis of global liberalism.

Jerusalem pushes back on the effort to impute so much good faith to the architects of the Iraq War in particular, making the reasonable point that nothing about liberalism or cosmopolitan values particularly suggests responding to a terrorist attack by attacking a country that had nothing to do with it.

I take the point. But I do want to beg for the mercy of younger progressives who have nothing but scorn for those of us who got caught up in war fever. If you can sympathize with the impulse to shrug off wild 2020-vintage takes with the line that “Woke 1 was crazy,” you understand the tremendous emotional impact of repeatedly viewing the footage of George Floyd’s killing. Consider watching thousands of people die. Bush used the considerable agenda-setting power of the presidency to frame the debate in a way that aligned his hawkish agenda with a kind of expressive maximalism about human equality and the universal appeal of liberal values.

It was a tremendous mistake, and not only is the world in general still paying a price, but so is the larger cause of liberalism. It’s why I think a revival will ultimately have to be led by people of Jerusalem’s vintage and younger, those able to learn from the mistakes of the past without being tainted with complicity in them.

Later this month on the pod, Jerusalem and I will be reading Friedrich von Hayek’s “The Road to Serfdom.” If you have thoughts or questions about the book you’d like us to discuss, drop a line in the comments below!

Paid subscribers can watch the ad-free embedded video at the top of this post and read the full transcript below.

WATCH THE EPISODE ON YOUTUBE HERE

New episodes post every Thursday.

Jerusalem Demsas: Hi, everyone. My name is Jerusalem Demsas.

Matthew Yglesias: I’m Matthew Yglesias.

Jerusalem Demsas: And this is The Argument. This week, well, tomorrow is the 25th anniversary of 9/11, and Matt and I want to talk about it. Matt, what was your argument this week?

Matthew Yglesias: So, my — 9/11 was bad. No, you know, I think obviously everybody knows that this was a big deal. It’s why we commemorate its anniversary. Twenty-five is a nice big round number. But, you know, I think that this is an event that, like, really changed the trajectory of world history in a way that, you know, was not just baked into the fundamentals of it, but that the specifics and the contingencies of the moment and the very early response decisions put us on a whole new course that I think is not the course Osama bin Laden wanted, but also was not a course that has ended up that well for the world.

Jerusalem Demsas: So, I was 6 years old when 9/11 happened. I don’t remember it. I feel like I really only learned about it in high school. And then also, as I decided to look into it for this episode, learned a lot of facts that I was unaware of. But what — so what is your take that it was underrated?

Matthew Yglesias: Well, I mean, you know, you’re talking about facts, and I think that this is important. You know, I remember I would just — I was in college, and it was kind of like the day before we were supposed to register for classes, and college students sleep in.

Jerusalem Demsas: Were you a freshman?

Matthew Yglesias: No, sophomore year. And I was always an early riser, even when people weren’t. And I walked and I went to the cafeteria and I was having some breakfast.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And somebody else there, like the jocks who were up early, was like, “Oh my God, planes flew into the World Trade Center.” And I thought, huh. It didn’t make that much of an impression on me.

Jerusalem Demsas: Wow.

Matthew Yglesias: And I was heading back, and I saw somebody who I knew a little bit from New York just sobbing on the street. And I was like, “What’s going on?” And she’s reacting very — she’s telling me the same thing that somebody already told me, but with, like, emotion.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And I’m like, “Oh.” And then I got back to my room, and I looked on the computer, and I was like, “Oh, shit. Like, this is a big deal. I better try to get — “

Jerusalem Demsas: Were you able to watch the video on your computer at the time?

Matthew Yglesias: No. I said I’d better get in touch with my parents. And so, I tried to call them and I couldn’t because the phone circuits in New York were all jammed. And then I went down to, like, a common room somewhere where there was TV. And we were watching it. And, you know, it’s both — I mean, a lot of —

Jerusalem Demsas: Did you watch the towers come down?

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. So, a lot of people died, and a huge share of the population watched it.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Live on television. And it had an incredibly strong emotional impact that I think then and now has sort of blocked out some of the specificity of what occurred and how sort of not obvious it was. I, as it happens, as it goes down, it’s like people are saying, like, “Is this terrorism?”

Jerusalem Demsas: And clearly if it is… Yeah, because people thought it was an accident at first. They’re like, when the first plane — yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. I mean, one plane hits a building, you think it’s an accident, right? Two —

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Clearly, something was going to happen. Like, it was a big deal. But, you know, the Bush administration chose very early on to sort of define what it was that had happened in a way that I think was, like, non-obvious. And they had some good reasons, I think, behind the choices that they made, but it really didn’t turn out well. And also just like the plot itself, you know, there was — some people tried to blow up the World Trade Center in [1993]1994, and it didn’t really work. And a half dozen people died.

Jerusalem Demsas: Six people and one unborn child.

Matthew Yglesias: OK. And so, I mean, I remember that too. Like, I was doing a tennis lesson in New York when that happened. And it, like — and I was like, “Oh my God.”

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But then, because it was only six people — I mean, this is the early ’90s. People were getting murdered in New York all the time. And, you know, there just wasn’t a huge…

Jerusalem Demsas: Like, thousands, like, I don’t know, thousands were injured. Like, it wasn’t like nothing. It was a big…

Matthew Yglesias: No, no. Yes. I mean, but that’s what I’m saying, that a terrorist attack that killed people and that injured many people, and they clearly could have taken down — had that worked, I believe the death toll would’ve been higher than actual 9/11 because the building was more crowded. But the fact that fewer people died meant that the emotional response was much more muted. And the policy response to that was like a shift in the trajectory of American policy towards Sudan and Afghanistan, but not like a revolution.

Jerusalem Demsas: So, I think it’s worth for people, whether you were alive or not alive, or you remember it, but you kind of have hazy details. There’s some study about it. People who say they remember 9/11 often get a lot of the details actually wrong because it was obviously an incredibly emotional moment, as you were saying.

So, 2,977 people die on 9/11. It’s 19 hijackers, or 19 men who are working for al-Qaeda. Al-Qaeda is, like, a transnational terrorist organization that comes out of the anti-Soviet jihad. And, as Matt was saying, the World Trade Center bombing — it’s not just that it was also a bombing in New York City. It’s the same guy who was the mastermind of 9/11 was, like, heavily involved in the World Trade Center bombing. He’s referred to as KSM. His full name is Khalid…

Matthew Yglesias: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

Jerusalem Demsas: In 1996, KSM suggests to Osama bin Laden, “Hey, we should consider using planes to go after the World Trade Center again.” A couple years later, Osama bin Laden’s, like, approved some version of this plan. And then, you know, it’s kind of remarkable. I think in total, when I was reading the 9/11 Commission Report of this, it cost, like, roughly $400,000 to $500,000. Yeah. For this entire thing to happen.

Like, all — most of these men come into the United States on visas. Some of them obviously lie on their visa applications, but they come into the United States on visas. They are living in and around the United States for a good amount of time before the attack actually happens. And it’s actually an incredibly — I mean, this sounds callous, but it’s a very efficient enterprise, right? Like, it’s not, like, a very — even very complicated thing they do. They get on a bunch of planes. This — as a result of this, of course, they harden the cockpit doors. But before then, it was much easier to break into the cockpit and take control of the planes.

You have two planes, of course, fly into the Twin Towers in New York. And over the course of, like, over 100 minutes, both towers collapsed. I think that’s one thing that’s, like — I feel like I did not — I didn’t — again, I didn’t watch it live. I only think I saw the footage for the first time when I was in high school. But I think it’s, like, super underrated, how long it took for that to happen after the planes had hit it. Which makes sense because the planes hit the building, it weakens a bunch of the supports. A bunch of fires kind of go off, which also the heat makes the floors sag, and then also is difficult for the supports. And then all of that leads to a collapse of not just one, but second one. And so, people are, like, riveted to their TV screens, and I’m like, obviously, from reading this, I did not remember this.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, yeah. No, but, you know, this is the point of my story.

Jerusalem Demsas: It takes 100 minutes for the second one [Tower 1] to go down. And so, people are just, the whole world’s, like, kind of stopped just watching TV. And I don’t think people thought it was gonna go down when it first gets hit. And because that was the original intent. And I think that connecting it again to the World Trade Center [WTC] bombing, the goal has been since the WTC bombing, at least to bring down these specific towers.

Matthew Yglesias: And I know, you know, human memory is, like, super duper fallible. So, I’m going to say that this is what I remember thinking 25 years ago, but maybe I’m duping myself. But my recollection is that I was watching it and I was thinking, “Well, they hit the building way too high, right? It’s not falling down.”

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Like, we can see there’s a fire burning.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But I mean, if you look at the video, the collision is high up on the tower. And I don’t know anything about engineering, whatever. You know, I’m a know-it-all. But it’s like, “Well, if you’d zoom down, this would be so much worse and the towers would be falling down. But it’s probably OK.”

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And then, you know, clearly it was not.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And so, yeah, I mean, there was just, you know —

Jerusalem Demsas: But it’s also, like, remarkable. I mean, obviously because it took so long, a lot of people were able to evacuate and get out of the —

Matthew Yglesias: …out of the —

Jerusalem Demsas: …out of the building, which is good. But I don’t know, 3,000 people. I mean, it’s a lot. I mean —

Matthew Yglesias: Also, one of the — the casualties were very heavily — a lot of police and firefighters died rather than office building workers. Because again, the long time meant it saved lives on net because they were able to do evacuation, but it meant that first responders were killed rather than if the buildings had, like, instantaneously vaporized or something.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: You know, it’s office workers, but — and, you know, all human lives are, like, beautiful and equal, but, you know, there’s a certain specific resonance to the firefighters and police officers who came in to help others and ended up sacrificing their lives and their families. I have tried over the past 25 years to become a rational person who says things like, you know, it doesn’t matter, like, objectively, whether you watched these people die on television or just heard that they died overnight. You know, which is true, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But part of that is because I know vividly that so much of the response in practice was because the emotional impact does matter.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Like, a guy tries to blow up a building that would have killed thousands of people if he had located it a little bit differently, provokes a totally different response from the building actually falls down and the people actually do die. Different amounts of people sobbing, different amounts of panic, and it’s a different world. And also, I mean, you see this very clearly in the 9/11 Commission Report, but it’s not like this was the — it’s not like this was such a great plot that there’s no way it could have been unraveled.

Jerusalem Demsas: No, I think that’s like — I think that’s part of — I mean, every time you read about almost any major event in U.S. history or in world history, whatever, the contingencies are really shocking. Reading the 9/11 Commission Report, seeing all the contingencies that came in in advance.

I mean, some of the more, like, absurd ones are there was a guy who was getting flight training in Minnesota. And he seemed suspiciously uninterested in both taking off and landing of planes, and he gets detained for a routine, like, immigration violation. And he’s actually detained through 9/11 itself. And people, and there’s reports that, you know, they wanted to search his laptop, and they wanted to do more intensive searching. But there’s, you know, there’s some — they don’t have the probable cause they need, and they’re like, “We’re just gonna deport him.” He’s supposed to be deported to France, which is where he, I guess, he came into the country from. And I don’t know what was on his laptop. We don’t know that. I don’t think, at least it wasn’t in the report.

But there were many things like that where it’s like, OK, well, we could have had this information. There’s of course the famous presidential briefing where it says, like, Osama bin Laden is going to be targeting the United States, and it’s just like it’s… There’s a sense of this was unthinkable that clearly pervaded the post-9/11 moment. But clearly many people actually were thinking about the potential for people to use planes to hijack them and to attack the United States.

Matthew Yglesias: So, you were referring to the Zacarias Moussaoui case.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: So, he had been flagged as suspicious by a flight instructor, was picked up on immigration charges, was in detention. They applied for a warrant, and it was ruled that it didn’t meet the FISA criteria.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But there’s a different guy who was in custody from the World Trade Center plot.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And after 9/11, they show this guy Moussaoui’s photo and they’re like, “Do you know this guy?” And they’re like — he says, like, “Yes, that’s Zacarias Moussaoui. Like, we trained together in al-Qaeda camp.” And so, if they had asked the guy, you know, they had this al-Qaeda source in custody, and they had another guy who the FBI in Minnesota thought was doing terrorism.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But they didn’t get the —

Jerusalem Demsas: But I mean, I don’t know. I don’t want to make it sound like these people should have figured it out.

Matthew Yglesias: No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. It’s just to say that the point of the 9/11 — the 9/11 Commission Report came out years after the event.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And it just — it paints a narrative which is like, there’s a bunch of these failure points. There’s this guy Khalid al Mihdhar, and the CIA tries to keep track of dangerous terrorists. And they observed him in Malaysia going to a, like, some kind of al-Qaeda summit with a guy who was involved in the bombing of the USS Cole, which was a naval ship. And so, they wrote down in their, you know, intelligence notebook, like, this guy is an al-Qaeda operative. He then applied for a visa to come to the United States, got the visa, came to the United States, was here for a while, left the United States, went to Yemen, went to Afghanistan, and then came back to the United States. And then he was hijacking one of the planes. So, again, you know, the 9/11 Commission Report, it raises the question of maybe if the CIA decides you’re a terrorist, that should go to the INS.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: So, that they don’t give you the visa, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Like, these things were just not integrated. Like, there were individual agencies that were aware of certain concerning pieces of information, and they were not — and there was some — one of the points the commission report makes is like, it was like it had to go to the president level in order to resolve a lot of these interagency issues.

Matthew Yglesias: And so, you know, this was like understood at the time, and the Patriot Act passed and was supposed to address some of these things. And after the World Trade Center bombings in [1993]1994, politics was different back then, but, you know, the Clinton administration was, like, really, really tough on crime.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And Republicans were more civil libertarian back then. And because of the Oklahoma City bombing and the World Trade Center bombing, they put forward a suite of counterterrorism surveillance proposals that Republicans mostly opposed.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And so, one of the things that happened on 9/11 was Republicans flipped on that, and the Patriot Act happened. But in part because it took a while to compile this information, go back through the files, the discourse, you know, one hour, one day, one week, one month after the attacks wasn’t like, we need to improve our procedures for identifying and catching —

Jerusalem Demsas: No, it’s like September 20th when Bush does his address. He says it begins with al-Qaeda, but it doesn’t end there. And I’m like, I don’t know. Again, my perspective on this is a bit, like, different because I mean not just because I was young, but because my parents grew up in the middle of a conflict that was in not in no small part blamed on the United States for intervening in the Ethiopian-Eritrean civil war. And so, from their perspective, they’re like, yeah, Bush’s father wanted to go after Saddam Hussein. This is the Gulf War, and Bush is now having an opportunity to finally do what his dad was unable to do, which is to kill Saddam Hussein.

And I remember — I don’t get — you know, I was a child. I don’t remember when this happened. I don’t remember the kind of whatever. But I remember my parents saying this to me and talking about this a lot. But it is remarkable in hindsight to go, like, nine days after a terrorist organization has killed 3,000 people in the United States. Terrorist organization, al-Qaeda. There is, like, no evidence at this point that al-Qaeda and that Saddam Hussein was involved in this plot.

Matthew Yglesias: Yes.

Jerusalem Demsas: We know now the best evidence that he was not involved in the plot on 9/11. But it’s clear that the hope — no, I don’t want to say hope. I don’t want to put it in, like, a, you know, they were happy about it, but they’re like, there is a view that this is a moment to take advantage of this emergency to do a broader intervention than merely responding to, like, there’s a terrorist attack. We need to, of course, make sure this never happens again. And then we need to find the specific people who perpetrated it and either capture or kill them. That is clearly not the goal nine days after a terror attack.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, and that’s why I think contingency is important here on a number of levels, right? Because again, imagine that this plot had been unraveled, right? That say they get this guy’s laptop and the laptop, who knows? Say even just the laptop specifies the thing about, like, well, we can use box cutters as weapons to hijack a plane. So, then, an emergency order goes out across the TSA that, like, we’re gonna, you know, the only policy change, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Is to strengthen the cockpit doors.

Matthew Yglesias: Is to strengthen the cockpit doors and change the rules about what you’re allowed to bring on a plane. And then these guys, because they’re fairly seasoned operatives, have to call it off because it’s not going to work. Now, that doesn’t mean that al-Qaeda goes away or that —

Jerusalem Demsas: No, they probably try again. Clearly, they’ve been trying forever.

Matthew Yglesias: Right, right. But so, you know, because there’s a view — I mean, there’s always been this discourse around 9/11 and how much we should understand it as blowback to other American — but so all that stuff would just still be in motion.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But very possibly, they would just never have been able to pull off something quite as spectacular as that. You come up with something else. You know what I mean?

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, other things they were suggesting were, they were thinking about going after targets in Israel. They were thinking about, you know, other non-American targets in American-aligned countries going after — I mean, I remember there was one comment about trying to go after Jewish targets in New York City. So, things like that would’ve been obviously terrible, but just not as — I think the visuals are really hard.

I think the first time I really got a sense of the visuals, when I went to the 9/11 memorial, and with the memorial, and this is now a, like, cold, cold, cold take. Insanely bad choice to make them, like, a convex, like, wound in the, like, in the middle of New York City. It’s like I don’t know. I feel like they should have just rebuilt the tower. I don’t know. That’s my take. All right.

Matthew Yglesias: I’m gonna leave that alone.

Jerusalem Demsas: But I think the visuals of it were like… That’s why they kept going back to the same place.

Matthew Yglesias: Yes. And I just — my point is, you could have — there just could have been this, like, whole other trajectory in which the basic structure of the ideological conflict is still there, but everything is much more, like, literal. You know, it’s like, we uncovered this plot, we prevented them from executing that exact kind of thing in the future. We started doing some changes to the visa system. They start going after softer targets. And it’s like, plop, plop, plop, plop, plop. Probably we would do something in Afghanistan related to that. There was a plan.

Jerusalem Demsas: We’d probably spend more time on trying to break down the al-Qaeda cells.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, yes, but also Richard Clarke, who had been the al-Qaeda coordinator at National Security, something like that, he had created some plan in the waning days of the Clinton administration that was like, we’re going to put a lot of money into the Northern Alliance and fight the Taliban. I don’t want to — I don’t want to libel anybody with getting this wrong, but I think — I think the basic call was like, we’re like a lame duck now. We’re going to just sort of forward this to the next people. And then it landed on the Bush people’s desk, and it was kind of like, eh.

Jerusalem Demsas: We have a lot going on.

I mean, I think around 4% to 6% of Black, white, Hispanic household high income households in these areas are using some form of tutoring or test prep outside of school, but like 9% of Asian households are. So, clearly there’s also, like, a different angle going on there.

Matthew Yglesias: You know, I — this is one of these papers where it, you know, I think if you exist in the world, especially if you’re a parent, it’s not, like, earth-shattering knowledge to learn that private supplemental instruction helps kids and that it is primarily done by more affluent parents and also that Asian families are, you know, at any given level, just, like, more jazzed up about this, that the non-Asian families. But, you know, I think the, like, policy upshot, which is outside the four walls of these research findings, is just to remind people how, like, actually inequitable it is when you dumb down public schools in the name of equity.

Jerusalem Demsas: Mm-hmm.

Matthew Yglesias: You know, because this is something that we’ve seen in a lot of school systems, this idea that if advanced coursework is disproportionately being used by white and Asian families, it shouldn’t exist or it should go away. But it’s the people with the most resources and the most commitment aren’t, like, what can I do? You know, it’s like, you get a private tutor, you get these chain things with Zoom, right? I mean, they are able to instrument on, like, did the private tutoring center open? But in the emerging technological paradigm, it’ll be much less bounded by that kind of thing. And so, it’s like you can give people in the public education system, good math instruction, and then we’ll see what happens. Or you can not give it, and we know what happens, which is, like, people able/motivated. It’s both and.

Jerusalem Demsas: It’s pretty, again, it’s pretty small numbers of people relative, like, you know, 4%, you know what I mean? It’s very small.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah.

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, I think what I will say is the thing that shocked me about this paper is that their estimated center entry effects explain nearly two-thirds of districts’ improvement in math scores from 2009 to 2019, which that means, from over a decade period, 66% of the improvement in math scores is due to the fact that a private tutoring center opened up in the district. And it’s about, the effect costs are $75 per district pupil, which is way less than we would spend to increase math scores through the public system.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah.

Jerusalem Demsas: I will say this, I think a lot of people are taking this paper to, I mean, I’ve seen some commentary about this and some of it is saying, well, we should just, instead of plowing even more money into the public school system, we should just pay for people to get this math instruction to go to Kumon or whatever it is. I think there’s some — I mean, I think it’d be good to have, here, we’ll pay for people to get math instruction from private tutoring or whatever. That seems like a fine policy idea to me. But I do think this paper speaks to only high-income students will increase their math scores if they get private tutoring.

Matthew Yglesias: Yes.

Jerusalem Demsas: It doesn’t necessarily tell us what would happen for what are potentially lower perform — what are likely lower performing students, if this would have the same level of impact. Like, it is easier in some senses to get someone from being, like, an eight out of 10 math student to a nine out of 10 math student than to — or maybe, well, let’s just say a similar six to seven out of 10.

Matthew Yglesias: Sure.

Jerusalem Demsas: Than it is to get someone who missed a bunch of foundational stuff because they have a bunch of shit going on at home, and now all of a sudden they need to get to, like, eighth grade level readiness. Like, that’s an incredibly difficult problem because you have to catch someone up on, like, eight years of coursework they just haven’t done.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. On the other hand, I could teach somebody multiplication tables, but I couldn’t teach somebody calculus. And, you know, that’s a funnel in instructional capacity that’s gonna exist out in the world. So, —

Jerusalem Demsas: But it’s like, my point is, I don’t know from this paper, I mean, we know that they’re doing math. I don’t know if they’re doing what kind of math they’re doing.

Matthew Yglesias: No, no, I agree. I agree. But look, I mean, it’s a reminder though that, you know, the structure of conventional public schools is just, like, really not optimizing to teach people stuff.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Now, some of that is, like, for good reason.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: You know what I mean? And things shouldn’t just all be maximizing everything all the time, but some of it is for, I think, bad reasons. And there is just a lack of focus on trying to do cost-effective instruction. And that’s bad. It’s sobering that these private companies are able to deliver this at so much lower cost. I’d recommend The Argument’s article about public sector labor unions, because you can also just see that between public school systems, that the, like, cost basis structure of different public school systems in America is, like, all over the map. And it holds. There is evidence that marginal funding increases lead to better educational outcomes. But there’s just also evidence that, like, cross-sectionally, the spending levels are uncorrelated with outcomes, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: And those are, like, a little bit hard to reconcile.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But it’s — you just — you —

Jerusalem Demsas: But it’s also like the — I mean, again, this is just repeating myself, but it’s just education’s not one problem. Like, the problem of educating a bright young child from, like, a healthy, rich family to be good at Calc 2 and ready to go to college, ready to take higher-level mathematics, is, like, a different problem than how do you take an eighth grader who never learned his times tables and get him ready to take the standardized test. They’re just different problems.

Matthew Yglesias: Yes. I mean, that is definitely true, but I just mean that I think we see over and over and over again throughout the educational system that there are just big fundamental cost structure issues that are not rationalizable, that if you somehow just zero-baselined everything and rebuilt from scratch, it just seems like things could be done much, much, much better. One thing that you cannot quite get at with the way this is instrumented that is always tricky in education is what is the instruction versus what is the motivation that is tokened by the instruction?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: You know what I mean? And so, —

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah. What do you mean?

Matthew Yglesias: The center opens. And some people go and others don’t go. And part of what’s happening is the people who signed up are signing up for — but I mean, it’s not just they’re different, it’s selected, but it’s like they are investing their own effort in the situation. And is there a world in which they just buy some book that’s even cheaper?

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, actually, there’s a historical analogy for you. Did you know — I learned this while researching for this podcast. In 1980, from 1980 to 1989 roughly, South Korea just banned private tutoring. Did you know about this?

Matthew Yglesias: No.

Jerusalem Demsas: OK, this, the — I forget what it’s called. The Chun Doo-hwan government in July 1980 imposed an extraordinarily broad ban on private extracurricular tutoring, including private lessons, the hagwons, or these private cram tutoring academies for entrance exams. Like, they banned them, and the rationale is largely about, like, financial economic playing field type stuff.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah.

Jerusalem Demsas: One study that I found found that you’re basically substituting hours spent by yourself studying for these — these people, like, they didn’t play more, they just studied by themselves and did some, like, study groups or whatever. There also was an illicit, like, risk premium private tutoring, like, you know, illegal mafia, I guess, or whatever that was, that was trying to provide this sort of thing at a higher cost for families that wanted to risk the law.

The impact of this is really interesting. So, there’s one paper that looks at the 1989 legalization as a natural experiment, and they find that admission to elite universities rises disproportionately in wealthy areas as a result. So, clearly there was — I don’t want to draw — a lot’s going on in South Korea in the 1980s or whatever.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah.

Jerusalem Demsas: But it is likely the case that there was some sort of leveling effect in terms of inequality of where people come from who went to the top university. But also at the same time, again, they’re very, very careful about drawing, like, too hard of a causal explanation from this. It does seem like school scores might’ve been, like, slightly lower in the years where you weren’t allowed to do private tutoring. Yeah. Which seems like —

Matthew Yglesias: Sure. I mean, I think about —

Jerusalem Demsas: But I think that’s like, I mean, that’s, like, super interesting.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah.

Jerusalem Demsas: I don’t know. They, like, did. And also I think it cuts against a lot of people’s intuitions around Asian Americans and Asians and private tutoring.

Matthew Yglesias: Sure. Yeah. I mean, when I was in college, I took the LSAT because there’s no money in journalism and no future in it. And I did a practice test and I got an OK score and I was like, ah, I better do better on this. And so, I got some LSAT books and I did it by myself and —

Jerusalem Demsas: Did you get better?

Matthew Yglesias: I got way better.

Jerusalem Demsas: What was your score?

Matthew Yglesias: What’s that?

Jerusalem Demsas: What’s your score? You’re going to share it?

Matthew Yglesias: I scored 179.

Jerusalem Demsas: Wow. That’s a really good score.

Matthew Yglesias: And so, then I…

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, what was the first score?

Matthew Yglesias: So, then I took it. I don’t remember, but I did way better. And then I came to D.C. and because there’s no money in journalism and I was like, what the fuck am I going to do? And so, I did some LSAT prep because I had a really — you don’t have to have gone to law school. You just need to…

Jerusalem Demsas: Wait, you did LSAT prep after you already got 179?

Matthew Yglesias: No, I taught it for money.

Jerusalem Demsas: Oh, you taught it. OK. Sorry.

Matthew Yglesias: So, you know, so I like to say, like, I’m better than a lawyer because I was an LSAT prep teacher. And, you know, because all you need to qualify to be an LSAT prep teacher is a good LSAT score. Yeah. My kids, they did better after they took my class, but I swear to God, all I did was be like, take the fucking practice test. You know what I mean? And so…

Jerusalem Demsas: That’s real. I mean, this is happening with AI tutoring now too. I have a friend of mine who’s like, yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right. So, it’s like, because I think people read this stuff both ways, right? And the more, like, progressive take is like, oh, this private tutoring, it does so much. And then the more, like, conservative, pull yourself up by your bootstraps take is like, you can literally just get these practice tests for free at the library.

Jerusalem Demsas: But that is do so much. It’s very, very hard to make yourself study.

Matthew Yglesias: I absolutely agree. I mean, it’s just that I think the tutoring works, but the main thing that works about it is it makes you practice. Is just, you’re like, you know, and it’s like the same thing. It’s like people take exercise, you know, have trainers, and it’s like, sure, yes, they give you some instructions and stuff, but the main thing is they make you do it. Yes. Right. Because we people tend to be a little bit lazy. And so, I don’t know, I’ve never been to a Kumon. My son doesn’t do that.

Jerusalem Demsas: He does tutors though, right?

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, math. Yeah. But it’s, like, getting the — getting, you know, like motivation is hard. Motivation is a scarce resource in contemporary society. And just like things that get people to do the work, even when it’s not, like, so galaxy brain, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah. I was not — I was not a studier of medicine.

Matthew Yglesias: You could just take — do the prep stuff at home by yourself for free.

Jerusalem Demsas: But what I will say about the South Korea thing is that it was super popular. So, they tested parents and it was 75% wanted the ban to continue. The general public, 68% wanted it. Students, it was 61%, and it was teachers, 56%. So, the least pop — I mean, it was still popular among teachers clearly, but, I mean, it kind of makes sense where you’re kind of like, I individually, a parent might be like, I kind of want it so my kid doesn’t fall behind. But they’re like, if nobody did it, then the playing field’s level. I don’t have to. And it’s like —

Matthew Yglesias: Positional competition.

Jerusalem Demsas: But it is. But it’s also like, I think it’s very hard to explain the benefits of, you really do want this really smart kid to be even slightly smarter. It helps you if he goes on to —

Matthew Yglesias: You don’t believe in externalities, innovation, growth, progress?

Jerusalem Demsas: No, I’m saying it’s hard to explain that to people. It’s hard to internalize that if you don’t already. I mean, because it’s not as clear as, like, hey, study culture’s, like, really bad and kids are, like, killing themselves over it. Or they’re like, you know, it’s ruining childhoods or whatever. Like, it feels very concrete to a lot of people, but maybe one of these kids will go on to be an engineer that’ll be part of a team that helps solve some electric car company problem. I mean, you just sort of, like —

Matthew Yglesias: I just think about the smartest people I knew, you know, when I was younger. And one of them, he’s, like, he’s working away at Nvidia building better chips to accelerate Doom. Yes. But the problem is — Another is in private equity, a heroic capital allocator. Making sure that our investments are maximized. It’s great.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah. Two very similar jobs. But I think that’s peer review.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. If you want to get ahead in a zero-sum positional competition against your friends, you need to — no, you need to like this podcast. You need to subscribe. You need to share.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: Tell your friends. You need to comment. All forms of engagement are valuable. Spread the good word.

Jerusalem Demsas: Every month we do a book club. This month we’re going to be reading The Road to Serfdom by Hayek. And leave a comment below if you have any questions or comments that you want us to address. Thanks! See you next week!

Bessent and the Bonds

Big talk, but he carries a very small stick

Paul Krugman
Sep 10
 
READ IN APP
 

Another short, wonky post. Too much going on for more.

“Speak softly and carry a big stick.” Teddy Roosevelt’s favorite aphorism made sense then and now. Policymakers should avoid being boastful or belligerent, not simply as a matter of good manners, but to save their credibility for moments when it’s really needed.

Obviously nobody expects Donald Trump to follow TR’s advice. No matter what the circumstances, Trump will always insist that he’s carrying a big stick, the biggest stick, a stick like nobody has ever carried before. But I expected a bit more circumspection from Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary.

After all, a young Bessent was working for George Soros in 1992 when Soros famously engineered a speculative run on the British pound. At the time British officials loudly and repeatedly proclaimed that they would never, ever allow the pound to be devalued — then caved in the face of market pressure, a humiliation from which Norman Lamont, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, equivalent to the U.S. Treasury secretary, never recovered. So Bessent should know the risks of talking big when you might not have the means to deliver.

Oh well. On Tuesday, Bessent — who has been deploying U.S. funds to support the Japanese yen, declared himself in control of the situation: “I am the house now … And you can bet against me if you want.”

So far markets haven’t challenged Bessent’s boasts about the yen. They have, however, tested his attempts to push down U.S. interest rates — and as the headline at the top of this post says, those efforts are failing with flying colors.

Now, I’d like to blame the Trump administration for rising interest rates. The truth, however, is that rates are rising everywhere. As the European think tank Bruegel says,

[The] problem with explanations centred on a breakdown in US institutions is that the rise in long-term rates is not uniquely American. US, German, French, Italian, United Kingdom and Japanese 30-year yields rose by 45-79 basis points in the six months to 28 August, with the US in the middle at 58bp.

Given the craziness of our leadership, America arguably deserves to be punished by the bond market, but the truth is that we can’t see that happening in the data (yet?).

So what is driving interest rates higher? It may not have much to do with policy at all. The simplest story consistent with the facts is that we’re seeing a surge in demand for funds as a result of the AI boom. We are in the midst of a surge in spending on information technology (information processing equipment and software) that is on track to be even bigger than the boom of the late 1990s:

And it’s worth noting that long-term interest rates were even higher then than they are now, even though inflation was low and we had a budget surplus:

As I said, although the Trump administration deserves blame for many things, I don’t think it’s responsible for high long-term rates, any more than Bill Clinton was responsible for high rates in the late 1990s. This looks like the natural market response to the rush to invest in AI.

It is, however, foolish of Bessent to imagine that he can beat rising rates back by talking big while waving his tiny, tiny stick. All he’s doing is further draining his rapidly diminishing reserves of credibility.
