The economy could survive a downtick in A.I.

Plus what happened to college and what’s wrong with Tucker Carlson

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 10
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Before moving on to an A.I. question I did get for the Mailbag, I want to answer one I didn’t. Tyler Cowen has been challenging A.I. risk worriers to make some investable prognostications about the looming clouds of doom.

I forecast that he will not find this answer satisfactory, but I think the problem here is that the real-world investment advice I have received from safetyists is mostly bullish. Advice I have taken that has paid off well was stuff like “buy Nvidia.” Advice I have not taken that would have paid off well is stuff like “go get a job at Anthropic and enjoy some stock-based compensation.” I know big safety-heads who advise making large investments in out-of-the-money calls on index funds — i.e., bets that the stock market will increase rapidly. The basic safetyist thesis, after all, is:

  1. A.I. capabilities will accelerate in a transformative way.

  2. This has a nontrivial chance of leading to human extinction.

Item (2) is the basis for policy recommendations but in financial market terms (1) is the dominant consideration. Now of course, mathematically whether you think (2) amounts to a “5 percent chance” or an “85 percent chance” makes a difference. But unless you’re a financial professional, the safetyists and the super-optimists are saying the exact same thing — that A.I. is going to be an incredibly powerful, incredibly transformative technology and not just a boost to coders’ productivity or a new way for kids to cheat on their homework. From an investment viewpoint, the opposite of the safetyist view is “it’s all a bubble,” not “A.I. is going to be really good.”

I think it is a little embarrassing for the safetyist view that it is not more clearly distinguished from A.I. optimism. At the same time, I think the optimists have done the world a disservice by insisting on labeling everyone who has safety concerns a “doomer” and then, rather than understanding what the actual belief is, wondering why the “doomers” aren’t behaving like people who believe the world is doomed.

M_McQ: A lot of people are getting concerned about accelerating AI, including me. I think slowing things down with an international agreement is the only way to avoid a race between companies and nations, leading to a variety of bad scenarios. But even if we could convince the administration that this is a problem, won’t an AI slowdown just cause the AI bubble to burst, tanking the economy? Will political incentives just force us to keep racing and hope for the best?

Ignoring the substantive question about A.I. governance, something that I keep seeing in discussions of A.I. and the macroeconomy is a lot of partial equilibrium thinking, where people look at one change while holding the rest of the economy fixed.

Someone will observe that a very large share of recent G.D.P. growth has been data-center construction, do a little basic subtraction, and then say, “Without the data-center construction, G.D.P. growth would be way lower!” This appears to me to have been the logic behind the Trump administration’s politically bizarre decision to come out swinging as the industry’s greatest friend rather than offer people any kind of reassurances around electricity prices or anything else.

But this is not how a dynamic market economy works.

What’s happening is that right now, A.I.-related activities are the highest-reward use of financial capital, so tons of investment funds are flowing into them. That financial capital is being used to buy real resources — land, electricity, chips, skilled labor, etc. — which are being diverted from other purposes. If data-center construction slowed markedly, interest rates would decline. More apartment construction projects would pencil out. Electricians and HVAC technicians who are currently building data centers would build apartments instead. The price of memory and other computer components would go down and people would build more gaming P.C.s and more video game consoles.

It’s important not to make the reverse mistake and portray the economy as purely zero-sum. The reason so many resources are being sucked into A.I. is that investors believe this is the highest R.O.I. use of the financial capital and the real resources that stand behind it. If regulators block data centers, there will be an economic cost. If the investors turn out to be mistaken (a “burst bubble”), we will end up with a worse economic outcome than the one projected by their current optimism. But it’s an exaggeration to believe the resources will just go idle or the economy will tumble into recession.

I’m old enough to remember Paul Krugman and others spending a lot of time during the Great Recession trying to remind people of the opposite. That when inflation is below target and interest rates are low and the Federal Reserve is at the zero bound, resources really do just sit around idle. Under those circumstances, mobilizing unemployed people to go do something is on net beneficial even if the “something” they do is far from optimal. But we left that macroeconomic world behind us a long time ago. Today, inflation has been persistently above the Fed’s 2 percent target. And while interest rates still aren’t particularly high by historical standards, they are definitely higher than they’ve been in the recent past, and the Fed’s policy rate is not at zero.

This generates a lot of aggravation and annoyance and public distress about the cost of living. But it also means the economy has a natural robustness to demand shocks. Blows will be absorbed by interest rates and inflation and the economy will bounce back.

None of this answers the question of exactly what to do about A.I., but it’s just to say that the macroeconomic take on A.I. is that politicians should do the right thing and not worry too much about the short-term economic impact of slowing or regulating A.I. progress.

Then to delve a little bit more into A.I. while also being a bit more speculative, I think the current “race to superintelligence” dynamic at the leading A.I. companies is probably hurting productivity growth. I don’t think it’s widely understood that right now the marquee job in the industry is “use A.I. to build the next great foundation model.” Of course, plenty of people are trying to use the existing A.I. models to build economically useful software applications that they sell to people. But the top priority at Anthropic isn’t “use Claude to revolutionize the tax prep industry.” It’s “use Claude to build a better Claude,” and the same is true at Anthropic’s competitors. That’s the high prestige work. A disproportionate share of the top people and the hardware resources are going to that work.

If you waved a magic wand and made it impossible to ever make a core model that’s better than Astra or Fable, it’s not like A.I. would vanish or all progress on it would cease. But right now the perception among A.I. true believers is that eventually the models will be good enough to achieve recursive self-improvement and an intelligence explosion. If you believe that’s possible, then racing to achieve that outcome is very important, and you dedicate a lot of resources to it. If further progress in core models becomes impossible, then those resources get redeployed to more prosaic questions like how to use Astra to make money by solving economically significant problems.

Mark: I’m YIMBY, you’re YIMBY, but just how far would you go? Would you bulldoze the West Village or Brooklyn Heights if it meant you could build 500,000 units over 8 years? I just watched Ninotchka so....

I always want to be extremely clear about this. If I were in charge of land use in New York City, I would not bulldoze anything. I would not do a big urban-renewal program in underbuilt neighborhoods. There would not be eminent domain of brownstone Brooklyn.

What I would do is make it legal to voluntarily replace older/shorter buildings with taller more modern ones if the owner of the building wants to do that. If you applied a policy like that throughout the city, you’d expect a good number of parcels to get redeveloped. But you would not expect to see whole neighborhoods leveled. I don’t think we really know, ex ante, if a 5 percent or 10 percent increase in the New York City housing stock would satiate demand for living there or make demand to live there even more robust or what. But redevelopment would only continue as long as demand remained strong.

It has to be either that demand is satiated before there is wholesale redevelopment of the city or else that on balance people like the denser version of the city, which is why demand for even more housing remains robust.

Share

Oliver: If you were entirely in charge of candidate selection as happens in European parties, how would you select congressional candidates? Assuming you could use assessment centres, exams, auditions or any tool you liked.

The main thing is I would give significant weight to prior electoral performance. The Democratic Party would run House candidates who were electoral over-performers in the state legislature. It would nominate House over-performers for statewide races. In the short term this would lead to modestly stronger nominees (Angie Craig rather than Peggy Flanagan), but in the medium term it would dramatically shift the incentive structure toward trying to put up strong electoral performances.

Testname: In general, I would be curious to hear if you have any thoughts on the Jason Arday affair (which has taken over my feed for a month now)

I am trying to be a little more mindful about not dipping into over-covered stories where I don’t have anything particularly novel to add or points that nobody else is making.

This story is of interest to people, though, because it touches on the broader question of the politicization of academia and/or the increasing political pressure on academia from the right. I had the privilege to read Neil Gross’s book “What Happened To College?” in galleys and blurb it. It’s now out for sale and I’d really recommend it to anyone who’s interested in the topic. Per the title, this is really about the undergraduate experience rather than faculty or research dynamics. But the thing he shows is that there’s a very significant and largely grassroots political polarization happening on campus. The minority of undergrads with conservative views are increasingly self-sorting into schools they perceive to be conservative-friendly, while progressives engage in the opposite sorting. The most prestigious schools tend to attract students who are both more progressive and more politically engaged than average. And what’s really unfortunate is that he has evidence that a lot of what’s driving the sorting is negative affective polarization — in other words, strong dislike of coexisting with people who you have political disagreements with.

He also shows that this sorting exists not only between campuses but also on a micro-level within majors and clubs. To quote his recent op-ed, “Fraternities and sororities, campus faith-based organizations, pre-professional clubs, and even a cappella groups can all become gathering points for students with broadly similar political outlooks.”

One upshot of this is that prestigious schools with left-wing student populations face nontrivial bottom-up pressure to become more politicized. This is partially balanced in an ecosystem sense by counter-signaling from conservative schools. But there actually isn’t a lot of demand for what you might consider an ideal of an apolitical university.

Separate from Gross’s findings, it strikes me that when I dip in to see Professor Bluesky, a lot of very smart people capable of doing high-level analytic work seem to turn that part of their brain off. Suppose that 98 percent of faculty do an excellent job of maintaining high standards and ideological neutrality in their teaching and research 98 percent of the time. That’s pretty good! These are human institutions and it’s not reasonable to expect flawless judgment in hiring decisions or totally flawless conduct from the typical employee. But then if 98 percent of the deviations from best practices all happen in a leftward direction, that’s actually a massive systemic bias that is going to look really glaring to outsiders. Even among solid researchers working in fields with high standards, I constantly see papers that would be improved by dumping the text into a good L.L.M., asking what a smart Republican would say about this, and then rewriting to at least try to address those concerns. People implicitly write for an audience, and if your implicit audience has no right-of-center people in it, you wind up addressing yourself in a weird way.

Matt Foreman: Do you think Tucker Carlson has real ideological convictions and is trying to win the fight for a nationalist Republican Party, or is he just trying to sabotage the Republican Party for fun? In his convo with Saagar Enjeti, their horseshoe agreement with AES on Israel was predictable. What surprised me was Saagar praising Zohran for “good governance” in disavowing defund, bringing down crime, improving sanitation and investing in infrastructure, with Tucker nodding along. Why compliment your adversary on issues where your party supposedly has the upper hand (unless you are just a wrecker)?

I can’t read Carlson’s mind, but I think it’s true that Mamdani is a controversial figure primarily because of Israel. He’s left wing on cultural issues in a way that Carlson obviously isn’t going to approve of but also in a way that any mayor of New York City would be. When Rudy Giuliani was mayor, he was pro-choice, favored gay rights, and was strongly pro-immigration and favorable to gun control. Michael Bloomberg, Bill de Blasio, and Eric Adams were all left wing in these exact ways and Andrew Cuomo would have been too if he’d beaten Mamdani.

So if you sympathize with Mamdani on Israel, then you have a guy with normal-for-N.Y.C. views on a bunch of stuff that conservatives don’t like who also seems to be leading a successful ongoing decline in crime and may be trying to do some helpful deregulation for small business. Why not say nice things about him, especially if your project is to try to realign the G.O.P. on Israel?

Share

Sean O: How much does the choice of world map projections even matter? Can a map projection be racist and colonialist? And why is there this widespread belief that map projections are some grand, nefarious conspiracy?

It’s pretty clearly true that the Mercator projection gives people a misleading sense of the size of Africa and Greenland. Does this “matter”? Probably not. It’s hard to think of anything that’s taking place in the world that hinges on people’s gut intuitions about the size of Africa’s landmass. Anyone who is interested in geography has seen a globe. I don’t like reflexively calling everything racist or colonialist, and I think there was a lot of lazy content produced in this vein in the 2010s. But in a world where there is no canonically “correct” way to project a 3D Earth onto a 2D plane, the preference for one that makes Europe, the United States, Russia, and Canada look really large does seem plausibly influenced by colonial mentalities.

My eighth-grade geography class had a giant map on the wall with the south oriented up (I forget which projection it used) in order to deliberately disorient the students and remind us that mapping conventions are just conventions. I thought that was a useful pedagogical exercise. Of course, as a media professional I still present normal north-is-up maps because my goal when I present maps is to illustrate things clearly and not to disorient readers.

Joseph Lord-Lieutenant of ORD: Is the concept of a firewall against the far-right to keep it from ever governing still a workable idea? Secondly, given that in Germany the BSW agrees to govern with the AfD, does this serve to prove the horseshoe theory?

The German firewall policy does not make sense. I obviously don’t approve of AfD, the country’s far-right party, on a whole bunch of levels, but as an American the biggest problem here is that I really don’t want AfD suddenly taking over the federal government and radically reorienting German foreign policy in a pro-Russian direction.

At the same time, you can’t just wish AfD and its voters away. Fortunately, Germany has a federal system and normally has coalition governments. The healthiest development would have been to have some coalitions of AfD and C.D.U., the major center-right party, in the eastern states where AfD is stronger. There’s nothing Earth-shatteringly terrible that the junior partner in a coalition government in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern could accomplish. We have strong precedents from Finland, Denmark, and the Netherlands that giving far-right parties the opportunity to participate in coalition governments tends to take some of the anti-establishment sheen off them and induce splits inside the far-right movements. Of course, it doesn’t magically cause tough-on-crime or anti-immigration sentiment to vanish. But it does normalize the functioning of multi-party democracy, restore the normal tendency for the political pendulum to swing from left to right and back again, and avoid lurching around in crisis.

In Saxony-Anhalt there’s now a situation where AfD is going to be extremely empowered without ever having been tested by practical governing responsibility. I’m not really sure what to make of a potential coalition partnership between AfD and BSW, a left-populist party that could be the kingmaker. The two parties’ main points of alignment — anti-immigration and pro-Russian foreign policy — are really issues for the federal government, so, on its face, teaming up in a state government doesn’t make a lot of sense. But to an extent, these kinds of anti-system parties tend to be led by unprincipled adventurers who do weird stuff.

The Long Decline of America

It began decades before Trump

Paul Krugman
Sep 11
 
READ IN APP
 

When the twin towers fell, it seemed to many like a second Pearl Harbor — a day of infamy, but one that would bring the nation together. And if you believed that, the state of the nation today must seem utterly shocking.

But the truth is that the seeds of where we are now had already been planted well before 9/11. There was an initial façade of national unity, but the ruthless political — and financial — exploitation of the attack began almost immediately. I wrote about what was really happening in a November 2001 column titled “An Alternate Reality” Here’s how it began:

Most Americans get their news from TV. And what they see is heartwarming -- a picture of a nation behaving well in a time of crisis. Indeed, the vast majority of Americans have been both resolute and generous.

But that’s not the whole story, and the images TV doesn’t show are anything but heartwarming. A full picture would show politicians and businessmen behaving badly, with this bad behavior made possible -- and made worse -- by the fact that these days selfishness comes tightly wrapped in the flag. If you pay attention to the whole picture, you start to feel that you are living in a different reality from the one on TV.

You can read the rest at the link. The past two years have been worse than almost anyone could have imagined, but the truth is that we were already well on the road to this MAGA nightmare on the day the towers fell.

It hasn’t been an inexorable downward spiral. The election of our first Black president really was a significant moment — the truth is that while there are plenty of haters, overall we are a better, more tolerant society than we were in 2001. The expansion of healthcare under Obama wasn’t just good policy, it represented real moral progress. Although there has been a concerted effort to smear the policymakers who responded to Covid, the truth is that we managed the economic fallout from that crisis very well, and the rapid development of a vaccine was a scientific and medical miracle.

But the evil now running wild in America didn’t begin when Trump descended that escalator. It has been building for decades.

We’re still underrating 9/11’s impact

Flukey events and eccentric decisions changed the world for the worse forever.

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 11
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

It was an incredibly bright and clear East Coast morning on September 11, 2001. I’ve always been an early riser, so even as a college student, I was awake and at breakfast when I heard a plane had hit the World Trade Center.

As for the rest of that morning, I don’t totally trust my own memory. But I do want to emphasize that quite a lot of us did literally watch thousands of people die on live television as the towers collapsed. And those who didn’t see it live saw it replayed endlessly in the hours and days that followed.

Hamas Factory Team
@420stonerman69
Millennials love pretending there were isolated shots of people jumping out of windows on live broadcasts of 9/11 and they could totally see that on the 21” CRT TV wheeled into their classroom. Most probably didn’t even have a TV in the classroom and are conflating memories.
Olivia Hofer @oghofer
It was a pretty big deal to watch people jump out of 90th story windows and plummet to their deaths on the sidewalk on live TV when I was in kindergarten, yeah.
8:49 AM · Sep 6, 2026 · 724K Views
499 Replies · 10 Reposts · 72 Likes

I don’t think anyone who didn’t experience 9/11 as an adult can fully understand how confusing that day was.

First it was one plane, then it was two. The first plane could’ve been an accident, but a second clearly wasn’t. The Pentagon was hit, but there were also false alarms about fires at the State Department and on the National Mall. The Capitol building was hastily evacuated. It was widely suspected early on that al-Qaeda was responsible, but of course nobody knew that for sure. So we were watching, and it was horrible.

And for all we knew, more buildings were about to blow up. A few weeks later, there was an anthrax scare at M.I.T. and an anonymous threat at the Harvard campus libraries. Researchers find that there was a pronounced increase in vacancy rates at the three most iconic office buildings in Chicago because people feared other landmark buildings would be attacked. It was a crazy, panicky time.

A few days after the attack, George W. Bush went to an Islamic center to reassure the country that Islam is a religion of peace and to try to tamp down on an incipient wave of hate crimes, many of which were mistakenly directed at Sikhs.

But while Bush displayed statesmanship and steady leadership on this front, his administration also moved the country helter-skelter into a war in Afghanistan that failed in its main objectives and into a war in Iraq that had nothing to do with the attack.

Critics are often reluctant to admit it now, but these were overwhelmingly popular moves at the time. Invading Iraq had 70 percent approval in March and April of 2003. Which of course doesn’t mean that a “let’s invade Iraq” sentiment spontaneously materialized in the minds of hundreds of millions of people as a result of what we saw on television two years before.

But it was an emotionally distressing time, and the range of possible outcomes was extremely wide.

If Bush had wanted to whip people up into an inward-looking demagogic fervor instead of an external-facing one, he clearly could have accomplished that, too. War on Terror 1 was crazy, and people were prepared to be led in all kinds of directions.

It’s on some levels obvious that we are all very much living in a world that Osama bin Laden made. But on others I think it’s still somewhat underrated how deeply contingent everything was.

An avoidable event

I think appreciation of the contingency starts with observing that the whole idea of hijacking airplanes in order to destroy the World Trade Center is eccentric.

We know Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, named as “the principal architect of the 9/11 attacks” by the official 9/11 Commission Report, is also believed by American intelligence to have been involved in the earlier 1993 effort to destroy the World Trade Center (that time with a truck bomb). So given our knowledge at the time that a group of violent Islamists thought destroying the World Trade Center was a good idea, the emergence of a new plot to do it was fairly predictable. But the details are still pretty weird.

Even if you see the rise of these kinds of jihadist movements as baked into the cake, orchestrating spectacular attacks on American civilians is not an obvious move.

I think that line of thinking gets occluded a little by right-wing types talking about a clash of civilizations and by people on the left talking about terrorism as “blowback” for America’s foreign policy sins. But Latin American leftists, who have a much more deeply entrenched beef with the U.S. government, have never done anything remotely like 9/11. And even though violent Islamist groups are very much still with us in the world, they seem to have largely abandoned this particular tactic. Part of how the Taliban came back to power in Afghanistan was that they credibly convinced the Trump and Biden administrations that they were no longer interested in hosting trans-national terrorist organizations.

And even in retrospect, the relationship between knocking down the towers and Osama bin Laden’s ideological goals is a little hard to parse. He was angry about America’s military presence in Saudi Arabia and our support for “apostate” regimes and Israel. But obviously the political reaction in the United States wasn’t to become less involved in the Middle East or just say, “Well, I guess we should let the people who did the terrorism take over the whole region like they want.”

In other places, he says his goal was to drag the United States into an endless unwinnable war in Afghanistan and bleed us dry economically. That kind of worked, but America is really rich, so it didn’t actually work.

The biggest win for al-Qaeda that resulted from 9/11 is that the invasion of Iraq created a huge new opening for Sunni jihadist operations in the western part of the country and contributed to destabilizing Syria, which created even more new opportunities. In the end, of course, ISIS was defeated and Syria’s al-Qaeda offshoot, like the Taliban itself, gained power in part by disavowing international terrorism.

There’s even more contingency in the fact that it’s easy to imagine worlds in which the attack was stopped.

The Afghan anti-Taliban commander Ahmad Shah Massoud tried to warn American leaders about a spectacular al-Qaeda plot. When Massoud was killed by suicide bombers on September 9, Vladimir Putin called George W. Bush with a similar warning. Zacarias Moussaoui, who likely planned to participate in 9/11, was already in custody, but the F.B.I. couldn’t get a warrant to search his computer. The C.I.A. was aware that Khalid al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi were terrorists, but they were allowed into the country — in al-Mihdhar’s case, multiple times. By August of 2001, the F.B.I. had decided they should actually find these guys, but according to the Justice Department Inspector General’s office, “even in August, the F.B.I.’s search for Mihdhar and Hazmi was not given any urgency or priority, and was not close to locating them by the time of the attacks.” Attorney General John Ashcroft issued a priorities memo earlier in 2001 that did not include any counterterrorism objectives.

I don’t want to exaggerate how easy it would have been to unravel the plot. Massoud was obviously a self-interested party in trying to get America to take this more seriously. Putin’s call was too late to do anything about it. It’s not obvious that a different priorities memo would have led to a more intensive August manhunt.

But certainly the attack could have been prevented.

It wasn’t a black swan event or the work of true geniuses who evaded America’s best efforts. The Bush administration’s response — and especially its decision to frame the problem in grandiose ideological terms — functioned in part to direct focus away from the banal law enforcement, intelligence, and border security failures. And the 1993 precedent shows that even though trying and failing to murder thousands of people is just as immoral as succeeding, the emotional response of the public to the failed attack was wildly different and the intellectual and political response in turn was extremely muted. A foiled 9/11 would have generated some kind of policy response, but not nearly the one we got.

A stack of contingencies

One reason I think today we should be skeptical that bin Laden got exactly the response he wanted out of the United States is that he could not have forecast George W. Bush’s response when the planning began before Bush was even elected. That race, which was razor thin and ended up hinging on factors as trivial as the design of the Palm Beach County ballot, was incredibly contingent.

I don’t really know how an Al Gore administration would have responded to 9/11. I doubt that Republicans and right-wing media would have been as kind to Gore in the wake of an attack as Democrats and the mainstream press were to Bush. I also think it’s possible that with Clinton-Gore continuity and without the early Bush-era decision to downplay terrorism as a priority, the attacks actually would have been foiled. But I’m very sure a Gore administration would not have responded in the precise way that Bush did.

One reason for that is that Bush’s own response was hard to predict based on the information available about him before the attack.

Foreign policy wasn’t a big issue during the 2000 presidential campaign, but to the extent that it came up, the main argument was that Bush accused the Clinton-Gore administration of overstretching American forces with too many nation-building initiatives. Bush’s father’s administration was characterized by realpolitik, interest in multilateralism and a “new world order,” moderate skepticism of the U.S.-Israel alliance, and a lot of interest in courting Arab public opinion. When I was an intern in the very pro-Israel Chuck Schumer’s office in the summer of 2001, we at one point sent out a press release that had something to do with Bush’s efforts to weaken the Iran-Libya Sanctions Act.

James Mann’s 2004 book, “Rise of the Vulcans: The History of Bush’s War Cabinet,” explains with the benefit of hindsight how the administration’s foreign policy turned out the way it did. But this was not how most knowledgeable observers saw this team when they were initially appointed.

More than anything, though, the circumstances of 9/11 created an unusual political situation.

Not only did Bush immediately become super-popular, but trust in the federal government soared, temporarily reversing the secular increase in cynicism that’s been happening since Watergate and the decline of the three-network news oligopoly. This provided Bush with a very unusual lack of political constraint. His presidency also occurred at a time after the fall of the Soviet Union but before China had risen as anything more than a regional power. No country is ever unconstrained in the international arena, but America was less constrained in 2001 than at almost any time in our history. These were the historical and political circumstances under which Bush was able to do some very good things like sell congressional Republicans on funding PEPFAR, which fights AIDS.

It meant that he had the opportunity to become a truly great president in a way that Bill Clinton and Barack Obama weren’t because they governed under much more cramped circumstances.

But … he wasn’t.

The consequences of the bad choices Bush made have been immense, not just in terms of their immediate human impact (though of course that matters a lot), but also in the collateral damage to vague notions of “the establishment” and to the good things that Bush stood for, like a Christian commitment to the brotherhood of all humanity and a belief that America should stand on high-minded principles.

Yet I really don’t believe there was anything inevitable about Bush making the choices he made, and certainly there was nothing inevitable about linking those ideals to the specifics of an extremely half-baked invasion of Iraq. Everything about that awful day and what followed was wildly contingent and hinged on the will of a handful of people.

Get the Middle East out of my politics!

A manifesto.

Noah Smith
Sep 12
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

The other day I saw a Harvard Harris poll on the favorability of various political figures in the U.S. Only RFK Jr. (sigh), Marco Rubio, and Mark Carney had net positive approval ratings:

While I understand that these polls all have methodological issues, I was struck by how three figures — Abdul El-Sayed, Zohran Mamdani, and Benjamin Netanyahu — had net approval ratings below almost any American politician. While Mamdani’s low rating might be partially due to his leftist policies and his association with the DSA, it struck me that all three of these unpopular figures had one thing in common — they are associated with the intrusion of Middle Eastern politics into American politics. And I thought: Maybe Americans just want to have nothing to do with the Middle East.

Today¹ is September 11, the anniversary of the terror attacks 25 years ago. Though I don’t agree with the leftist line that those attacks were blowback from American involvement in the Middle East, it’s unquestionable that 9/11 inaugurated an era of heavy U.S. involvement in that area of the world — the Iraq War, the follow-up war against ISIS, the War on Terror, greater support for Israel, an increased military presence in the region, and finally the war against Iran.

I don’t believe that all of that involvement was a bad idea — in particular, as I’ll argue, the War on Terror, including the fight against ISIS, was generally successful and necessary. But overall, the era of heavy U.S. involvement in the Middle East has been a disaster for U.S. power and prestige, and it’s time for that era to end.

This is not a recent conversion on my part; I’ve been in favor of general disengagement from the Middle East for a very long time. Five years ago, in the early days of the Noahpinion Substack, I wrote a post called “How to fix U.S. foreign policy”:

How to fix U.S. foreign policy

Noah Smith
·
February 27, 2021
Read full story

In that post, I wrote:

[D]espite modest progress, we still remain too tied up in Middle Eastern conflicts…The U.S. will never be able to ignore the Middle East entirely, but we can remove ourselves much more than we’ve done…[W]e need to draw down engagement in the Middle East, and increase engagement in Asia.

Since then, things have gone from bad to worse, making my message far more urgent than it was at the time. Most obviously, there’s Trump’s disastrous war in Iran, which continues to waste U.S. military resources and make the U.S. look weak while failing to accomplish any significant objective. Recent polls show that a very strong majority of Americans think that the Iran War is not worth fighting.

There’s also Israel’s intensified campaign against the Palestinians. This has become the rallying cry of the American left, which has prompted a backlash and crackdown by the Trump administration. As a result of that conflict, Middle Eastern politics is increasingly becoming the focus of American domestic politics.

The controversy around Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, for example, has nothing to do with his policy stances, or even American culture wars — it’s entirely about his stance on Israel/Palestine and his ally Hasan Piker’s comments making excuses for 9/11 and Islamic terrorism. El-Sayed recently apologized for tying a synagogue shooting to Israeli warfare in the Middle East.

Many analysts believe that Zohran Mamdani, meanwhile, won the NYC mayorship primarily because of his outspoken stances on Israel/Palestine. And more is on the way. Organizations like CAIR Action that are linked to the Muslim Brotherhood — a sort of international equivalent of the Christian Coalition, but for Islam — are now supporting political candidates throughout the U.S., using the Palestine issue to recruit candidates and win votes. Muslim Brotherhood figures are cheering this effort on from overseas. AIPAC and other Israel-supporting groups, meanwhile, are pouring money into races in order to stop those candidates.

Our media, too, is increasingly filling up with the Middle East’s cultural and religious conflicts. Leftist shouters like Hasan Piker, Mehdi Hasan, and Cenk Uygur constantly urge progressives to base their politics around Palestine. Every day, Americans are bombarded with rhetoric like this:

This is simply bad for America. We have so many pressing issues to worry about — Trump’s corruption and authoritarianism, inflation, AI, etc. We should not be nominating Democratic politicians based on whether they support Israel or Palestine; we should be nominating them based on their stances on issues of direct relevance to Americans, and on their ability to oppose Donald Trump. Furthermore, mobilizing Muslim and Jewish voters to vote based on Israel/Palestine, rather than on issues of importance to Americans in general, provides fuel for rightist attacks on both groups.

What the United States needs, now more than ever, is general disengagement from the Middle East — an end to military adventures, a dialing back of support for Middle Eastern “allies” (including Israel), and a forceful rejection of Middle Eastern issues in American domestic politics.

Fortunately, conditions in the world have shifted. The kind of disengagement I’m calling for is a lot more feasible than it was twenty or even ten years ago. The Iran War has shown that Middle Eastern oil is a lot less important for the global economy than it used to be. And the success of the War on Terror and the general decline of Islamism reduce the necessity for further interventions.

The U.S. doesn’t need to protect Middle Eastern oil supplies anymore

For many decades, the main justification for U.S. intervention in the Middle East has been to keep oil prices low and stable. The Middle East is one of the world’s largest oil producers, and its low extraction costs mean it functions as the world’s “swing producer”. Supply disruptions from the region can cause global price spikes, endangering industrialized economies that depend on petroleum. Oil was a big reason the U.S. intervened to stop Saddam Hussein’s invasion of Kuwait in the early 90s, for example.

Obviously, oil is still a very important commodity. But it’s a lot less important to the U.S. than it used to be. Here’s what I wrote when the Iran War began:

Blanchard and Gali (2007) looked at economic responses to changes in oil prices in the U.S., and concluded that the economy of the 2000s was only about a third to half as sensitive to the price of oil as the economy of the 1970s had been. Their reasoning is that modern economies are more flexible in general, that they have better monetary policy (i.e. we don’t try to print a ton of money in response to a supply shock), and that we depend on oil less.

By their estimates, a 10% increase in the price of oil now (or at least, if “the 2000s” means “now”) leads to only a 0.25 percentage point increase in the CPI and a 0.3 percentage point reduction in GDP over the course of a year or so. Since oil just spiked by 50%, then if that’s sustained, we might expect to see inflation go up by 1.25 percentage points, and GDP go down by 1.5 percentage points over the next year. That would mean inflation would go to around 4% and GDP growth might go down to 1.5% — frustrating and annoying, but not catastrophic…Other estimates seem similarly modest. For example, in a recent roundup, I flagged a paper by Känzig and Raghavan (2025) that looked at the closure of key shipping chokepoints.

In addition to having a more flexible economy, better energy efficiency, and more reasonable monetary policy, the U.S. is now a net oil exporter. That means when oil prices go up, the benefit to the energy sector cancels out at least part of the harm to other sectors of the economy.

But on top of all that, the fact is that the Iran War simply hasn’t raised oil prices that much! Despite Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and Trump’s retaliatory blockade of Iranian oil shipments, oil prices haven’t even reattained their highs from the early 2010s:

And in real terms, the spike is even less impressive. If we divide oil prices by average hourly earnings for production and nonsupervisory workers — basically, how many hours an average American worker would have to work in order to afford a barrel of oil — we see that prices really aren’t that high at all:

No wonder the U.S. economy is still doing fine, and inflation has only risen a little bit (and some of that may be due to demand from the data center boom).

Nor does the U.S. have to worry about oil cutoffs in the long term, if it disengages from the Middle East. Yes, in the 1970s, OPEC injured the global economy with its embargo. But the cartel’s power was broken in the 1980s and never recovered. In a world of globalized oil supply, Middle Eastern countries simply need to keep selling their oil to survive. And if Iran cuts off the Strait of Hormuz in the long term and raises global oil prices, it will arouse the ire of China, its main patron and customer.

Actually, China gives us one more reason to be less concerned about Middle Eastern oil supplies over the long term. China is racing to become less dependent on oil by adopting electric vehicles en masse, which is causing its petroleum usage to plummet:

In fact, falling Chinese demand is a big reason global oil prices haven’t risen more in response to the Iran War. China’s drive to reduce oil use isn’t going to change, which will put downward pressure on oil prices for everyone else as well. And China’s exports of electric vehicles will cut petroleum use all over the world.

Thus, economically, the Middle East is already not nearly as relevant as it used to be, and it’s going to become a lot less relevant in the years to come. The 1970s taught America that we needed to maintain a robust presence in the region in order to keep the oil flowing; half a century later, that’s simply no longer the case.

The War on Terror was successful (and now we can go home)

When the War on Terror started after 9/11, a lot of people assumed it would be a losing proposition — that the more America went after jihadists abroad, the more they would multiply. Calling it a “forever war” was very common. And yet when we look at the results a quarter century later, it’s very hard to avoid the conclusion that the U.S. won the War on Terror, and that radical Islamism is on the wane.

The clearest fact is that the two main organizations that prosecuted the War on Terror from the Islamist side — Al Qaeda and the Islamic State — have been effectively defeated. Al Qaeda’s leadership, including everyone involved in the planning and execution of the 9/11 attacks, has all been captured or killed. The Islamic State was defeated on the battlefield, and its territory wiped off the map.

Both organizations survive only as brands — names that a few hundred random local jihadists can claim to be affiliated with in lawless backwaters like the Sahel. The U.S. and its allies will continue to hunt these down, but much like the smattering of communist guerrilla movements that persisted around the world after the end of the Cold War, they lack the ability to do any real damage.

Perhaps the clearest way to see the victory in the War on Terror is to look at the plunging number of terrorist plots and attacks around the world. Here’s an estimate, which makes it clear that the battle against the Islamic State was actually the peak of the conflict:

And here’s a dataset from CSIS that includes plots and threats as well as attacks:

I’ve been talking about this victory as if it were America’s alone, but I really shouldn’t. Most of the fighting was actually done by people in the Middle East, South and Southeast Asia, Africa, and so on — regular, normal folks who adhere to the Muslim faith but wanted no part of what the Islamists were selling, and were willing to put their lives on the line. Here’s what I wrote in 2021:

Remember how in the wake of 9/11, commentators used to always demand that moderate Muslims condemn jihadists? Well, folks, they did one better — they shot the jihadists.

In the U.S., too, sympathy for Islamic radicalism is dying. Charles Kurzman of UNC Chapel Hill has kept tabs on reports of Muslim American involvement with extremism. There was a wave of verbal support for Islamism after 9/11, and a wave of violent attacks in the mid-2010s, though neither wave was very large at all. Then the waves died down, and jihadist activity in America basically vanished:

Europe is seeing the same pattern — the big deadly attacks were all in the mid-2010s, at the same time as the conflict with the Islamic State. There remains a smattering of low-level, low-casualty attacks — perhaps about a dozen a year throughout the EU, with annual deaths in the single digits.

Many European societies are currently experiencing anxiety about their ability to absorb large numbers of Muslim immigrants, but that’s very different from the kind of threat posed by Islamic State and Al Qaeda. In particular, it doesn’t require any sort of involvement in the Middle East — in fact, the people experiencing the anxiety over Muslim immigration would probably also want to have less to do with that region of the world.

In other words, there’s little reason for the U.S. to maintain a high level of involvement in the Middle East in order to thwart Islamism. The war has been won, and what remains is low-level monitoring and clean-up. That can be accomplished with low-key coordination between intelligence services, rather than with military bases, invasions, and so on.

America’s “alliance” with Israel has outlived its usefulness

Beyond oil and Islamism, the other reason often given for continued American involvement in the Middle East is to help our ally, Israel. Israel is not a treaty ally of the United States, like Turkey or Japan; we are not obligated to come to its defense, or vice versa. The U.S. has unilaterally designated Israel to be a “Major Non-NATO Ally”, but that’s simply an indicator of our attitude toward the country, not any kind of a pact or treaty. Israel is an “ally” only because we choose to regard it as such.

But is this attitudinal alliance still worth what we’re paying for it? I have my doubts. First of all, there’s the matter of Israel’s obvious human rights abuses. Americans used to consistently sympathize much more with Israel than with the Palestinians, but this has recently reversed:

Some part of this is undoubtedly due to the leftist movement, and their relentless — and often dishonest — campaign of anti-Israel agitation. America’s progressive media is clearly biased against Israel to some degree. But Israel isn’t just losing the war of public opinion because their opponents are better at lying. Americans simply can’t ignore the country’s human rights abuses any longer.

Forget about the war in Gaza for a moment, and consider the situation in the West Bank. Israel keeps large numbers of the Palestinians in the West Bank stateless; these people are citizens of nowhere. The Palestinian Authority administers much of the day-to-day business of governance in the Palestinian parts of the West Bank, but Israel actually rules; all real power in the territory is held by the Israeli military.

That by itself should be considered a crime, but it gets worse. The West Bank Palestinians are denied freedom of movement — kept penned into their villages and cities, often unable to move around to other parts of the West Bank. Much of the territory is held by Israeli settlers — Israeli citizens who have the (sometimes explicit, sometimes tacit) support of the Israeli military occupation. These settlers commit frequent, sporadic acts of violence and theft against the stateless Palestinians in the territory — basically, pogroms — and often receive protection from any retaliation by the Israeli military.

This state of affairs has been likened to apartheid, and honestly the metaphor is apt. It’s a slow campaign of conquest, land theft, and racialized and religious violence against a people who have been forcibly denied a place in the community of nations. It’s not quite as brutal as what Russia is doing in the occupied territories of Ukraine, but it’s in the same general vein.

Why would the United States of America want to associate itself with that sort of villainy? Why would we give almost $7 billion a year — more than we give to any other country, more even than we give to Ukraine — to a nation that carries out campaigns of mass dispossession and conquest like the one Israel is executing in the West Bank? I realize that America is no longer a champion of human rights under Donald Trump, but the American people can still tell when they’re being asked to support crimes against humanity. (And note that I didn’t even deal with Gaza at all; I don’t have to even mention it in order to make my point.)

In addition to Israel’s human rights abuses, there’s the question of what, exactly, the U.S. is getting out of this alliance. Granted, Israel’s failure to offer aid in Afghanistan or Iraq wasn’t its fault — the U.S. asked it not to get involved, so as to avoid adding a religious aspect to those conflicts. But the only reason Israel refused to help Ukraine was out of fear of alienating Vladimir Putin, with whom Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been friendly for many years. Nor has Israel helped the U.S. prepare for a Chinese onslaught in Asia.

In the Middle East, it’s now mostly America who does the helping. Netanyahu reportedly helped persuade Trump to attack Iran — a course of action that has been distinctly to America’s detriment. Leftists have been accusing America of conducting wars in the Middle East at Israel’s behest for decades, but this time, it looks like it might sort of be true. Trump undoubtedly had his own reasons for wanting to attack Iran, but the fact that Israel’s leader seemingly goaded him into taking the plunge should make the U.S. much more skeptical of its relationship with that country.

Essentially the only thing Israel might have to offer the U.S. — other than some defense technologies that we can almost certainly replicate ourselves — is the promise of cooperation to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. Prior to the current war, that argument held some water. But months of joint action by Israel and the U.S. have failed to cripple Iran’s nuclear program. So it’s unclear how much help Israel is even capable of offering in this regard. If the U.S. is going to prevent Iran from getting nukes, it isn’t going to do it via joint Israel-U.S. bombing campaigns.

An ally that refuses to help you with your biggest challenges, but which goads you into engaging in risky, ill-advised conflicts on its behalf, all while committing large-scale human rights abuses with impunity, is simply not a very good ally. So it seems like it’s time for the U.S. to pause or dial back its close relationship with Israel.

What does that mean? Most obviously, it means cancellation of foreign aid to Israel — money that is invariably used to maintain the intolerable situation in the West Bank. It also means removing Israel’s designation as a “major non-NATO ally.” The aid and ally status can be restored if Israel ever stops its campaign of dispossession and violence in the West Bank and agrees to support U.S. interests in Europe and Asia.

That does not mean I think the U.S. should reorganize its foreign policy around opposition to Israel, as the leftists would have us do. Israel’s enemies — Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran — are even more savage than Israel is. Hamas would absolutely commit genocide on the Israelis, given the chance. Leftists like Hasan Piker and Mehdi Hasan who urge us to think of Hamas as the lesser of two evils simply want us to switch our support for one brutal Middle Eastern regime to an even more brutal one.

Instead, what we need to do is to reduce American involvement in Israel’s conflicts with its neighbors. If there aren’t pressing national interests that can be served by throwing our support to one side or another, and if supporting either side requires endorsing human rights abuses, then the right answer is just to be less involved.

The Middle East will be fine without us, and vice versa

All of this might make it seem like I dislike the Middle East, or view it with disgust. On the contrary, I think the Middle East has a bright future ahead:

Why I'm long-term bullish on the Middle East

Noah Smith
·
January 18, 2025
Read full story

What I think is that the Middle East had some problems that caused it to lag behind some other regions in terms of political and economic development. Over-reliance on oil inhibited industrialization, while Islam was slow to recognize the importance of the separation of church and state.

But I believe the region is in the process of starting to overcome those initial conditions. The constant series of quasi-religious wars that has engulfed the region over the last few decades is reminiscent of Europe’s Wars of Religion and Thirty Years’ War in the 16th and 17th centuries. Eventually, Europeans tired of fighting over God, and Middle Easterners will as well.

In fact, it’s already happening in some places. After over a decade of horrifically destructive sectarian civil war, Syria is slowly rebuilding itself under a moderate government (despite the occasional Israeli airstrike). Middle Easterners are, for the most part, not religious fanatics who want nothing more than to die for Allah; they are regular people who want to buy bread at the store and have a roof over their heads and go to work and raise their children in peace.

Meanwhile, the region’s economic future is more promising than people realize. Solar power will allow it to remain an energy powerhouse even as the world shifts away from oil. Permissive land-use policies will allow it to build data centers when other countries block them. Falling fertility has primed most Middle Eastern countries for a demographic dividend that will boost growth, even as Europe and Asia age rapidly.

The best thing the U.S. can do to further this process along is not to interfere with it. The Middle Easterners — Israel, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Egypt, UAE, and all the rest — have to simply realize that eternal war isn’t doing them any good, and then work out a regional architecture for security and economic cooperation among themselves. Military interventions by distant powers will only delay that maturation process.

Meanwhile, U.S. politics will be healthier if we can ignore the activists and demagogues who constantly harangue us about the Middle East. Right now, with Trump executing his doomed misadventure in Iran, and American aid supporting Israel’s campaign of conquest in the West Bank, it’s very hard for anyone in American politics to avoid constant debates and discussions about the Middle East. Making it easier to avoid those debates and discussions should be a conscious goal of our politics and our policy. It’s time for America’s Middle Eastern era to end.
