But here’s where I think I need to try to explain American politics to tech industry workers.

I would like to avoid labeling Anthropic the “good guys” of the A.I. industry and their rivals the bad guys. That’s wildly oversimplified in both directions.

What is true, though, is that as a matter of engagement with American electoral politics, there is a big difference. When Donald Trump apparently entertained the idea of doing something meaningful in terms of federal regulation, Mark Zuckerberg called him up to talk him out of it. If you’re working at Meta and feel concerned about A.I. safety, I think you have an obligation to take collective action with your fellow concerned colleagues and ask your C.E.O. to stop doing this, and if he won’t, you have to walk.

More insidiously, OpenAI’s official position in its communications to its employees is that OpenAI is not behind the anti-regulation super PAC Leading the Future.

But nobody working professionally in American politics believes this.

Leading the Future is funded in large part by OpenAI’s President Greg Brockman and his wife. It was conceptualized, by all accounts, by Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer. I should say that while I don’t by any means know Lehane well, he’s a veteran of the moderate Dem political space and I broadly like him and approve of his work.

Unfortunately, his expertise in helping tech companies win regulatory fights in blue states — an endeavor I normally support — is in this particular case gravely endangering humanity.

Leading the Future has dumped huge amounts of money into primaries to try to defeat candidates who advocate for A.I. safety regulation. More than that, though, it’s trying to chill the whole topic. It exists not so much to spend money in the midterms as to convey to Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer something like “nice anti-Trump thermostatic backlash you’ve got there … would be a shame if hundreds of millions of dollars came off the sidelines to be used against all your frontliners because party leaders embraced A.I. safety.”

So, again, if you work at OpenAI and believe that collective action is needed to address this problem, you have to understand that your company’s executives are massive stumbling blocks. Putting out fake statements distancing the company from Leading the Future is worse than doing nothing. You and your colleagues need to work together to demand that the company cease and desist from this effort to chill federal regulation. If the company won’t do it, you need to walk.

By contrast, while I would never in a million years say that Anthropic’s conduct as a company is beyond reproach or above suspicion — that’s the whole reason we need actual regulation here and not just to root for the “good guys” to win the race — their political conduct is consistent with the view that collective action is desirable.

What is to be done?

Regulating the A.I. industry — which is to say slowing down the race to make sure that we learn more about advanced A.I. before we create an A.I. powerful enough to automate its own improvement and end up in a situation where humans have genuinely no understanding of what’s going on — is a difficult problem. Difficult not just in the sense that it’s hard to defeat the vested interests at play, but genuinely difficult on the merits.

I think a huge failure mode for progressive politics is looking at a difficult problem like climate change that can only be addressed through a mix of hard international coordination problems and hard technical problems, only to decide that it’s really just a political question of beating the fossil fuel industry. It’s not. Making airplanes fly without burning jet fuel or finding cost-effective zero-emissions ways to manufacture cement or conduct the Haber-Bosch process are genuinely difficult technical problems.

By the same token, with A.I. we need to take the complexities seriously. But this shouldn’t mean paralysis.

I think the right order of operations is something like:

  1. For American frontier companies, start with relatively light-touch rules focused on things like transparency and model evaluation. [Between when I wrote this draft and its publication, Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, and Sam Altman all came out in favor of this.]

  2. The rules in (1) are bad for American companies, but in exchange for accepting them we can help those companies by imposing stricter export controls on chips (especially those headed to China) and taking action against Chinese “distillation” — using American models to train theirs.

  3. Because (2) should really slow down Chinese development and increase America’s lead, we can then afford to tighten the screws and slow the rate of American frontier development.

  4. Having acted credibly against our own industry in (1) and (3), we can go to China with arms control proposals that could be mutually beneficial.

  5. Then, and only then, with (4) in place, we can really try to impose an ambitious end-stage regulatory framework.

This is all incredibly challenging and moderately unlikely.

In particular, even if you could achieve steps (1), (2), and (3), which would already be hard, it all might totally fall apart at (4). I’ve heard different things about the attitudes of Chinese leaders and industry figures to this whole question, and it’s impossible to know for sure. But it’s sure worth trying!

Subscribed

So in summary, congratulations to Jacob Coxon for getting the world’s attention. Unfortunately, responsible technologists quitting their jobs unilaterally is unlikely to actually solve the problem.

But if responsible technologists at Meta and OpenAI and other companies that lobby against regulation work together — which might include quitting — that could greatly contribute to solving the problem. And Congress should be holding hearings where concerned employees can explain their fears and working toward bipartisan legislation on domestic regulation, on distillation, and on chips. President Trump should worry less about the short-term economic impact of any of this (if short-term economic issues are the concern, focus on ending the war with Iran) and deploy his knack for knowing when to reject intense right-wing policy demands and just give the people what they want.

In this case, I think that’s some kind of assurance that this industry will not be allowed to transform the world in a totally unaccountable way.

The MAGA Plot(s) to Destroy Humanity

On AI and climate, it’s the same story of mass destruction

Paul Krugman
Sep 14
 
READ IN APP
 

Will AI lead to the destruction of humanity? Over the past year a number of top AI researchers have warned that AI was quickly attaining the capacity to wipe out humankind.

These warnings aren’t entirely new. At first, however, Anthropic was virtually alone among the top LLM companies in highlighting the dangers that unregulated AI poses. And in return for its conscientious objection to allowing its models to be used for AI-agentic warfare – a clear means of humanicide – Hegseth’s Pentagon tried to retaliate by designating the company as a security risk. Fortunately, a judge saw through this ploy.

Still, until very recently other AI companies — in particular Elon Musk’s Grok and ChatGPT — were willing to dance to the Trump administration’s tune to get a competitive advantage Currently, Grok is used by the U.S. military to assist targeting in Iran – a clear pre-cursor to situation in which the machines, not humans, decide who is the target.

But now, quite suddenly, Musk and ChatGPT’s CEO Sam Altman are falling in behind the call by Daron Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, to acknowledge the existential dangers of AI and to put on the brakes. Notably, Amodei explicitly calls for government regulation if other AI companies refuse to cooperate:

The most effective method of pacing is via regulation that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily.

Regardless of why Musk and Altman are having a sudden attack of conscience, I applaud their new position. As many people think, perhaps this was due to the Hugging Face hack by rogue ChatGPT AI-agents. But I also think Musk and Altman’s volte-face was influenced by the changing political environment, with the near-certainty that Democrats will take the House and a very good chance that they will take the Senate.

For in a real sense, Amodei isn’t just trying to protect humanity from rogue AI, he is also trying to protect humanity from Donald Trump. It’s important to remember that, under the Biden administration, government policymakers tried to formulate some basic AI precautions. But removing those precautions was literally one of the first things Donald Trump did when taking office the second time. And that’s a history worth revisiting at a moment when the AI industry itself is sounding the alarm, but Trump is dismissing the risks:

You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen.

Well, I’m glad to know that he’s sure that bad things won’t happen. But last I heard, Trump wasn’t a technology expert. And his recent record on rosy predictions — wasn’t the Iran war supposed to be over in a few days? — hasn’t been great.

In any case, here’s the history you should know.

The current age of AI is often considered to have begun with the public release of ChatGPT on Nov. 30, 2022. However, the potential economic and social implications of large language models were already becoming apparent during the first year of the Biden administration, which began implementing a series of rules and executive orders intended to limit the potential damage from the technology. The Economic Policy Institute maintains a comprehensive list of these actions.

The centerpiece of the Biden agenda on AI was Executive Order 14401, issued on October 30, 2023, titled “Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence.” The document declared that

Harnessing AI for good and realizing its myriad benefits requires mitigating its substantial risks. This endeavor demands a society-wide effort that includes government, the private sector, academia, and civil society.

Would we be less panicked now if there had been a serious effort to put that executive order’s recommendations into effect? It’s basically impossible to say, because precautionary policy toward AI never got a chance. Trump revoked Executive Order 14401 on Jan. 20, 2025. Yes, you read that right: He literally removed all safeguards on AI on his first day in office.

Just three days later his administration issued a new executive order, “Removing barriers to American leadership in artificial intelligence,” which might be summarized as “Damn the social and existential risks, full speed ahead.”

Some of this determination not to limit the risks from AI reflected industry influence. A week before Trump took office, NVIDIA combined an appeal for deregulation with slavish praise for the incoming administration:

The first Trump Administration laid the foundation for America’s current strength and success in AI, fostering an environment where U.S. industry could compete and win on merit without compromising national security.

But there was also a social aspect to Trump’s anti-regulation stance. You won’t be surprised to hear that hostility to DEI was right at the heart of the agenda. Literally the second sentence of the order declares that

we must develop AI systems that are free from ideological bias or engineered social agendas.

I think this was a thinly veiled plug for Grok, which by all accounts is vastly inferior to offerings from Anthropic and OpenAI but which Elon Musk has tried to sell in part because it supposedly isn’t “woke.”

In any case, Trump’s dismissal of the risks from AI, even at a time when experts and industry insiders are in hair-on-fire mode, is simply a continuation of the position he has taken from the beginning.

It is also, not coincidentally, completely consistent with his attitude toward the other existential threat facing humanity — a threat that isn’t at all hypothetical and is rapidly becoming acute.

The contiguous United States has just experienced its hottest summer on record, with July the hottest month ever. Across the Atlantic, Europe has been ravaged by droughts and heat waves. Here’s a headline from yesterday’s Wall Street Journal:

And everything we know about climate change suggests that what we’ve seen so far is just a foretaste of the disasters to come.

Yet last year, speaking at the United Nations, Trump dismissed climate change as a “con job,” while calling renewable energy sources such as solar and wind — which met almost all of the world’s growth in electricity demand last year — a “scam.” And this disdain is being reflected in policy. As I and many others have written, the Trump administration has been actively trying to block wind and solar power projects. And today the administration is reportedly planning to eliminate all restrictions on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.

There is a lot to be said about the reasons our current government seems so determined to rush into disaster, even when the very survival of humanity may be at stake. Climate denial, we know from decades of experience, is fueled by an unholy trinity of financial interest (fossil fuel companies determined to keep their profits flowing), ideology (conservatives hostile to any form of regulation) and psychological insecurity (real men burn stuff.) AI-risk denial presumably reflects a similar mix of factors.

So let’s applaud leaders like Amodei for speaking up and applaud the growing willingness of other CEOs to warn about the dangers of their technology, even if their attack of conscience partly reflects the looming prospect of Democratic subpoenas.

Sanctions on West Bank settlements aren’t enough

Unfortunately, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict turns out to be a difficult problem.

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 15
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Last week, the United Kingdom, France, and Canada all announced new sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. From the standpoint of the likely goals of the political leaders of those countries — to express moral disapproval of something bad that is happening without doing anything too costly or provocative — this seems like a good idea.

That said, one of the luxuries you have as the foreign minister of, say, Canada is that you get to weigh in on various international controversies without anyone necessarily expecting you to solve them.

A genuine difficulty facing American policymakers is that as leaders of what is still the preeminent global power with unparalleled global reach, people expect our policy initiatives to be efficacious.

Back in October of 2025, for example, the government of Italy put out a strongly worded statement expressing “grave concern at reports emerging from El Fasher of widespread atrocities, summary executions, and deliberate acts of violence against civilians committed by the R.S.F.” This of course did not stop the Rapid Support Forces, a Sudanese paramilitary group — and in fact by the summer of 2026, there’s whole new rounds of atrocity in a different part of the country. But nobody really expects the prime minister of Italy to be able to halt a civil war in Sudan.

The United States faces higher expectations.

So thinking about these West Bank settlement sanctions and the possibility that a future Democratic administration will do something similar, it’s worth pointing out that this kind of measure is almost certainly inadequate to the scale of the problem.

The people actually doing the land theft and terrorizing Palestinian villagers are the most hardcore ideologues in Israeli society. There are some Israelis living just east of the border basically because they got a good deal on housing. But the people living in the further-flung settlements and certainly the people building new outposts aren’t there by happenstance, and they’re not going to turn around over a minor economic inconvenience.

The issue is that while mainstream Israelis are not doing this stuff, they also aren’t stopping it.

They have no real sympathy for or interest in the Palestinians as human beings, they’ve given up on a peace process or a two-state solution, they’re furious about hostile coverage of Israel in the global media and what they see as a double standard, and they just don’t care. The current Netanyahu coalition is dependent on small parties that are overtly supportive of irregular anti-Palestinian violence. The opposition coalition has pivoted toward criticism of the worst excesses of the violence, but settlement expansion continued apace under prior non-Netanyahu governments, and the legal landscape in the West Bank is inherently tilted against Palestinian civilians in a way that most Israeli politicians show no interest in dismantling.

Which is just to say that if Americans want to actually change the situation, as opposed to expressing disapproval over it, we almost certainly need to go further than targeted sanctions aimed at settlements. We need to do something that inflicts pain on nicer, more sympathetic Israelis in Tel Aviv and Haifa, something that makes them want to actually change course and meaningfully alter the situation.

Getting to yes

In American discourse about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, I often notice an elision between taking a position on an issue — there should be a two-state solution, there should be a unitary democratic state, etc. — and making policy choices that will cause that to come about.

When Barack Obama was president, he announced a declarative policy that the United States favored a freeze on all Israeli settlement expansion, including the so-called “natural growth” of established communities. This did not cause settlement expansion to halt. After months of wrangling, he eventually got Israel to agree to a partial moratorium that lasted 10 months and was not renewed.

The basic problem here was that Obama’s declarative policy had no teeth.

The implicit precedent was George H.W. Bush holding up loan guarantees for Israel to pressure them into attending the Madrid Conference. But the politics of 2009 (and the structure of American aid to Israel) were different, and Obama did not have support in Congress to apply meaningful leverage.

The politics of 2026 (and presumably 2029) are again different from the politics of 2009. If Democrats win, it will almost certainly be politically possible for a new Democratic administration to wield meaningful pressure against Israel in a way that wasn’t really the case for Obama, and in fact, it’s something that a big segment of the Democratic Party base is going to demand. And obviously because the United States, unlike France or Britain or Canada, provides a lot of direct financial assistance to Israel, we have a tool that’s broader and more potent than targeted sanctions aimed at settlers.

In 2029, in other words, it should be possible to pull off what Obama couldn’t and really yank American aid unless and until Israel takes steps in the West Bank that the American government approves of.

But that raises the question: What if it works?

In other words, what if the Gavin Newsom administration loudly demands that Israel restrain settler violence and genuinely halt expansion and says that if it doesn’t, there will be real consequences, and then Israel does what Newsom asks? Now we have to keep sending the aid. But even though this would be a real win for the daily lives of Palestinians in the rural West Bank, it obviously would not end the occupation or address the concerns of pro-Palestinian activists.

U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s statement rolling out the new government’s new approach is, I think, quite eloquent and morally righteous across a wide range of dimensions.

But it’s also a little weirdly unclear on what the precise conditionality is. With a coercive policy that you’re expecting to work, you need to say, “Here is what I’m doing to you and here is what you need to do to get out from under it.” The new British policy doesn’t include that because, again, it’s essentially expressive.

Britain isn’t a great power anymore, and no one really expects Miliband to get results — he’s just taking a stand. But Americans need to think clearly about what we’re trying to achieve. If we want to coerce Israel into making modest policy adjustments, that’s relatively achievable. But the only way to achieve it is by taking yes for an answer if Israel complies.

If you’re not going to be satisfied with small changes, you need to make bigger asks. But that may mean you fail to obtain the small changes.

What are we trying to achieve?

As long as critics of Israel have been far from wielding political power in the United States, they’ve also been free of the burden of deciding what exactly they’re trying to accomplish.

Abdul El-Sayed, for example, has described himself as an America First candidate because he wants to stop giving money to Israel and spend it at home instead.

I think that this is a deeply correct view and I agree with him entirely.

I often see people exaggerating the actual extent of American assistance to Israel, which is bad because accuracy is important, but Israel is an unworthy candidate for foreign aid and we should cut them off.

That said, most of the people who I see complaining about aid to Israel aren’t deficit hawks; they’re advocates for Palestinian interests. But while a unilateral aid cutoff would save American taxpayers money, it wouldn’t really do anything at all for Palestinian interests. To use aid as leverage to secure Palestinian interests, you need to threaten to cut the aid off but then be willing to keep paying if Israel takes the pro-Palestinian steps you’re demanding.

So either you don’t successfully change Israeli behavior or else you don’t save any money. You can’t achieve both of those things simultaneously.

Subscribed

Of course, we could cut off aid to Israel entirely as a baseline and then start coercing them from there. We could curtail arms sales to Israel. We could apply economic sanctions. There’s a wide variety of tools in the coercion toolkit.

Still, sanctions aren’t magic. One of the wars Donald Trump claims to have ended is a conflict in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo where a rebel group called M23 has been operating with Rwandan assistance. This war has, in fact, not ended, and the administration has been hitting Rwanda with a series of sanctions to try to get them to pull their troops back across the border. The administration is pursuing a fairly limited objective that would not comprehensively resolve the conflict or even involve M23 laying down its arms. They are nonetheless struggling to get Rwanda — a very poor country — to comply.

Sanctions, famously, have not gotten North Korea to give up nuclear weapons. We’re in a war with Iran right now because sanctions weren’t achieving what Trump wanted there. We’ve been waiting a loooong time for economic coercion to generate regime change in Cuba, and while it seems like it might happen someday soon, that underscores how hard it is to achieve large policy changes through this kind of coercion.

The kind of sanctions the United Kingdom is applying won’t be enough to get Israel to get tough on settler violence, but I’m pretty confident the United States of America could pull this off by applying broader economic pressure.

Again, though, to achieve that, you wouldn’t just need to apply the pressure — you’d need to back off if Israel did what we want. Pro-Palestinian activists obviously want much larger changes than Israel just stopping the active theft of West Bank farmland. But if you insist on bigger changes, you may end up with nothing.

Cleaning our hands

Just to be clear, if I were voting in Israel’s upcoming elections, I would back The Democrats, a now rather small left-wing opposition party that favors a return to real diplomacy and an effort at a two-state solution. But they are not the largest or even the second-largest party in the anti-Netanyahu opposition. If the voters turn the current government out, they will do so rather narrowly, and the new prime minister will be an avowed opponent of a two-state solution. What’s more, even if Gadi Eisenkot (who would likely become prime minister if Netanyahu lost) did change his mind about this, his coalition would depend on other figures like Avigdor Lieberman, which would make it basically impossible to deliver.¹

Given Israel’s proportional electoral system, anti-Netanyahu voters face no tradeoff between backing The Democrats and trying to beat Bibi. The fact that they have so little electoral support in that context indicates that, authentically, the vast majority of Israeli Jews — including a majority of anti-Netanyahu Israeli Jews — are not interested in pursuing peace in a way that I think they should be.

And beyond that, there’s an even larger gap between two states as conventionally understood and the standard Palestinian demands for a “right of return” and revisiting the facts of Israel’s founding in 1948.

By contrast, there’s a lot of reason to think that an Eisenkot government would crack down on irregular settler violence, especially if it faced meaningful international pressure, which would also offer domestic political cover. An American government could cut off aid unilaterally and unconditionally as fiscal policy and then go further, deploying U.K.-style sanctions and threatening to withhold arms sales in order to achieve policy adjustments here.

But no matter how willing the next administration is to confront Israel, the same basic tradeoff exists: If you make relatively modest asks, you stand a good chance of getting the result you want. But then we have to uphold our end of the bargain and return to selling weapons or whatever it is we withheld.

If you push for gigantic Israel policy shifts — and certainly if you push, as anti-Zionists want, for the dissolution of the Israeli state — then you might cause Israel’s military defeat (though it’s a nuclear weapons state), but you most likely won’t achieve anything at all, as with U.S. policy toward Cuba.

What’s more, if we do withdraw aid (which we should), it raises the question of how involved in this we want to be at all.

A standard argument about Israel starts with a Jewish person complaining that the Jewish state is singled out for criticism not given to other problems in the world, arguing that the disproportionate focus is antisemitic. The counter is that America, through its relationship with Israel, is uniquely culpable for humanitarian tragedies and human rights violations in Palestine in a way we are not for problems in Sudan or Myanmar or wherever else.

That’s a very reasonable reply! But if you reduce complicity by ending aid and revisiting some of the intelligence sharing and military R&D partnerships and making sure our hands are clean of direct economic support for settlement expansion, then the singling-out claim becomes more true the further we go. Pakistan has blasphemy laws, a sectarian basis for the state, “honor killings,” and all kinds of other problems, but we have a normal diplomatic and economic relationship with them because it’s not a hostile country or a geopolitical adversary.

And in the shorter term, it’s completely unclear whether isolating Israel economically over maximalist Palestinian nationalist goals makes life better or worse for people in Gaza and the West Bank. You don’t need advanced weapons to steal land from Palestinian peasants or cut off aid to Gaza.

If you’re just doing position-taking as a poster — or even as the U.K. foreign minister — you don’t necessarily need to worry about the tradeoff between having a constructive impact at the margin and standing on principle. But the next American administration, like every other administration that’s tried to involve itself closely in the conflict, will find that it’s a very hard problem.

Why Is Trump Still Boosting AI?

Because it’s the only thing he has left

Paul Krugman
Sep 15
 
READ IN APP
 

For the next couple of days I will be a Frankfurter — that is, attending a conference at the European Central Bank. So posts, if they come at all, will be short and erratic in timing.

Will AI transform the economy? The jury is still out on that one: So far there is little evidence for either the massive job losses or the soaring productivity growth industry leaders threatened/promised, but it’s still early days.

But AI does seem to be transforming U.S. politics. I can’t think of a technology that has inspired so much hate across such a wide political spectrum. Even the leading AI companies are warning about the dangers of their technology and pleading for government regulation to slow it down.

Which makes it more than puzzling that Donald Trump is going all in on AI, claiming that concerns about its dangers are a “hoax” and opposing any kind of regulation.

In so doing, he’s taking a wildly unpopular position. Here’s recent polling from UMass Amherst:

Notice that even a large part of Trump’s base is deserting him on this issue, with a quarter of Republicans disapproving.

So why is Trump posting stuff like this?

Robert Reich has a good post on the subject, urging us to follow the money: As he notes, members of the Trump family have personal financial stakes in the industry. And one motive one should never, ever dismiss in current U.S. affairs is Trump’s personal greed.

I would, however, add two more points.

First, I think Reich is too glib in dismissing the idea that Trump imagines that he knows what he’s doing. “It can’t be,” Reich writes, “that he knows very much about AI.” But does he know that he doesn’t know? That Truth Social post above, in which Trump declares himself perfectly able to manage this wild new technology because he is a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”, is like a textbook illustration of the Dunning-Kruger effect, in which incompetent people are highly confident in their own judgment because they’re too incompetent to realize that they’re incompetent.

Second, it’s important to realize how much Trump needs an AI boom.

Trump came into office believing that his tariffs would produce a huge boom in “manly” jobs. In fact, job growth has been weak — and more than all of the job gains have gone to women. Meanwhile, tariffs have driven up consumer prices.

And then there’s the Iran war, which has been an economic as well as a strategic disaster. Diesel prices are now well above $6 a gallon. Trump officials love to say that gasoline was over $5 a gallon under Biden, which was true — for one week.

Yet one thing did seem to be going right under Trump II. Enthusiasm for AI was generating a huge investment boom and supporting stock prices. Trump officials, notably Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary — who Edward Luce of the Financial Times now dubs “the Pete Hegseth of the Treasury” (ouch) — had taken to claiming that AI will solve all their problems, ending inflation by reducing costs and curing the budget deficit by generating huge economic growth.

The backlash against AI, then, is taking away the one thing the Trumpists thought they had going for them. So in a way it’s understandable that Trump is trying desperately to hold on to the magic (and possibly endangering the future of humanity, but he doesn’t care about that.)

But of course it won’t work. The AI boom, once Trump’s last remaining political asset, is now a huge liability.

The anti-American Right

Bo French’s rightist movement is a dead end for our nation. Fortunately, it’s beatable.

Noah Smith
Sep 15
 
READ IN APP
 

After days of thinking about the possibility that AI might kill all of humanity, it’s almost a relief to be able to write about a lighter topic — like how the xenophobic Right is threatening to tear my country apart.

Who is Bo French? No one of much consequence. He’s a mostly failed Texan politician — the heir to an oil company, born with a silver spoon in his mouth, who alienated his business partners, who lost two Republican primaries for the Texas House of Representatives before finally becoming the chair of a county-level party chapter. He finally got his first political success this year, when he won a narrow primary victory and became the GOP nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner. He currently trails his Democratic opponent in the polls.

Bo French isn’t that important, but this week he set off a national firestorm when he tweeted the above photo of a bunch of Indian kids celebrating University of Texas football at a Longhorns game, along with some alarmist anti-Indian rhetoric:

Bo French
@bofrench
I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.
12:52 PM · Sep 13, 2026 · 47M Views
7.7K Replies · 4.64K Reposts · 54K Likes

It was hardly a surprise that French tweeted something like this. He’s tweeted plenty of stuff along the same lines in the past. Here are two famous examples:

He’s also repeatedly called for the deportation of 100 million people; since there are only 50 million foreign-born people living in the United States, this means French was either getting his numbers wrong, or (more likely) calling for deporting tens of millions of American citizens. Reading his tweets, it’s not hard to imagine which citizens he’d choose for deportation.

It wouldn’t be fair to say that French’s race-war ideology has taken over the GOP. Plenty of Texas Republicans, including outgoing Senator John Cornyn, Senator Ted Cruz, Representative Jared Patterson, Representative Lacey Hull, and others publicly denounced his tweet. Karl Rove declared that he’d vote for the Democrat over French. Governor Greg Abbott, who has endorsed French despite his history of similar tweets, was milder in his criticism, but still affirmed the fundamental Texan-ness of the football fans in the picture:

“That is not my message,” Abbott said. “A selective picture of Longhorn fans celebrating our biggest home victory-ever-actually shows a way that Texans unite. We all support our college football teams.”

“The way we win the state is the same way we win football games,” Abbott added. “We unite under the brand of Texas.”

But despite these official condemnations, it’s easy to tell which way the wind is blowing among the GOP base. All of the Republican tweets denouncing French were heavily attacked on X. Rightist journalists, activists, and even a few GOP politicians poured out of the woodwork to support French and affirm his message. Here are a few examples:

Representative Nico Rios
@oilfield_rockhd
Eat shit you fucking loser. Go off to your retirement home and enjoy all the riches you made selling our country out.
Senator John Cornyn @JohnCornyn
This is the Republican nominee for statewide office. Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized. This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad.
6:02 PM · Sep 13, 2026 · 71.6K Views
104 Replies · 396 Reposts · 7.9K Likes
Sean Davis
@seanmdav
Bo French is awesome. John Cornyn is an anti-American loser hell-bent on looting America on behalf of foreigners.
6:14 PM · Sep 13, 2026 · 180K Views
133 Replies · 723 Reposts · 7.3K Likes
Auron MacIntyre
@AuronMacintyre
@JohnCornyn Our home is not yours to give away you traitorous catamite
3:01 PM · Sep 13, 2026 · 40.3K Views
25 Replies · 305 Reposts · 8.6K Likes
Jack Posobiec
@JackPosobiec
The cuckservatives are crying, screaming, vomiting all over themselves over Bo's tweet Get in the hotel chair
Dustin Burrows @Burrows4TX
You can oppose immigration policy without demeaning people because of their race or ethnicity — this post has crossed the line. Delete it @bofrench
5:47 PM · Sep 13, 2026 · 101K Views
82 Replies · 302 Reposts · 4.39K Likes

French himself, who had been pressured to delete his poll about Jews and Muslims last year, now felt encouraged enough to double down on his anti-Indian tweet.

I can’t tell you whether the New Right — represented by French and his supporters in the right-wing media — will prevail over the Republican establishment. But watching the movement go after a bunch of Texas college football fans tells us something important about the New Right as a movement.

What it tells us is that if you’re a nonwhite immigrant, or the child of nonwhite immigrants, it doesn’t matter what you do — the New Right will still view you as an enemy and as an invader.

It doesn’t matter whether you or your parents came to this country legally. How many times have we heard rightists shout “Illegal vs. legal!!” in response to anyone who defends immigration? Many regular Americans care about “illegal vs. legal”, but the New Right does not. Everyone in that UT photo either came to America legally, or was born to parents who came here legally. It didn’t matter to Bo French, or the people who defended him.

It doesn’t matter whether you’re high-skilled or low-skilled. How many times have we heard rightists complain that immigrants come to America because they want welfare benefits? And yet everyone in the UT photo is going to spend their lifetime paying taxes to support native-born Americans on Medicare and Medicaid and Social Security Disability. Indian Americans in general are the highest-earning group in the country, and those who go to a good college like the University of Texas are going to beat that average.

That matters to many regular voters, but it doesn’t matter at all to the New Right. Yes, they’ll shout about poor (nonwhite) immigrants on welfare. But when they encounter nonwhite immigrant groups who make lots of money, they suddenly pivot to accusing those groups of stealing their jobs and their spots in colleges. There’s just no way to win.

It also doesn’t matter whether you assimilate or not. Yes, if you speak a foreign language or build a Hindu temple or wear traditional Indian clothing, the New Right will scream their heads off about it. “Alien invaders!!”, they’ll cry. But if you put on a University of Texas sweater and go to football games, they’ll still scream “Alien invaders!!” when they see you in a photo. It’s who you are that bothers them, not what you do.

Nor does it matter whether your entire ethnic group is well-behaved. Indian Americans are incarcerated at only 25% of the rate of non-Hispanic White Americans. And basically none of the people in the photo that frightened Bo French will ever go to jail. That probably matters to some voters, but not to the New Right.

In fact, it doesn’t even matter if you vote Republican. As a matter of fact, Donald Trump won a pretty solid victory among Asian people in Texas (which includes Indians):

It’s not clear whether Bo French and his fellow New Rightists are even aware of this fact, but what is clear is that it didn’t matter to them at all.¹

This is why there is no pro-immigration argument that will ever sway members of the New Right. You can give them research showing that high-skilled immigrants raise employment and wages for native-born Americans, and they’ll either disbelieve it or (usually) ignore it. You can talk about Nobel-winning scientists and Operation Paperclip all you want, and it won’t make a dent. You can cite statistics about immigrant entrepreneurship and job creation, you can talk about how Satya Nadella saved Microsoft and Sanjay Mehrotra is the reason why America still has a presence in the memory industry. They will counter with some fabricated anecdote about how their friend got fired from their company because Indians came in and only hired other Indians.²

So why am I even talking about this? If the New Right can never be persuaded to stop thinking of brown faces as invaders, then why discuss this topic at all?

Well, two reasons, actually. First, it helps us more clearly understand the New Right as a movement — how they think and what they want. Most importantly, they see the world in terms of collective zero-sum competition between groups.

To the New Right, if Indians get into the University of Texas, it means that White people must have been “replaced” at that university — or at American universities in general. Bo French himself tweeted that the presence of Indian students at American universities is evidence that “they hate white Americans and prioritize everyone else”. They do not even consider the possibility that the Indian kids got in because of individual merit. If an Indian American succeeds, that represents not the success of that singular individual, but a win for Team Indian in general.

And the New Right worldview sees any win for Team Indian — or Team Asian, or Team Hispanic, etc. — as a loss for Team White. Nowhere do they consider the possibility that the system might not be zero-sum. The fact that the number of freshmen admitted to UT grew from 15,000 in 2011 to 19,000 in 2021 means nothing to them. The historical fact that Italian and Jewish and Polish and Japanese Americans attained economic success sixty years ago without consigning WASP Americans to poverty is lost on them — as is every other example in which immigrant groups and existing groups succeeded in America side by side.

Crucially, this zero-sum assumption is why the New Right constantly shrinks their tent instead of expanding it. In principle, even if you see the world as a collective interaction between groups rather than individuals, that interaction doesn’t have to be zero-sum — you can have alliances between groups, for mutual benefit. The Christian conservatives of the 1970s and 1980s accepted Catholics, “white ethnics”, and some Jews into their coalition as “co-belligerents”, and won many battles as a result.

The New Right had a golden opportunity to do something similar after Trump’s victory in 2024. Hispanic and Asian voters (and even some Black voters) shifted strongly toward the Republicans, and toward Trump specifically. But instead of embracing that influx of new voters and building a big conservative tent to defeat wokeness and progressivism and the Democrats, they went all-in on race war.

Stephen Miller relied so heavily on racial profiling for his mass deportation efforts that many Hispanics felt that Trump had betrayed them. Muslim voters might have gone back to the GOP, but rightists made resistance to Muslim immigration a “civilizational” crusade. Jewish voters turned off by the antisemitism of the Left might have switched their allegiance to the GOP, but the New Right allowed Nazi apologetics to fester within their ranks.

Now it’s Indians’ turn to feel the sting of unprovoked rightist attacks. All those kids in Texas wanted to do was to cheer for their football team; instead, a political movement is calling for their ethnic cleansing simply because they showed up at the stadium. As a result, despite the best efforts of Republicans like Cornyn, the GOP is poised to mobilize and piss off a group of Americans who are just about as numerous as Jews — and who earn even more money.

It’s this pathological inability to understand alliances and coalition-building that will ultimately doom the New Right. Like the far Left, this is a movement built to exclude and divide and splinter — both because of the querulous personalities of rightists themselves, and because of the intransigence of a racial ideology that abhors any impurity. If they ever managed to see off the Hispanics and the Asians, the rightists would start in on the Greeks and the Italians, and so on. There’s no victory in sight — only eternal conflict. These are not nation-builders; they are nation-dismantlers.

Coming to grips with the extremism and intransigence of the New Right also helps us understand what an unpopular fringe they really are. The New Right screams and shouts and acts very aggressive on X, but this aggression is just a way of concealing their numerical weakness. Most voters are not part of the New Right, and they don’t think that immigrants are invaders or that immigration is “replacement”. Most Americans say that immigration is a good thing as of today:

Essentially none of that 73% majority is going to be part of the New Right, and some portion of the 21% minority probably isn’t either. That means the New Right is a fringe movement — a very loud, very aggressive group of people who are adept at bullying regular Americans on certain social media platforms, but who ultimately lack the numbers to overcome the mainstream in a direct contest.

Just watch some of the reactions of the UT students who were targeted by Bo French and his racist social media hordes:

Ryan Chandler
@RyanChandlerTV
“We all bleed orange… all the people in that video, all my friends, were either born in Texas or the United States.” As many assumed, the students in the photo @bofrench shared are native Texans - and some of our very brightest. Hear from one student in those stands @NBCNews :
10:28 PM · Sep 15, 2026 · 37.3K Views
31 Replies · 104 Reposts · 472 Likes

Consider how regular and non-alien those young people seem, compared to the screeching bigots attacking them on X for going to a football game. I guarantee you that the majority of regular, normal, non-internet-poisoned Americans will watch those videos and just want to say “Hook ‘em Horns”.³

That means that the immigration argument is winnable. A reasonable liberal position on immigration — one that respects the law, honors the democratic will of the people, and treats immigration as a privilege rather than a human right — has a good chance of winning over the majority of the country. The New Right can only succeed if they manage to divide and conquer the pro-immigration majority, as they did in 2024; immigration supporters should focus on making common cause with the persuadable center, in order to make sure 2024 isn’t repeated.

That means not treating all immigration skeptics the same. Republicans like John Cornyn, who like to see Indian American kids cheering for Texas football but who hate to see asylum seekers rewarded for illegally crossing the border, should not be lumped in with those who simply see any brown face and think “invader”. Xenophobes exist, and they are growing more powerful within the GOP, but not every Republican voter is a xenophobe, and not every restriction on immigration is xenophobic.

If Democrats understand and accept that fact, I think they will be able to turn the tide.⁴ Throughout America’s history, pro-immigration forces have won a lot more battles than they’ve lost, but it was never easy. It always required compromise, reassurance, moderation, and coalition-building. This is not the time for Democrats to respond to the maximalism of xenophobes like Bo French with maximalism of their own.

Destroying women’s sports in order to save it

Dems are quietly becoming more reasonable, and Republicans are revealing their true colors.

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 16
 
READ IN APP
 

There are people on Bluesky who believe I am “obsessed” with the issue of trans women participating in women’s sports, which is not the case. I am, rather, frustrated by Democrats’ tendency to take a No Compromise With the Electorate Approach to a question that while nuanced, doesn’t require a doctorate to understand and that also involves low stakes compared with other questions related to trans rights.

So I’ve been heartened to see Rob Sand, James Talarico, Amy Acton, and Josh Turek take a more pragmatic approach to this issue. And it’s especially heartening to see that while there is of course some blowback against these candidates, it’s mostly not being led by anyone with real clout or power.

In particular, we’re not seeing safe seat Democrats blast these politicians for their more moderate stances.

That is, in a lot of ways, the most important aspect of the politics. Democrats — including Democrats in safe blue seats who hew to activist orthodoxy on this question — are making it clear that the tent includes a diversity of opinion and that holding the same views as a large majority of the public does not make you a proto-fascist.

This will hopefully allow for some refocusing of attention on the question of who actually is supporting women’s sports and why.

For example, note that even Sophie Cunningham, who has spoken out against the participation of trans women in women’s sports, does not appreciate Enes Kanter Freedom’s efforts to troll his way onto a W.N.B.A. squad. It’s the difference between a woman who is a professional athlete giving her view about a policy question that is, currently, totally hypothetical and a person trying to gin up controversy and draw attention to himself.

An even more egregious example comes from Washington state, where conservative activists have put a trans sports initiative on the ballot that would require affirmative sex verification in order to participate in girls’ school sports. This is not the standard practice even in the many red states who’ve adopted rules on this topic, and by creating new barriers to participation, the new rule would likely generate fewer opportunities for girls to play sports.

It’s not entirely clear to me why the Washington initiative is written this way. In Rachel Cohen Booth’s reporting, the proponents just deny that it says that, but it appears that they are wrong. Advocates for the initiative did not provide Booth with any legal experts who would back up their account, and when I asked Grok (seeking a “based” analysis of the controversy), anti-woke artificial intelligence agreed with her.

It’s basically impossible to know what they were thinking when they drafted this, but it’s clear that they weren’t thinking about the best interests of girls’ sports or female athletes.

Which in a lot of ways is the natural order of things. Promoting women’s sports is and always has been a progressive cause. Lately, this topic has been a political godsend for the right, but conservatives were never actually going to center women’s sports as a cause worth fighting for.

Destroying the village in order to save it

In most of these political arguments, progressives’ point that there are actually very few trans athletes is pretty unpersuasive. You still need a rule about who can play on which teams, and people are entitled to care about what the rule says.

But when it comes to an implementation and verification regime, the underlying rareness really is a relevant consideration.

To justify doing something that will inconvenience, embarrass, or possibly deter a huge number of girls from participating in sports, you need to be addressing a quantitatively significant issue. And this just isn’t one. Under the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association’s current policy of gender self-identification, there are 10 trans athletes out of 200,000+ kids playing middle school and high school sports in the state.

What’s more, by an overwhelming margin, these trans athletes are not people who’ve snuck surreptitiously onto sports teams. They came out as trans and that identity is known to parents and school officials.

If Washington state and its voters want to change current policy, that’s fine (my wishy-washy take is that stringently enforced sex segregation for middle school is probably unnecessary but that for high school it typically is). You can, though, just make a new declarative policy without subjecting everyone to a verification regime. In 99.9 percent of cases, there’s going to be zero controversy. If somebody wants to make a big deal about a specific athlete’s status, it’s not that hard to do an SRY gene test with a cheek swab, which is used as a proxy for biological sex. But in the real world, this is almost never going to come up.

I did a double take when I saw this story because I know Democrats have been in the habit of raising the prospect of universal genital inspections as a reason to oppose a chromosomal definition of sex for the purposes of sports. But obviously there’s no actual need to do that! And yet, here the authors of the Washington initiative seem to have done it.

Republicans don’t care about women’s sports

In what I think is a related development, earlier this year the Heritage Foundation put out a report blasting the whole idea of Title IX parity for male and female athletes in American schools.

I was glad they did it. Not because I agree, but because this is the actual conservative position on gender and sports!

I’m old now, so I remember back in 2003 when the Bush administration considered gutting Title IX parity but backed off under pressure. But then in 2005, with Bush’s re-election secured, they grew bolder and wrote new guidance to make it far easier for schools to say there just wasn’t interest from female students in playing sports. In 2010, the Obama administration reversed the Bush rule. This is politics! Democrats pushing an ambitious vision of social change and equality; Republicans pushing for traditionalism.

Subscribed

And unlike the trans issue, the implications of basic Title IX rules are far reaching. There’s a reason the U.S. women’s ice hockey team does better in international competitions than their male counterparts and the women’s soccer team does much better than the men — America has made unusually large investments in athletic opportunities for girls and it pays off. American men do very well overall at the Olympic Games, for example, but American women do even better because most of the world is behind us in women’s sports.

Like anything else in life, it’s perfectly fair to debate this. But my point is that this is a fairly big-picture, fairly long-running debate. It has intersected recently with L.G.B.T. policy in a way that landed Democrats on the wrong side of common sense and public opinion. But it’s pretty clear who stands where in the broader debate.

The endgame

This larger dynamic also helps explain why Sophie Cunningham was getting booed at games after speaking out in favor of the principle that only cisgender women should play in the W.N.B.A. The actual fanbase for most women’s sports in the United States in general, and certainly for the W.N.B.A., is quite left wing and disproportionately queer. They understand Cunningham to be doing right-wing politics, and they don’t like it.

By the same token, the family and I were at the Washington Spirit women’s soccer game last weekend and there was quite a bit of advocacy material in the section for the die-hard Spirit supporters. The video that introduces the team at the start of the game starts with a paean to the diversity of the district and depicts everyone getting to the game on the metro. It’s a very progressive fan base!

Notably, though, there are no trans women playing in the National Women’s Soccer League or the W.N.B.A. In both cases, the written rules could be construed as either barring them or not. And I think that status quo serves the business interests of these enterprises, as an explicit ban would probably antagonize a bunch of fans but an influx of players with XY chromosomes would mess up the competition. This is why Kanter Freedom’s intervention reads as obnoxious to fans of the league — he’s trying to embarrass people and make it hard for the W.N.B.A. to please all its stakeholders, not addressing an actual problem.

The thing I would urge progressives who are not sports fans to understand about high-level sports is that these are literally zero-sum competitions to which generic progressive interest in inclusivity does not apply. If there had been a trans woman in the U.S. Open draw, that would have almost certainly mechanically squeezed out a cisgender woman.

Conversely, I think it would be constructive for non-opportunistic conservatives to admit that they’ve won the argument about this.

Subscribed

The Women’s Tennis Association tour does not admit trans women. The W.N.B.A., regardless of its ambiguously worded policy, is in fact not full of people self-IDing into the league. The International Olympic Committee has adopted a rule using SRY testing. The N.C.A.A. has a simple declarative policy with no specific verification process. Democrats are not objecting to any of this or promising to reverse it. People don’t like to admit they made mistakes, so don’t expect Democrats to explicitly acknowledge that it was the Obama Department of Education that put on the table the idea that there needs to be a uniform national policy here. But they really have retreated from that view and seem content to let all kinds of sports bodies adopt rules on their own accord, and the trajectory of those rules is pretty clear.

When conservatives move toward something like mandatory sex verification for middle schoolers, though, that puts the debate back in more traditionally progressive terrain.

That’s a rule that’s only going to reduce girls’ participation and burden female athletes and their families for the sake of, I guess, rooting out the occasional extremely rare case of someone with an undiagnosed difference of sex development. And the broader Title IX fight is a classic left/right political battle, where conservatives just want to shrink opportunities and funding for girls’ sports.

How to stop Hitler

Read Hayek, but don’t listen to him about the specifics of the rise of fascism.

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 17
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Hey guys! For a while now I’ve been hosting a podcast, called “The Argument,” with Jerusalem Demsas, the editor in chief of The Argument magazine. We realized that rather than sending everyone a separate podcast email each week, it would make more sense to incorporate the Thursday podcast releases into the morning’s article.

The podcast itself has a few different episode formats, but once a month or so we do a “book club” episode where we read a classic book. This week’s was Friedrich von Hayek’s 1944 book “The Road to Serfdom.” In our conversation, Jerusalem and I really dug into Hayek’s ideas. But as someone who’s interested in history, I also wanted to write in greater depth on the specific historical argument of the book.

For an 80-year-old book written by an Austrian guy in a language he didn’t speak natively, Friedrich von Hayek’s 1944 book “The Road to Serfdom” is incredibly engaging and accessible. It’s also crackling with insights on nearly every page — I kept furiously highlighting passages that reminded me of contemporary controversies and phenomena so I’ll have quotes and points for future articles on everything from antitrust policy to Waymo to health care.

What’s remarkable is that even though the book is really good and I strongly recommend it to anyone interested in the future of liberalism in these fraught times, its ostensible core thesis also seems totally wrong.

Hayek wrote it in the middle of World War II, when lots of people in America and especially Britain were looking at the semi-planned wartime economy and seeing it as a model for peacetime. He thinks this is a bad idea (this part holds up) that if implemented will lead to a totalitarian regime (this part does not) and also that German retention of planning concepts from World War I during the interwar period is causally responsible for the rise of Adolf Hitler, which I think is so clearly wrong that I can’t help but quote from the introduction, where Hayek writes that “few are ready to recognize that the rise of fascism and Naziism was not a reaction against the socialist trends of the preceding period but a necessary outcome of those tendencies.”

I want to emphasize that the book is not at all a detailed survey of German politics in the 1920s and 1930s; it’s a book about economics and political theory.

And that’s why it’s a good book and why on the podcast we mostly talked about the insights we think hold up. But I think this impulse to gild the lily and attribute the rise of Hitler to deep intellectual trends is an example of a pretty common fallacy of assuming that an incredibly important world event must have incredibly important roots.

One point I tried to make last week about 9/11 is that while Osama bin Laden was swimming in some big currents of violent Islamist political thought that have deep roots and semi-broad sociological appeal, the specific theory whereby blowing up office buildings in New York City would advance that cause was quite weird. It’s easy to imagine a world where the same basic ideological currents are in the mix but nobody ever says that and all of world history is different.

By the same token, Hitler was a fairly marginal figure on the eve of the Great Depression. It was poor short-term economic management plus the questionable short-term political calculations of the non-SPD German parties that brought the Nazis to power. It was a very big deal for world history, but not an inevitable consequence of the whole structure of German intellectual life.

The real story of Hitler’s rise is mostly a history of contingency — bad choices by specific influential politicians first wrecked the German economy and then handed power to Hitler.

Paying subscribers can find the rest of the article beneath the paywall, along with the transcript for this week’s episode of “The Argument” podcast. The embedded video below is also ad free for paid subscribers. The public version of the episode is available on YouTube here.

The Nazis were a minor party in 1928

You often hear from Germans that the hyperinflation of the early 1920s broke the back of the Weimar Republic and laid the groundwork for Hitler.

John Maynard Keynes’s 1919 book, “The Economic Consequences of the Peace,” is also quite popular and influential. In it, Keynes argues that the reparations imposed on Germany would be economically destabilizing and lay the seeds for future conflict rather than preventing it. Hearing about these things sometimes creates the impression that the whole Weimar era was a doomed series of disasters. But in fact, the hyperinflation ended in 1923 and a new stable currency was introduced. Keynes’s book is famous because his insights were accepted by American leaders who implemented the Dawes Plan to make reparations manageable and set things aright. Dawes won the Nobel Peace Prize and the German economy recovered.

In the 1928 German federal election, the Nazi Party got 2.63 percent of the vote, putting them in ninth place.

Prussia, by far the largest state in Germany with over 60 percent of the country’s population, also had an election in 1928. There, the Nazis got 1.8 percent and also finished ninth. In Bavaria, the second largest state and home of Hitler’s original base, they got 6 percent and finished fifth. Saxony, the third largest state, didn’t have elections in 1928, but in their 1929 Landtag election the Nazis got 4.96 percent — good for seventh place. In the fourth biggest state, Württemberg, there was a 1928 election where the Nazis were tenth with 1.8 percent of the vote.

I don’t need to bore you by going further down the list. But if you actually want to analyze the political events in Germany in the years leading up to Hitler’s rise, you do have to engage with these details.

Over the past decade, tons of bad takes have attributed the rise of populist-right political parties to economic hardship when it’s pretty clear that actually a large minority of voters agree with their anti-immigration tough-on-crime message. But one reason these takes are popular may be a kind of historical memory in Europe of the interwar period when there were basically no political debates about immigration. There is plenty of evidence that lots of German people held antisemitic attitudes and were angry about World War I. But very few people had any interest in voting for a violent, demagogically antisemitic, pro-war political movement until the Great Depression.

The Weimar Republic really did have a number of structural weaknesses, starting with the really goofy federalism of a system with one state that had a majority of the population and then tiny states like Lippe with 164,000 people (the Nazis finished ninth in Lippe’s 1929 election, by the way, behind the Reich Party for Civil Rights and Deflation). They also had a persistent block of 10 percent or so of people voting for the Communists even during the good economic times. Catholic and Protestant right-wingers had trouble working together. German liberalism was relatively weak and yet divided between two different political parties. The Social Democrats were stuck between rhetorical radicalism and the practical realities of governance.

But there’s no reason to think things couldn’t have trundled along with the various party leaders getting more sophisticated at the art of representative government over time. The problem was the economy went to shit.

Germany tumbled into economic and political disaster

In the 1925 German presidential election, Paul von Hindenburg, backed by a coalition of right-wing parties, defeated Wilhelm Marx from the Catholic Centre Party, who was mostly counting on Social Democrats for votes. Hindenburg won with only 48 percent of the vote because the Communists insisted on running a spoiler candidate who got 6 percent. That’s an annoying turn of events, but also just normal politics in a democracy. Everyone is dealing with the basic issues of coalition management, and it superficially appears that the ability of the Communists to retain a core base of loyalists no matter how ridiculous they act is the primary problem for the German center-left.

But shortly after those 1928 elections in which the Nazis did so poorly, the Great Depression hit.

Unemployment increased massively, which eroded the popularity of almost all the mainstream political parties. It also created a large bloc of idle young men with time on their hands to join either Nazi or Communist paramilitary organizations to achieve some sense of purpose and meaning in life.

By the time new elections were held in the fall of 1930, industrial production had fallen by over 25 percent, and it’s not a huge surprise that both the Nazis and the Communists saw their vote share rise. This new parliament made the political situation extremely difficult, but even so there was hope. As Barry Eichengreen has famously shown, most countries began to recover rapidly from the Great Depression once they ditched the gold standard and allowed their economy to reflate.

The exception is Germany, where, uniquely, an end to gold led not to reflation but to a massive wave of bank failures that further pummeled the economy.

What happened here? Well, Thomas Ferguson and Peter Temin argue persuasively in their 2001 paper on the crisis that the key problem was Hindenburg’s determination to pursue an aggressively nationalist foreign policy, which screwed up the opportunity to get the long-term loan from France that Germany needed to stabilize its budget.

Cut off from international capital markets, Germany ended up going off gold in a way that panicked foreign depositors and exacerbated the economic crisis. The Nazis had made huge gains in the 1930 elections, and when Germans went to the polls in 1932 the economy was worse than ever. Though Hitler was still well short of a majority, he did lead the largest bloc in parliament. And at that point, Hindenburg and the rest of the German right decided to throw in with Hitler rather than work with the socialists.

Practical management matters a lot

This is a lot of words to say that while I think Hayek’s book provides an incredibly powerful critique of central planning, I really don’t see how you can avoid the conclusion that powerful elements in German society — in the military, in the old aristocratic class, and in the business community — did do what he says they didn’t do and turned to the Nazis as an alternative to the socialists.

But the reason anyone was even in a position to make a choice like that was the extremely bad macroeconomic management in Germany. This was in part just mistaken ideas about economic policy from the people in charge and in part Hindenburg’s perverse decision to prioritize things like a customs union with Austria and heavy cruiser construction over maintaining a pragmatic economic relationship with France.

All of Germany’s problems were also in part downstream of the parallel economic collapse in the United States, which was also likely mostly avoidable if Herbert Hoover and the Federal Reserve had made smarter choices. The American Depression, of course, also generated massive political change — we just had a much more benign opposition. It’s also one of the unfortunate twists of history that the Nazis just genuinely had pretty good judgment about macroeconomic policy in the mid-1930s and ended up gaining a halo of prestige and public support from driving an effective economic recovery.

Where I think Hayek is persuasive is that having seized power, attempting to do a (“national”) form of socialism turns out to work a lot better if you’re also willing to implement a brutal dictatorship.

Something that really resonated for me in the book across the generations is his point that a kind of nice-guy liberal socialism has a lot of superficial appeal to intellectuals but doesn’t really make sense. The more you want to organize the economic system around telling everyone what to do, the more you need an overwhelming consensus about values that can’t really be secured through liberal means in a liberal society.

And to this day, I see people like Matt Stoller tossing off ideas like “China, by contrast, where the superrich are not in control, and which has a coherent governance model, the same kind of existential fears about A.I. simply do not exist,” as if the presence of a totalitarian regime is incidental and a Chinese regulatory model could be easily replicated in a Western democracy. What I think we learned from post-WWII history, though, is that rather than efforts to introduce state ownership and comprehensive price regulation in Britain leading to authoritarianism, it simply didn’t work well.

The United Kingdom actually did a bunch of the stuff Hayek warned them against in the late 1940s, and he was right that it wasn’t sustainable or workable. But the upshot was it mostly got dismantled because it was done by wishful thinking liberal socialists, not by the hard men of a fascist movement. Authoritarianism didn’t come into Germany via a slippery slope; it came quite suddenly because a non-authoritarian government catastrophically mismanaged a massive economic crisis. The route to the Bolshevik takeover of Russia was totally different but similarly involved catastrophic mismanagement of an urgent crisis that allowed a group of people to rapidly leap to power from the margins of society.

There’s something unsatisfying about “don’t lose a huge war” or “if your country tumbles into recession, make things better rather than worse” being the big takeaways from epic political disasters. After all, everyone agrees you shouldn’t do those things, and it would be more interesting and emotionally satisfying if these cataclysms related more to deep intellectual arguments. But the shallow stuff matters a lot.

It’s making a lot of good points, but as an account of mid-century totalitarianism, like, I don’t know. I don’t buy it, but he’s a really smart guy. You learn a lot. He has not convinced everyone. I guess that’s the difference with Friedan. She really has just won the argument.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: I mean, people disagree about that. We still have value pluralism, but I would say her ideas are dominant today, whereas Hayek’s ideas are falling into some abeyance in a way that we could benefit from elevating.

Jerusalem Demsas: All right. Well, thank you all for listening to this episode of The Argument. If you have book suggestions for our next book, please let us know. We have taken those in the past. You can do that in the comments of The Argument, of Slow Boring, tweet us, share this podcast with your friends on social media, and we’ll see you next week.

Matthew Yglesias: Bye.
