Forwarded this email? Subscribe here for more
 
Watch now
 

A Globalist Comeback?

Hints of a business break with MAGA

Paul Krugman
Oct 1
 
READ IN APP
 

Transcript

On September 28th Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase, one of the most prominent, most successful financial figures in the United States, published an article in the Wall Street Journal titled, “The Hell with Trump, Let’s Go Back to Globalism.”

Okay, that’s a lie. That wasn’t what the article was titled, but it was, in effect, what it said.

And it was a very interesting message to be coming at this moment in time. I think Dimon’s op-ed can be viewed as a harbinger of a big shift in the business community’s political positions and its attitudes that may be coming in the very near future — in effect a bet that Trump and MAGA in general are going to be in the rearview mirror, not too far from now.

Now, a word about Dimon. He’s an extraordinarily successful financial leader. He navigated the 2008 financial crisis and aftermath better than almost anyone else in Wall Street. He had the good sense to limit JP Morgan’s exposure to the practices that helped to create that financial crisis.

He is also a very, very smart political operator. He has had a talent for not making enemies, for staying at least on decent relationships with administrations from both parties, which is no mean feat in 21st century America. He certainly did not join the cavalcade of business leaders rushing to prostrate themselves at Trump’s feet after the 2024 election, and yet he was subtle enough about his restraint to not get put on Trump’s enemies list. So,you know, his political judgment should be trusted.

His economic judgment, all right, being a great businessman is not at all the same thing as being a great economist. And there’s no particular reason to think that he is always right about economic affairs. But that is, in a way, mostly beside the point.

So what did Dimon call for? Well, he basically said, we need to repair theWestern alliance. We need to bring the Western world, the advanced democracies, above all the United States and Europe, back together in part as a way to stand up against the threat of a rising China. And his proposal for how to do that was to negotiate a free trade agreement between the United States and the European Union.

That’s quite something. That’s a very un-MAGA position to take. You want to bear in mind that, first of all, we’re currently under a government of people who do not at all believe in the virtues of free trade. In fact, are extremely hostile to globalism. Certainly don’t believe in binding international agreements. Maybe they want agreements that bind other countries, but not them.

And they are also not of the mind that we have a lot of shared values with the democratic governments of Europe. The MAGA position, if anything, is that they like the anti-democratic forces in Europe. J.D. Vance essentially campaigned for Viktor Orban in Hungary. Trump officials have been quite clear that they have sympathy for the AfD in Germany. So if we have common values with some Europeans, the Europeans with whom they have common values are neo-Nazis. And Trump’s de facto support for Putin in his invasion of Ukraine has been alarmingly clear over the past two years.

What we’re seeing here is Jamie Dimon basically saying that I don’t care about any of that. I don’t believe that you people are going to be in charge. And I think that we can go back to trying to rebuild bridges to Western Europe.

Now, it’s kind of interesting the way he phrases it. He puts a lot of it in terms that I suspect are intended to appeal to economic conservatives in the United States who are not MAGA types. He sells his proposal in part as an incentive for Europe to conduct pro-business, pro-economic reforms. He cites the Draghi report on European Competitiveness, which has been very influential in Europe. And points to him for even knowing about it! There are probably not a lot of people in the United States who have read the Draghi Report, absorbed its lessons.

I myself have read it. I have had some criticisms of some of the analysis in the Draghi Report, but the reforms that Draghi proposes, which have a lot to do with completing the European internal market, making the capital markets in Europe more flexible and responsive and so on, are very much in the right direction. So this is a good thing. And I’m glad to see someone in the United States, someone prominent, actually taking European affairs seriously and wanting the Europeans to do things that will improve their own position.

Dimon is almost surely overstating how important a free trade agreement with the United States could be. The reality is that the obstacles to European reform are internal — as are the obstacles to all the reforms we should be making here. Politics is real on both sides of the Atlantic.

And we are not as important to Europe — or they to us — as a lot of people imagine. The fact of the matter is that Europe only exports around 3% of what it produces to the US. And we were pretty close to free trade with Europe until Trump II came along. We had our average tariffs of only something on the order of 2% on European products. So it’s not as if he’s actually offering a tremendous benefit to Europe, something that would radically dislocate their internal politics and move them in a positive direction.

But, all right, it’s a good proposal. And I think that, as I understand it, Dimon believes that the process of negotiating towards a free trade agreement would in itself help to improve politics. That it would be a signal that the ultra-nationalist, anti-democratic, often anti-European policies of theTrump era are behind us.

So he’s looking forward to the day when we can start to try to repair some of the immense damage that has been done to our international relations during the Trump years.

Dimon is a smart political operator. I’m reasonably sure he would not have written this op-ed if the polls weren’t pointing towards a Democratic blowout. And of course, he could be wrong in believing that that’s going to happen, as we all could. But I’m sure that he is looking at the situation and envisaging a Democratic Congress — almost surely the House and quite likely the Senate — after the November election.

And a reasonable president, not necessarily a Democrat, but most likely, but in any case a reasonable president after Trump has gone from the scene.And a president and Congress that would be interested in trying to rebuild the Western alliance. Because ultimately, although Dimon’s proposal is economic in the narrow sense, it’s really political. It’s about rebuilding an alliance.

That won’t be easy. The fact of the matter is that the United States did just casually rip up solemnly signed trade agreements. Almost everything that Trump has done on tariffs is a violation of agreements made over several generations. Also, it’s not just Trump. The American people elected Trump twice, and the rest of the world is not going to forget that.

But free trade agreements can be a way of not just of enhancing trade, which is important, but maybe not as important as economists would like to think. But they can also be a way of binding countries closer together. They can be a gesture of alliance. And Diamond obviously thinks that this is possible, or at least thinks that it might be possible — close enough to being something that would really be on the table, that it’s worth making a case for it, and that it’s worth positioning himself and his institution for a post-MAGA era. And as Isaid, Diamond is a smart guy with a very, very good political judgment.

So that op-ed was one of the most encouraging things I’ve seen in months.

On that happy note, take care.

A “Who You Gonna Believe?” Election

If you’re arguing, you’re losing. Trump is arguing.

Paul Krugman
Oct 2
 
READ IN APP
 

They’re still doing it! Click on any White House press release and the image above pops up. The tone-deafness is almost surreal. Even if you’re a Trump loyalist who really believes that things are going great in America, surely you have to be aware that this isn’t how most voters see it. Here’s what the latest AP-NORC poll says:

A note here: When Kyla Scanlon introduced the term “vibecession” during the Biden years, Americans generally had a much more positive view of their local economy — which they could observe with their own eyes — than they did of the national economy. That’s no longer the case: Americans are as down on their local economies as they are on the national situation. This downbeat view of the state of the nation isn’t a media narrative concocted by the “fake news”: it’s what people see all around them.

And while I’m not a political consultant, I don’t think “Who are you gonna believe, me or your own eyes?” is a winning strategy.

But then again, who in this administration would be willing to risk Trump’s ire by taking that popup down?

Tomorrow I’ll post a conversation with G. Elliott Morris and David Nir about what polling and other political indicators say about the midterm elections. Today I thought I’d complement that discussion in advance by talking about several economic indicators that are also really, really bad news for Trump and his party.

First, the obvious: prices at the pump:

.

Voters famously blame whoever is in the White House when fuel prices are high, even though presidents normally have very little influence on these prices. In this case Trump, with his disastrous war of choice in Iran, really does bear full responsibility for high energy prices — and voters know it.

However, fuel prices and inflation in general aren’t the only reasons Americans have a negative view of the Trump economy. Official measures of employment and unemployment look good by historical standards, but perceptions about the state of the job market have dramatically worsened. Every month The Conference Board asks Americans whether jobs are “plentiful” or “hard to get.” The difference between these two answers is almost always positive — we are an optimistic nation — but the “labor market differential” has plunged. Americans perceive the job market as being the worst it has been since Covid:

Finally, how about those interest rates? We often hear about elections being swung by an “October surprise,” and maybe Trump still has something up his sleeve. But the big economic news of the past month has been a “September surprise” on interest rates, including rates that matter a great deal to ordinary Americans — such as families trying to buy houses. Here’s the 30-year mortgage rate:

So where are we as we head into the final month of the midterm campaign? Election models based on political polls are almost surreally favorable to the Democrats, who Elliott Morris gives a 99 percent chance of winning the House. But it’s not just the polls. Even though the U.S. economy looks OK by some measures, the overall economic environment looks really bad for Trump and his party.

Oh, and there’s the small matter of that disastrous war.

Yet the Trump administration insists that this troubled environment is a Golden Age. This isn’t just bad politics. It’s an indication that Trump is living in a bubble of fantasy and sycophancy, in which nobody dares suggest — even as a matter of cynical political strategy — acknowledging that things are less than perfect.

And remember: When voters make it clear that they aren’t buying into Trumpist triumphalism, he won’t blame himself. He’ll blame America, and look for people to punish.

How blue-state Republicans can be relevant again

Plus alternate Bonaparte and some Lee Kuan Yew takes

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 2
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Before we get to the questions, I wanted to flag the unveiling of a new bipartisan permitting reform deal in the Senate. I don’t know that I have a whole column about this, but I do want to say that it seems like a very strong package that blends provisions to make electricity transmission a lot easier, provisions that are tech-neutral and would improve speed and certainty around energy project permitting, and some good ideas around data centers to make sure new large loads pay the cost of grid upgrades.

I also need to say that I misjudged Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, whose push to get people to talk more about climate change seemed misguided to me but apparently was coupled with a determination to negotiate a really good piece of substantive legislation. I still don’t literally agree with his take on “hushing,” his term to criticize Democrats who avoid talking about climate change, but he was actually doing the important thing here.

Now, Congress should pass the bill!

The risk is that people who at heart don’t want a deal kick it into the next Congress by arguing that there will be a better deal next spring and then we waste another year or two spinning our wheels rather than giving the next Democratic administration a chance to hit the ground running with renewables build-out.

If you’re a person who cannot countenance a bill that makes any concessions to the fossil fuel industry, then you will not like this bill. But you won’t like any bill that Donald Trump could conceivably sign in 2027 or 2028, or any bill that could conceivably pass the Senate — even a hypothetical filibuster-free Senate — in a world where Democrats are counting on Texas and Alaska to deliver their majority.

Whitehouse and Senator Martin Heinrich negotiated a ton of wins for electrification and renewables and geothermal in this bill, and it’s time to pass it.

B Wilder: You’ve given advice in the past for Democrats in red states to make inroads, but what would your advice be for Republicans in blue to states in order to provide checks and balances on the state legislature?

I think this is a sort of under-discussed issue, in part because in a lot of ways I think the playbook for blue-state Republicans is a lot easier and more obvious than the playbook for red-state Democrats.

After all, if you look at federal politics, the main Republican idea is to deploy culture war issues for maximal electoral benefit and then do business-friendly economic policy. In 2004, when opposing gay marriage was good politics, Republicans ran hard on it. By 2016, when it was bad politics, they dropped the issue like a rock. Federal Republicans don’t spend down political capital on cultural issues — they wield them to try to win races. All you really need to do to be sporadically competitive in blue states is just apply that exact same formula to an electorate where the median voter is more left-wing. Every single state has business owners and business executives and people who’d like to pay less in taxes. And the bluer states are in fact more likely to have wasteful spending that’s worth cutting.

We used to have a lot of guys like that.

When I was a kid, Rudy Giuliani was mayor of New York City. He was vocally pro-choice, favored gay rights, and was very clear that his vision of “tough on crime” politics included gun control. He was also, in a way that reminds me more of Zohran Mamdani than Bill de Blasio or Eric Adams, very celebratory of the 1990s version of actually existing New York as an aspirational city of immigrants and diversity. Richard Riordan was also mayor of Los Angeles during this time period and had a similar profile — even tending to brag that he was supporting marriage equality before the vast majority of national Democrats.

By 2026, I would say blue-state Republicans are suffering from three problems.

One is that Donald Trump personally is such a titanic issue. It’s not just that Trump is a really big deal and also super-unpopular in blue places. It’s that he does inappropriate and abusive things that insert himself into local affairs. His habit of trying to cheat in and steal elections, for example, gives people reason to believe that if California had a Republican governor right now that he might be pulling shenanigans to subvert the integrity of the midterm House races. The successful blue-state Republicans of the Trump era have taken clear anti-Trump stances, but most Republican Party voters sincerely love Trump. Charlie Baker had a successful run as a Trump-critical moderate governor of Massachusetts, but rather than the state party seeing him as a model for success, they went in an explicitly MAGA direction post-Baker even though there is no universe in which that was going to work in the Bay State.

This Trump divide can play out in different ways in different institutional contexts, but it keeps being important. Consider the California governor’s race. Matt Mahan, the successful moderate Dem mayor of San Jose, tried to run as a tough-on-crime, business-friendly reformer. If he’d taken second place and made it to a runoff against Xavier Becerra or Tom Steyer, I think there’s a reasonable chance that Mahan would have won. But California Republicans wanted to vote for Steve Hilton, a Fox News contributor and a Trump supporter, so Mahan didn’t make it to the runoff. Now it’s Hilton in a runoff with Becerra that Becerra is obviously going to win.

Whether it’s internal to G.O.P. primaries or in tactical decision-making around these jungle primaries, you’re just not seeing a spirit of pragmatism among blue-state conservatives.

This then just raises the question of whether conservatives actually want to win races in these states or just prefer to complain. I get the sense that a lot of right-wing people are annoyed that Zohran Mamdani has taken a pragmatic approach to law enforcement and crime keeps falling. They would sort of rather see New York City be punished for its sins with far-left governance that causes the city to fall apart. Conservatives on the merits think the California wealth-tax proposal is a bad idea, but I think a lot of them will be happy if it passes — they would enjoy watching the state’s economy suffer a crisis more than they would enjoy getting their way on the issue.

Last but not least, most Republicans in the urban Northeast seem to conceptualize a critical economic policy issue — land use regulation — as primarily a culture war topic.

When Mikie Sherrill ran in New Jersey she endorsed some very tepid YIMBY ideas and for her trouble got denounced by her Republican opponent Jack Ciattarelli, who characterized the state as suffering from an “overdevelopment crisis.” Republicans in the state legislatures of New York, Connecticut, and Maryland have likewise been uniformly hostile to zoning reform. I understand the political psychology of this. Blue-state Republicans are emotionally oriented in opposition to urbanity and to the state government, so the idea of preemption to facilitate density is anathema. At the same time, it simply makes no sense to have a pro-business, pro-growth agenda in these states while ignoring what is by far the largest regulatory barrier to growth. NIMBY conservatism in the context of the actual urban/suburban American Northeast is just a crank movement rather than a problem-solving one.

Unfortunately, I see a lot of conservative elites who live in the Northeast Corridor and ought to know better engage in apologetics about this rather than try to reorient their state parties. I know it would be tough for the Manhattan Institute to just plainly say that New York Republicans are on the wrong side of the single most important economic issue facing the state, but the fact is they are.

Kevin Zielnicki: Patterns of overreach, backlash, and political blunder have me thinking about the original Thermidorians and an alternate history hypothetical. We follow our timeline up to 9 Thermidor Year II and the overthrow of Robespierre. From here, something diverges (better constitutional design? better monetary policy? better foreign policy?) such that instead of the fatally unpopular Directory leading to Napoleon’s coup, France gets a government that will mature into a stable liberal democracy. What does an enduring First Republic look like? And how does this alter the broader political trajectory of Europe?

When I took a French Revolution class in college, the professor took a very narrow view of the revolution and ended it with the overthrow of Robespierre rather than exploring the period between his overthrow and Napoleon’s seizure of power. But I think the most plausible point of departure here may be the Coup of 18 Fructidor.

What happened here is that the Directory, the five-man government that ruled France after Robespierre’s fall, was, as you said, unpopular. As a result, in the elections of March and April 1797, monarchists of different stripes won a majority of seats. Rather than accepting these results, three of the five directors along with Foreign Minister Talleyrand and Napoleon and his allies in the military staged a coup and purged the legislature. This was essentially a “destroy the village in order to save it” moment for the French Revolution, which left in place a regime with limited popular support and no ideological legitimacy whose whole base of support was just the army. Devolving from there into a dictatorship led by the army’s most popular and successful figure was a logical progression. But the coup itself was a somewhat non-obvious move. The immediate impact of purging the monarchists was to shift political control back to the left, contrary to the original purpose of having established the Directory in the first place. The plotters themselves did not necessarily like each other all that much or have aligned views about the direction of policy. If they’d just been less cooperative with each other, it’s not that hard to imagine the newly elected deputies taking their seats.

In theory, a monarchist majority might have meant an end to the revolution and the restoration of the monarchy. But the experience of the 1871 French elections, which generated a monarchist majority and no coup, suggests a different possibility. What happened in 1871, at the dawn of the Third Republic, is that the monarchists were themselves divided about exactly what kind of system they wanted to set up, nobody could secure majority support for anything, and France ended up becoming a durable republic.

Flash back to 1797, and the monarchist deputies-elect seem to have been a mix of hardcore absolutists who wanted a return to the ancien regime from before the French Revolution and people who were more like advocates of the kind of constitutional monarchy that the French Revolution had originally tried to set up. It strikes me as very likely that had the new deputies taken their seats, the median members would have been constitutional monarchists who would have found that the Bourbon royal family itself had no interest in being constitutional monarchs. The deputies would have ended up needing to try to manage a republican form of government that simply held some conservative attitudes toward things like religion. Bonaparte’s coup in the main timeline was, in part, an effort to shift policy back to the right after the Fructidor coup swung things to the left. Without the original coup there is less demand for the subsequent one. And it is at least possible that the mix of Napoleonic military success with relatively conservative government in Paris means that the revolutionary wars come to an end.

In real history, the Treaty of Campo Formio, signed between France and Austria shortly after the Fructidor coup, basically restored peace in Europe. But Britain did not join the peace, and eventually a new broader European war broke out. Perhaps with constitutional monarchists awkwardly running a republic, Britain signs a deal. With Europe at peace, Bonaparte is a celebrated war hero but not actually commanding an army or having further adventures and ends up going into civilian politics — like a French version of Andrew Jackson. In this timeline he is an ideal front man for the avowedly pro-republic, pro-revolution forces who want to regain a majority in parliament and need a respected popular leader.

From there any number of things could have happened, including Napoleon establishing himself as dictator. But I choose to believe that a peaceful transfer of power from non-Jacobin republicans to constitutional monarchs and then back again might have created a sufficient democratic norm to stabilize the situation. To me, though, the point is that the Fructidor coup is a key turning point because it’s the moment when the people with the correct “republic good, Reign of Terror bad” take turn against their own principles and create a situation where there’s really no rescuing the project.

Wandering Llama: Let’s say SlowBoring uses an AI for a research task. The AI agent seeks to find the answer to the best of its ability, and finds out a classified government report has the best answer. It hacks into the government system to get it and provides you with the output.

Questions:

1. Was a crime committed?

2. Who is liable? SlowBoring or the AI provider?

3. Should the government charge anyone? What is an appropriate punishment?

The genius of common law is that the answers to (1) and (2) are discovered by humans through the trial processes depending in part on prosecutors’ discretion around (3). I would say as a voter that it would be unreasonable for a district attorney to charge an L.L.M. user with a crime for an innocuous prompt. We’re looking instead at some kind of negligence charge against the maker of the L.L.M. The punishment would be financial penalties and, ideally, a consent decree around model behavior.

In practice, though, a big part of the solution to A.I.-enabled hacking is going to be A.I.-enabled cybersecurity. That’s especially because it’s easy to imagine a world where a lot of people end up using open-source models where this kind of liability deterrent may not be efficacious.

Broadly, though, I would say that a transition to a world where A.I. means “lots of random computer hacking happens” would be a process that generates a lot of grief and dramatic news stories but ultimately lands in a fine place. The main thing is really just that there are currently thousands and thousands of American institutions that can afford to be fairly casual about their information security and are going to need to tighten up practices — including by using A.I. to do the tightening. That’s a big deal, but I also think focusing on it excessively is a little bit like looking at the invention of the automobile and thinking, “What happens if criminals use cars to speed away from the cops? What if they use them to move rapidly from city to city doing crimes?” Those things obviously did both happen, but law enforcement officers also use cars. More broadly, you’re sort of missing the forest for the trees if you’re thinking about the impact of cars on society primarily through this lens.

To me, the big problems with A.I. are all about the possibility of an intelligence explosion and deceptive alignment leading to a genuine loss of human control. The hacking concerns fit into a “normal technology” bucket, and I think the common law is robust enough to address these issues.

Matt Dreyer: I’m going to D.C. indigenous people’s day weekend with a 7 year old and a 10 year old who have no recollection of being in D.C. in their lives. What should I prioritize in two days? They love the songs from Hamilton which makes Revolutionary War adjacent sites slightly more appealing though it’s not a strong preference.

I would say kids of that age are really in the sweet spot for the National Zoo and the Smithsonian’s Natural History (dinosaurs) and Air and Space museums, all three of which are conveniently free. A cooler fall day in particular is an ideal time for the zoo. Also I really like the zoo.

In terms of “Hamilton”-themed attractions, there is of course the Jefferson Memorial (which can be a great walk if the weather is nice or an annoying slog if not) and George Washington’s estate, Mount Vernon, which is just a bit out of town and I think a good visit but maybe too time consuming for your schedule. If you happen to be nearby, a lot of downtown hotels are very close to the Alexander Hamilton statue that’s due south of the Treasury building, which I personally like a lot. I think the U.S. Botanic Garden at the far southeastern end of the National Mall is a kind of underrated site, personally, and a good place for kids. A seven-year-old may love the carousel that’s right by the Smithsonian Castle.

Oliver: I want MY’s opinions of LKY.

That’s Lee Kuan Yew, Singapore’s founder and longtime leader, for those who aren’t hip to the nickname.

Singapore seems pretty great to me by the numbers, and I enjoyed it when I visited. I remember when I was in Russia in the summer of 1998 hearing a bunch of smart, angry Russian people saying that Boris Yeltsin was a disaster and the country needed a strongman leader like Lee Kuan Yew who could fix problems. They got Vladimir Putin instead, who I would say has not really shown the same level of technocratic rigor or level-headed decision-making. There’s this big list of policies, starting notably with Singapore’s early and aggressive use of congestion pricing, where it seems like “everyone” knows it’s a good idea, and yet the voters never seem to want to do it. Or, like, clearly the Singaporean mix of harsh anti-corruption measures in the public sector paired with genuinely very generous compensation for key officials is correct. But, again, the voters. So it’s very tempting to think we should just have a strong leader who does the good policies and it will work out for everyone just like in Singapore. But if I’ve heard the good news about Singapore and you’ve heard the good news about Singapore and random Russian dudes in 1998 have heard the good news about Singapore, then clearly there are some deeper reasons why relatively few countries are pursuing this approach.

I really liked Stefan Dercon’s book “Gambling on Development: Why Some Countries Win and Others Lose,” which tries to take seriously the question “if pro-growth reform is good, why doesn’t everyone do it?” After all, it’s not just that Singapore’s trajectory has been better than that of the vast majority of post-colonial regimes — this success has been very good for the personal interests of the leaders of the People’s Action Party! It’s not like doing good policy was some tremendous act of self-sacrifice. All kinds of leaders, democratic or authoritarian, would seem to be better off making smarter policy choices. Dercon’s main point about this is that even very positive growth trajectories can be bad for the interests of a range of incumbent elites and that aligning the stakeholders to believe that growth will be win-win is just very difficult. Part of the Lee story, I think, is that he’s an actual brilliant politician and not just a technocrat.

Oliver: Where does the $52,000 per pupil spending go at a failing New York school?

There are a lot of aspects to this, but one broad structural fact to consider is that very high per-student spending is often a downstream consequence of a school being bad.

Say you have a school where they are spending $40,000 per student but then, for whatever reason, the school is no good and enrollment drops by 5 percent. Well, a 5 percent drop in enrollment doesn’t actually reduce the cost of operating the school, so per-pupil spending goes up. But the 5 percent of families who leave are probably coming from the top of the distribution in terms of having smart, organized, attentive parents who care a lot about school. So per-pupil spending has gone up, but average test scores go down. Because test scores are getting worse, enrollment falls further. The only way to really address this is to close down the under-enrolled failing school. But the political backlash to school closures is intense. Some of that is labor union politics, but a lot of it is very authentic — people tend not to like it when their neighborhood school closes down.

Damian: What do you make of Peter Gray’s new book that asserts that the decline in youth mental health is due to academic pressures and school structure? If you agree then what does that mean for the future of schooling?

It’s annoying to comment on books that you haven’t read, but just going by the publicity materials, one of the things he argues is that “children need something that seems to be missing from modern childhood: the freedom to play, explore, solve problems, and take age-appropriate risks without adults constantly directing them.”

I agree with this, and it’s one reason even though it of course made me a little nervous, I was thrilled to have my 11-year-old start riding the city bus to and from school with no adult supervision. But I do also think that when childless adults wax nostalgic for the good old days of “go outside and play and come back in time for dinner” they are being a little bit out of touch with exactly how fun and engaging and affordable and ubiquitous contemporary video games are. To a first approximation, what unsupervised kids given “freedom to play” are going to want to do is play Fortnite. That doesn’t mean you need to let your kid play Fortnite for hours a day every day. But it does mean that you are in one way or another operating in a sphere of parental control if you want to get kids off their devices. They’re not going to just get bored with their games the way I got bored with my Nintendo.

This is also why I don’t quite buy the view that what’s driving the decline of independent play for kids is that we have, as the book’s publicity materials say, “made their lives more achievement-oriented” in pursuit of “helping them find success in the increasingly competitive adult world.”

Part of what you see when you participate in a diverse urban public school is that there is a wide range of parenting styles out there and a very large number of working-class families that are not at all focused on intensive parenting or raising achievement-oriented kids. These kids are sort of being parented with 20th century norms, but that doesn’t mean they are behaving like 20th century children. They have 21st century technology and, realistically, are spending a ton of time watching TikTok on their phones. And while you don’t need to give your kid a phone (Kate and I haven’t given ours one), you again get the tension between independence and the desire to control technology access. One thing our admirably independent 11-year-old does on the city bus, I think, is watch short-form videos over the shoulder of classmates who do have phones.

Siddhartha Roychowdhury: Is the Brightline bankruptcy the beginning of the end of delusional fantasies about HSR being a commercially viable project in most parts of the country outside the northeast corridor?

Brightline is not now and has never been high-speed rail! This drove me insane during the Brightline hype era and is now driving me insane in the Brightline non-hype era. It’s a conventional-speed regional rail project that has no implications whatsoever for high-speed rail in any part of the country because it is not high-speed rail.

It is also true that I don’t think the prospects for a Florida H.S.R. network are all that bright. If you eyeball the distances and the city sizes, then an Orlando-centric starfish network with branches to Jacksonville, Tampa, and Miami seems like it might make sense. But the issue is that if you live in any of these four cities, you probably have a car and you are probably going to want a car at any of the destinations, so it’s just really hard to beat “drive your car” as a proposition across those short distances. Obviously trains can compete with planes across a distance like Miami to Jacksonville — I think that if such a high-speed train existed, people would ride it. But what’s the point of building it? There’s no actual problem with flying.

So I agree with the conclusion: High-speed rail makes sense in the Northeast Corridor thanks to the unique conditions there. The key thing is that New York City has an enormous population, low rates of car ownership, an overcrowded airspace that literally cannot accommodate any additional plane flights, and is an extremely annoying place to take a car as a destination. Supplementing this is the fact that Boston, Philadelphia, and D.C. are all sort of halfway between New York and Jacksonville in terms of car ownership and utility. And then while you would not build a train purely for the purposes of serving population centers of the scale of Providence, New Haven, Wilmington, or Baltimore, the fact that you can serve these cities “for free” just because they happen to be on the way is a big win. The existing train has a lot of ridership on these routes and if it was faster, even more people would ride it. If you ended up with fewer intra-Northeast plane flights, the slots would be reallocated to serve flights to other cities and everyone would win.

Back to Brightline, though. As I understand it, the train operations are in fact profitable outside the cost of the debt that was incurred to build the train in the first place. This is, roughly speaking, what the bankruptcy process is for. I expect that what will emerge from this is a profitable regional passenger rail service that people in South Florida are glad exists but that investors lost money on. That’s kind of the genius of capitalism. Private investors took a swing at this project, seem to have lost their bet, but the state will still be better off for the fact that they took the swing.

The second Trump presidency is a world-historic failure

How did Trump fumble so badly?

Noah Smith
Oct 3
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

There’s a large market for “Trump is bad” posts. I wrote one of them back in May:

Are you tired of the Trump era yet?

Noah Smith
·
May 25
Read full story

It’s easy to tune these posts out, for at least two reasons. One is partisanship — as a reader, I’m sure you know how hard it is to separate “Trump is bad” from “Trump made me mad”. The second is fatigue — you’ve heard the familiar litany of all of Trump’s outrages, and reading it one more time is both redundant and depressing.

Today I’m going to do something a little different, which is to ask: Why, exactly, has the second Trump presidency been such a failure?

Trump is a failure in the eyes of the nation

Before I do that, we should establish that in the eyes of the nation, Trump’s second presidency has been a failure, at least so far. His approval rating, going into the midterm election, is at historic lows:

2:01 AM · Sep 26, 2026 · 683K Views
57 Replies · 274 Reposts · 1.27K Likes
Nate Silver
@NateSilver538
Trump approval now at -22.4, his low point for the term and now lower than at any point in his first term, even after Jan. 6. By comparison, he was at a "mere" -11.6 at this point in 2018.
5:21 PM · Sep 23, 2026 · 478K Views
122 Replies · 606 Reposts · 4.28K Likes

America was mildly disapproving of Trump in his first term; now, only his base is staying loyal. And even that base is eroding. On the cost of living — one of the key issues in 2024, and likely to be a key issue in the midterms — Republicans now disapprove of Trump:

InteractivePolls
@IAPolls2022

📊 IPSOS/REUTERS - Trump Approval Pres. Trump Approve: 32% (-3) Disapprove: 66% (+4) His lowest approval by Ipsos in either term —— 17% approve on cost of living 9/17-20 | 1,277 A https://t.co/ILSAuUtWdN
6:39 PM · Sep 21, 2026 · 72.5K Views
15 Replies · 105 Reposts · 473 Likes

Hilariously, a modest but growing number of people who voted for Trump in 2024 now say they never voted for him.

And despite the widespread belief that Trump’s cult of personality dominates the GOP, Republicans now tend to say they support the party rather than the president himself:

But nevertheless, the GOP is going to suffer from Trump’s unpopularity in the midterms. Prediction markets are increasingly sure that Dems will take the House, and they now also give Dems a better-than-even chance of winning the Senate, despite a very difficult map:

Polls showing Senate races moving toward the Dems might be overstating things, but polls have ended up understating Democratic support in special elections since Trump returned to power. Trump has resorted to desperately promising $5000 checks to every U.S. citizen if Republicans win the midterms. But so far, these wild bribe attempts are falling decidedly flat — in fact, they’re actively driving voters away.

All this is all the more remarkable because Democrats themselves are in disarray. The party has torn itself apart over Israel/Palestine, and the public is still deeply skeptical of Dems’ “woke” progressive ideology. But whereas Americans still trusted Republicans more on many issues in 2025, now they tend to trust Democrats on issues like the economy and immigration:

The GOP was more popular than the Dems as of one year ago; now that has reversed.

Even some of Trump’s most prominent allies are now distancing themselves from the president. Here’s Peter Thiel, one of the godfathers of the Tech Right:

Sheel Mohnot
@pitdesi
Thiel on Trump: “There are a lot of things I got wrong... was crazier than I thought. It was more dangerous than I thought.” “You wish they’d appointed more competent people.” “administration is… staffed by not very smart but very loyal people”
6:38 PM · Sep 26, 2026 · 3.79M Views
622 Replies · 881 Reposts · 6.37K Likes

I can’t rule out the possibility that someday we’ll all look back on Trump’s second presidency as a success. Perhaps winning the AI race will prove to be so much more important than everything else that Trump’s decision to stall AI regulation ends up swamping everything else he ever does.

But I don’t find it very useful to indulge in this kind of “too early to tell” speculation. The blunt fact is that Trump’s second term has already failed in the court of public opinion. This is an incredible, world-historic failure. And it didn’t have to be that way — Trump simply made a bunch of avoidable errors, for a mix of ideological and personal reasons.

Trump didn’t have to fail

Liberals and progressives — who constitute the majority of my own social circles and friend group — hate Trump with a passion, and always have. But when I analyze his performance in office, I try to be as nonpartisan as I can. When Donald Trump returned to the presidency, I noted that his first term actually hadn’t gone that badly:

The best-case scenario for Trump's second term

Noah Smith
·
November 28, 2024
Read full story

Trump’s first term was marked by a lot of shouting and social division, but yielded surprisingly benign results. The economy grew very solidly, though Trump (predictably) passed up the chance to cut the budget deficit. America’s economic response to the Covid shock was among the best in the world, though it ended up fueling inflation later. Trump’s administration showed surprising competence in developing a vaccine for Covid. And although Trump did nothing to reshore U.S. manufacturing, his election and his protectionist policies did produce a needed shift toward seeing international economics through a geopolitical lens.

Trump came back to office in 2025 with a modest but real mandate, having won the popular vote for the first time. He could have essentially run the same playbook from his first presidency — done a lot of shouting and blustering, purged the government of wokeness, halted the flood of asylum-seekers (i.e. “secured the border”), put some more tariffs on China, supported tougher policing in American cities, and called it a day. This is basically what America elected Trump to do, and it’s what I think most of his supporters probably envisioned for his second term, given how the first had gone.

Progressives would have hated it, of course, and high Democratic turnout might still have produced a modest blue wave. But I think that if Trump had stuck to this plan, the nation would have rewarded him with popularity and a grudgingly positive place in the history books. Only because he deviated so radically from this basic playbook is his presidency failing.

And although I don’t like it, I am forced to admit that many of the things that piss me off about Trump don’t seem like big factors in his low popularity. For example, I’m horrified by the administration’s anti-vaccine turn under RFK Jr. But despite the resurgence of measles in America, RFK’s crusade against Western medicine seems like only a minor electoral liability.

Nor does America seem particularly enraged about Trump withdrawing support for Ukraine, distancing America from NATO, or cozying up to Vladimir Putin. His bullying of Ukraine and his threats to invade Greenland are deeply unpopular, but don’t seem to have caused significant downward movements in his approval rating.

Other outrages seem to have had even less of an impact. Trump’s dismantling of USAID was unpopular, but the blame has mostly fallen on Elon Musk, who acted as a sort of ablative shield for Trump by removing himself from the political sphere. His purges of generals, his abuse of presidential power to attack law firms and media outlets, and his pardons for the perpetrators of the coup attempt of 1/6/2021 all seem to have flown below the radar of anyone who doesn’t follow politics closely or already hate Trump.

It’s possible, of course, that all of these things have contributed to a sort of general background distrust of Trump that has slowly eroded his approval rating over time. But Trump’s big second-term failures — the things that Americans say they dislike about his presidency — are basically just inflation and the Iran War.

Trump showed that he didn’t care about inflation

It’s barely exaggerating to say that Trump was elected in 2024 to address two things: inflation, and immigration. Those two issues dominated the polls in advance of the election, and of the two, inflation loomed larger. Trump was generally given better ratings on his ability to handle the economy — which, to most voters, meant the rising cost of living. Voters who emphasized economic issues broke hard for Trump.

But Trump failed to fix the economy. Inflation under Trump hasn’t been as bad as it was in 2021-22, but it has remained at around 3%, compared to 2% in Trump’s first term. And since the Iran War started, inflation has accelerated:

The surprise inflation has sent real wages back into decline for the first time since 2022, meaning that American workers are now getting poorer again:

Inflation has many causes, of course, and some of these are beyond Trump’s control — in particular, the massive AI investment boom that’s driving up prices for materials, electricity, and so on. But from the very start, Trump showed very clearly that he didn’t really care about bringing inflation down.

First, there were the tariffs. Everyone knows that tariffs raise prices for American consumers. Trump knows this too — when the price of beef rose earlier this year, Trump temporarily lowered tariffs in order to bring prices down.

Tariffs have defined Trump’s approach to economic policy during his second term. Although walkbacks, “deals”, court rulings, and plenty of exceptions have blunted the negative impact of tariffs, they’ve still raised prices somewhat:

A 0.5% increase in inflation is not huge or catastrophic. But it sends a very clear signal that inflation isn’t Trump’s top priority.

Nor was it the only such signal. Trump let deficits rip, boosting spending even as he cut taxes. Americans may not instinctively think of deficits as inflationary (as many economics models do), but they understand exactly what it means when Trump says that higher inflation is helpful for paying off the debt:

[I]n a recent interview with Time…Trump also said something that will prick the ears of economists: "You know, inflation, certain levels of inflation, will also pay off that debt very rapidly. Very rapidly." [emphasis mine]

Intentionally running up debt and then using inflation to “pay off” the debt — which is actually a soft default rather than “paying” anything back — is the classic way that governments set off hyperinflationary spirals. So when Trump runs up the debt and then talks about inflating it away “very rapidly”, people know what that means. Even if an actual hyperinflation never happens, the fact that Trump was willing to prioritize handing out fiscal goodies over bringing down the cost of living probably makes an impression on at least some voters.

But of course Trump’s most inflationary move was the Iran War. In Trump’s first term, gas was $2.50 a gallon. When he took office it was around $3, but after Trump recklessly went to war with Iran, it shot up to over $4:

Expensive gasoline feeds through to the rest of the economy in plenty of ways, since gasoline is so important for transporting people and goods. So expensive gas is definitely feeding into the higher inflation we’ve seen in 2026. But there’s also evidence that Americans care about gas prices even more than they care about inflation in general. This is probably a big part of why the Iran War is the most unpopular war since Vietnam.

So time and again, Trump has shown that inflation is low on his list of priorities. He was elected to bring down inflation, and instead he willfully made it worse, through a combination of protectionism, fiscal profligacy, and military adventurism. No wonder inflation is the issue where Americans give Trump the lowest marks:

As they’ve realized that Trump has no intention to actually attack inflation, even Republicans’ economic mood has begun to sour:

Joe Weisenthal
@TheStalwart
THE FIRST INTERESTING SENTIMENT SURVEY IN YEARS Surveys like UMich and Conference Board don't get the attention they used to, because the numbers have been so rancid for so long. But the collapsing mood among Republicans with an R-White House is a real development.
5:51 PM · Sep 11, 2026 · 93.6K Views
22 Replies · 86 Reposts · 559 Likes

Alternative measures of economic sentiment, which had held up much better than the standard University of Michigan numbers, have now also gone into steep decline.

America is tired of leaders who stoke racial division

The #2 issue that Americans wanted Trump to address was immigration — specifically, the flow of quasi-legal asylum seekers across the southern border. This has, in fact, been accomplished, with border encounters going from a quarter million per month to approximately zero almost the instant Trump took office:

Trump could have taken this victory and called it a day. Instead, he decided to engage in a program of mass deportations. And instead of focusing on deporting illegal immigrants who committed crimes — as Barack Obama had done — he sent ICE to round up anyone they could find who might be in the country illegally.

Naturally, this involved a large element of racial profiling. ICE just ended up grabbing any Hispanic-looking person and demanding to see their papers. This has made many Hispanic voters realize that immigration enforcement isn’t just coming for the immigrants. Polls show that ICE’s overreach is a big reason that Hispanic voters are shifting back toward the Democrats this cycle, after trending Republican for years. Stories about Hispanics who regret having voted for Trump have become commonplace.

This is an enormous electoral own goal for the Trump movement. In 2024 it looked as if the GOP were succeeding in converting Hispanics to their cause, thus neutralizing the threat of the “emerging Democratic majority” that so many had feared. Without Hispanics on board, MAGA’s path to victory looks a lot more difficult:

Trip Gabriel
@tripgabriel
NYT's Nate Cohn: A strong erosion of Trump's support with Hispanic voters imperils the party in more than a dozen districts Trump won by double digits, while cueing up Texas and Florida to "become ground zero for a possible Democratic tsunami"
nytimes.com
Hispanic Voters, Abandoning Trump, Are Transforming the Midterm Map (Gift Article)
7:43 PM · Sep 22, 2026 · 500K Views
52 Replies · 419 Reposts · 1.86K Likes

But Trump’s missteps on immigration have gone far beyond what ICE is doing in the streets. It has become abundantly clear that MAGA sees immigration policy through a fundamentally racial lens. Trump has promised to stop all immigration from “third world” countries, even as he hurries to roll out the welcome mat for white South African refugees. JD Vance has spoken about his desire to cut off legal immigration. And the Trump administration has put gigantic fees on H-1B visas, making these much harder to obtain.

Trump’s crusade against H-1Bs, despite strong Republican support for higher levels of skilled immigration, is especially telling. These visas have become identified with Indian immigration, and the GOP base has rapidly become more openly racist against Indians specifically:

The anti-American Right

Noah Smith
·
Sep 16
Read full story

Scholars from the Manhattan Institute — hardly the most racially oriented of the conservative think tanks — are now releasing podcast episodes on “The Indian Question”:

The American public doesn’t like this sort of thing. After Texas Railroad Commissioner candidate Bo French denounced the presence of Indian American fans at a UT Austin football game, polls showed a strong negative reaction among regular Texans:

The combination of rampant racial profiling of Hispanics and pure animus toward Indians leaves no doubt about what Trump’s anti-immigration campaign is all about. It is a campaign to racially re-engineer the American populace. Karl Rove, hardly anyone’s idea of a screechy woke progressive, now says the GOP is being taken over by “Nazis”.

It’s hard to say how much the GOP’s turn toward race war has hurt its electoral chances. But it’s notable that in Trump’s first term, his decline in popularity set in after the Unite the Right rally. A decade ago, Americans really disliked racism and were inclined to punish it in the polls.

Between then and now, progressives massively overreached on race. They embraced explicit racial discrimination in hiring, promotion, and every other walk of life, in defiance of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and often of the 14th Amendment. Endless discussions of race, with guilt and “privilege” assigned collectively instead of to individuals, became standard in progressive circles.

Americans punished the Democrats in 2024 for their extreme views on race. That gave an opening to elements of the Right who wanted to prosecute their own race wars on the stage of American politics. But Americans didn’t simply oppose the leftist version of racial struggle — they oppose all such divisive efforts, and want to be treated as individuals. They don’t want to simply trade one set of race warriors for a different set — but they’re quickly waking up to the reality that this is exactly what they did in 2024.

Corruption is starting to break through to the public consciousness

In general, anger at inflation and the Iran War is the most important reason Trump’s presidency is being rejected, and souring on his approach to immigration is probably #2. His rightist foreign policy, anti-vaccine policies, and general authoritarian overreach are probably smaller factors, but contribute to the general impression of a failed presidency.

But there’s one more issue that I haven’t seen much polling on, that I suspect might be contributing to Trump’s loss of popularity: corruption.

By any reasonable reckoning, Donald Trump is by far the most corrupt president in U.S. history. Here’s a good summary of all the main ways that Trump has used the office of the presidency to increase his personal fortune — rampant insider trading, misuse of personal property for government functions, giving government contracts to his relatives, giving his own companies lucrative foreign deals, and so on. But all you really have to do is look at a chart of Trump’s personal wealth, which has increased by $5 billion since he returned to the presidency:

Note the giant red “cryptocurrency and liquid assets” bar at the bottom of that huge pile of ill-gotten gains. As I warned last year, crypto has become the perfect vehicle for corruption — people can essentially bribe Trump by buying his memecoins.

I had been pretty pessimistic about all of this breaking through to the public consciousness. Americans are constantly being bombarded with allegations of corruption — Hillary and Bill Clinton were both prime targets, as was Nancy Pelosi. My default assumption was that this had made the populace so numb — so used to either believing all of those allegations or tuning them out entirely — that they would ignore real, massive corruption when it came along.

But perhaps I was wrong. Perhaps Americans are starting to wake up:

It’s not inconceivable that this is another reason America is turning away from MAGA and the GOP.

Of course, seen in this light, calling Trump’s presidency a “failure” might be a bit of a misnomer. He’s failed the country and failed his party. But perhaps he was never very interested in doing right by either one. If Trump’s purpose was always just to make himself rich and powerful, his presidency has been a spectacular success. Maybe that’s all it was ever about.
