The dream of Blue Texas

Plus my “Moby Dick” limited series and the problem with primaries

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 9
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Before I get to this week’s Mailbag, I’ve gotten some questions about whether or not we have an updated list of donation recommendations since the slate we published back in July. And the answer is — no, I think those recommendations hold up.

To be clear, though, the presumption of the recommendation is that you are a normal person interested in making small- to medium-sized hard-money contributions to candidates. We identified a list of people based on a balance of how pivotal/strategic their race is, how much extra money is actually needed, and how aligned the candidate is with Slow Boring’s priorities and worldview. To make a list like this useful, I think it’s important to keep the list short, and that means that plenty of perfectly good candidates running in important races end up off the list.

If you’re a billionaire who can easily afford to give to more candidates, you should by all means do that. I feel bad to not be recommending Scott Wiener (who’s been on our list in the past) in his runoff against Connie Chan, for example. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who’s running for governor of Alaska, is amazing. I’m very intrigued by what Adam Hamilton is cooking up in Kansas. There’s a wide range of worthy House challengers associated with the Blue Dogs and Welcome PAC who I like a lot. I wouldn’t want anyone to assume that the failure to include someone who seems broadly Slow Boring-aligned reflects a negative judgment on them as candidates. It’s just that I think the list is most effective when it’s really selective and reflects judgment not just about the candidates but about where your hard money is most likely to make a difference.

Speaking of which, we’ve raised nearly $1 million for the slate so far. That’s a ton in a cycle when fundraising has generally been a problem for Dems. Thanks for everything you do!

Greg S: There are many ways to gauge influence but one is access to powerful people. How many US Senators would take your phone call directly?

I have the phone numbers of exactly three senators. I don’t know that they’d pick up if I called out of the blue, but I try to text judiciously.

Neil Mehrotra: Can Gina Hinojosa really win Texas governor’s race? Her profile as a state legislator would not have seemed to position her to win statewide, but she seems to have successfully positioned herself as a moderate. Is this just an example of the Abbott campaign being slow to respond?

The polls show her within striking distance but definitely behind. For her to win you’d need there to be a meaningful polling error in Democrats’ favor (which is conceptually possible but I wouldn’t bank on it) or for something new to happen in the race that deals a further blow to Abbott. The betting odds heavily favor Greg Abbott, and I don’t see any reason to doubt that.

If the final result ends up being like the polls — which is to say close-ish but not exactly a razor-thin margin — I think people will think of it as a missed opportunity on two levels.

One is that while Hinojosa has run an extremely smart campaign with some very based campaign ads touting her law enforcement endorsements, featuring a January 6 participant who’s supporting her, and portraying herself as an advocate of low taxes, she’s not really someone who has a pre-campaign reputation as a moderate. The ideal profile for a statewide Democratic candidate in Texas would be a Hispanic moderate from South Texas. Vicente Gonzalez or some equivalent type of guy in the state legislature or former Representative Filemon Vela would be my top choices.

The other is just that while Democrats had a big financial edge in the early Trump election cycles, the money now favors Republicans. If this were the 2018 or 2020 fundraising environment, I think there’d be a strong case for investing a lot of money in Hinojosa’s gubernatorial run. She could conceivably win, and a win there would be very high value. Spending on her campaign would be complementary to spending on a key Senate race and a couple of key House races. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s just hard to make the case for it in a world of financial scarcity where Democrats are at a financial disadvantage all across the board.

Why is it competitive at all despite a non-ideal nominee and scarce money? Well, for one, again, Hinojosa doesn’t have a perfect profile but she’s running a smart campaign. Another factor that she (like Rob Sand in Iowa and Amy Acton in Ohio) has going for her is that when it comes to wrong-party gubernatorial candidates, you have a built-in margin of comfort. That is, if you’re sick of Abbott and you’d like to see Texas public policy get a little bit less right-wing but also don’t trust progressives, you don’t need to believe that Hinojosa is a moderate deep in her heart to vote for her. You know that it’s just the case that the policy status quo in Texas is very right-wing, that the legislature is very right-wing, that other statewide elected officials will be right-wing, that all kinds of commissions will be full of legacy Abbott appointees, etc. There is zero chance of Texas state government becoming an off-the-rails progressive policy zoo. And her actual agenda is fairly limited. Hinojosa is promising to roll back the voucherization of the high-performing public-school system that George W. Bush and Rick Perry built. She’s going to be more skeptical of data centers. She’ll try to expand Medicaid. It will be an uphill struggle for her to achieve even these goals, so if you like that agenda, you can comfortably vote for her and not worry too much about the risk that she may secretly harbor further-left views.

Beyond that, Abbott’s problem is that he’s been in office a long time and he’s the third Republican governor in a row and there’s been a G.O.P. trifecta for a long time and it’s just hard to govern for a really long time without eventually overreaching and pissing people off. The longer any party coalition governs, the more scandals accumulate and the more undisciplined its leaders become. It gets easier for voters to take for granted whatever they like about them and harder for aligned interest groups to take “no” for an answer about their most unsound ideas. You see a version of this in the relatively tight polling for the Oregon governor’s race. I think Tina Kotek will probably pull it off, but if there were a Democrat in the White House, she’d be in real trouble.

Paul: Is a jury of your peers really the best way to achieve just outcomes?

Probably not. But it does seem good at achieving what I think it is meant to achieve, namely making it difficult to abuse criminal prosecutions for political purposes.

Kirby: What do you think of sortition systems? It seems like the average voter is more civically minded than the median voter, if that makes sense.

I am very interested in sortition, which is basically jury duty for legislative functions.

A common American form of municipal government, for example, is the council-manager system. I wonder if it wouldn’t make more sense in most of those cases to have a council selected by sortition. The actual governing of the city would be done by a professional city manager, but the manager would need to present an annual budget that he talks through with a randomly selected council of residents and those residents would also have the power to fire the city manager and hire a new one.

Mechanical Buttons: If you were extremely wealthy and had decision- making power at one of the streaming services, what show would you have made? Assume you don’t need to recoup the costs.

The answer is that I would like to see someone make a “Moby Dick” limited series.

For starters, C.G.I. has progressed to the point where it’s probably cost-effective to do the whale-hunting action stuff in a way that looks decent in a television context. Beyond that, though, this classic American novel is really something that doesn’t work as a movie. “Moby Dick” is long, it’s digressive, and more to the point the digressions are integral to what the book is. Trying to chop it down into a streamlined adventure story doesn’t make sense.

The way to do it is to take advantage of the fact that television as a medium allows you to have episode-to-episode inconsistency in the style and tone of the program. It’s common for modern shows to be shot like a very long movie with a lot of stylistic continuity. But think about how “WandaVision” would deliberately play with the format. Or how “Buffy” had a musical episode. Or how “Star Trek: The Next Generation” would sometimes be a costume drama inside the holodeck. “Moby Dick,” in particular, should just have certain segments that are mockumentaries about whales or the whaling industry.

Share

Some other thoughts:

  • The documentary segments should be narrated by John Hodgman and done in the tone of “The Areas of My Expertise.”

  • The iconic line “Call me Ishmael” should be spoken dialogue, not voiceover. It should be the narrator trying to make conversation with an indifferent fellow traveler on a boat to New Bedford.

  • The theme music should be “Gigantic” by the Pixies.

Last but not least, they should try to cast Americans in the American roles rather than the HBO thing of constantly casting British people (I love Kelly MacDonald, but that was an insane accent in “Lanterns” for a Midwestern sheriff from Gotham City).

But just in case any executives are out there reading, I don’t think this is some kind of crazy “if I had a billion dollars and money was no object” scheme. I think this is actually a good idea and it would get a lot of attention and people would watch. There is just honestly not that much equivalently iconic intellectual property out there waiting for someone to grab. Obviously there is a history of people attempting to do adaptations of “Moby Dick,” but none of them are well-regarded, and I think the fundamentals of “really long story that involves whale hunts” have just basically not been realizable until the modern era. Under today’s conditions, though, I don’t see why you couldn’t do it.

Tom Scheinfeldt: Swim dad here. Age group swimming can be pretty intense, swim parents especially. How’s everyone in the Yglesias household holding up?

Our kid is on what counts as a relatively low-key swim team by D.C. area standards (which still means four practices per week, some of them very early), so I haven’t seen any unhinged parental behavior. It’s a slightly weird sport as a spectator because it’s such a high ratio of sitting around to actually watching your kid compete, but two things I like about it are that it’s extremely healthy with minimal injury risk and that the basically objective nature of swim times means that they can’t lie to you about your kid’s prospects.

Bloodknight: What was the point of the Alliance to Restore the Republic? In both timelines the New Republic fails in roughly thirty years either because of the Star Tek villains that are the Vong or to the clear mishandling of the post-Imperial transition under Mon Mothma. Does the continuation of Coruscant as the seat of government matter? Absent the out of nowhere Vong invasion does Leia outperform the Canon timeline version of Mon Mothma as head of the Republic?

George Lucas originally described the Rebel Alliance as inspired by the Viet Cong (worth keeping in mind for complaints that later iterations of the franchise got too woke), which was a highly disciplined and ideologically unified movement. More recent depictions have shown what was actually a quite fractious set of disparate opposition forces.

In particular, the prequels show a strong axis of conflict around centralization versus decentralization operating within the context of the Old Republic. Palpatine himself originally gains power as an advocate of centralization within the context of republican institutions, only later seizing power by transforming the Republic into a personalistic dictatorship. So you always have a tension inside the rebel movement between the idea of reclaiming power for the Senate rather than an emperor and the idea of decentralizing authority. This is closer in spirit maybe to the situation in Afghanistan, where both the mujahideen resistance to the Soviet Union and the later alliance against the Taliban were mishmashes of groups with competing ideas that were unified against a common enemy but not really pursuing a common goal. That sort of rebellion is prone to collapsing after winning.

Oliver: If you were running Malaysia or Uganda in the 1960s, how would you deal with the extreme disparity of wealth and business control between the majority and the minority without destroying the economy?

I don’t really know anything about Malaysia, but clearly whatever they did worked a lot better.

cp6: I got into an argument with some relatives recently. I said that privatizing federally owned ranchland would be a good idea, and they claimed that this would lead to all the ranches being sold to developers and converted to suburbia. I tried to tell them that this would only happen to a small number because it wouldn’t make economic sense for most of them, but they simply didn’t believe me and insisted that I didn’t know what I was talking about and all the ranches would definitely get developed.

If they were talking to you, what would you say to them?

The right way to think about privatizing non-park federal land is that it would make other western states look more like Texas, where there is very little federally owned land. It is true that the existence of vast stretches of privately owned ranch land in Texas facilitates suburban sprawl because where housing demand exists, there is a strong tendency to sell the land off to housing developers. This is also, as I said on Tuesday, a major reason there is a lot of renewables development in Texas.

That being said, it’s not like there are no ranches in Texas. Outside of the Northeast Corridor and California, most land in the United States is not particularly valuable, and its highest and best use is in fact as some kind of agriculture. So it’s both true that privatizing more western land would facilitate more suburb-building and also that the land mostly would not be turned into housing subdivisions.

In general, I think people underrate the benefits of land use flexibility. I think you should be allowed to construct gigantic Billionaires’ Row-style supertall apartments on all the residential land in the United States. Obviously, though, there is almost nowhere that someone would actually want to do that. Most people do not want to live in supertall buildings, the construction cost per square foot of such buildings is high, and most land is not that expensive. It’s just that the deadweight loss of quantity restrictions on housing is very large, the question of where demand exists is not entirely predictable in advance, it’s not the worst thing in the world for the occasional investor to go bust via overbuilding, and patterns of demand change and we all ought to be flexible. But when you say “unlimited density on all residential land,” there’s a tendency to imagine every parcel being suddenly converted into Hong Kong or something. Even in literal New York City this mostly wouldn’t happen, just as Texas mostly isn’t suburbs of Dallas. You just want maximum flexibility to build the housing that there is demand for, rather than the current dynamic of constraints on all sides.

Share

Eliot: In your interview with Jon Favreau, you argued that moderates need to be “looser” to attract attention in a Dem presidential primary, citing the appeal of Platner’s unpredictability and Gallego as a mod who might pull it off. But don’t Platner’s unraveling and the emerging view that there’s something “shady” about Gallego illustrate the risks of that approach?

To be clear, yes. Primary elections are bad. The nature of the primary is to hand inordinate power to advocacy groups and media figures who lack any kind of accountability and responsibility, and everything that is helpful to winning a primary is anti-correlated with attributes that are useful for winning general elections and governing effectively. That’s my whole point. General election voters love candidates who are both boring and moderate.

Primary electorates are skeptical of moderates, but beyond that, the only way to win a primary is to get a lot of attention. I was arguing that a good way to get attention and be “exciting” without adopting a ton of dumb issue positions is to be looser and less scripted as a public figure (see Donald Trump). Literally none of this is a good idea, though. The best way to pick a 2028 nominee would be to run a boring-but-popular red- or purple-state governor. The issue is that we don’t pick nominees that way. Given the system that we have, you have to try to come up with the least-damaging approach. What Steve Bullock and Amy Klobuchar tried in 2020 — just be an obviously strong electability choice and hope that electability-minded voters will vote for you — doesn’t work. You need to come up with some kind of razzle-dazzle.

Now I do think it’s true that in a world where politicians are advised to be very cautious, there is going to be a certain correlation between a loose media style and an overall lack of discipline. But that’s a contingent relationship. If the conventional wisdom about ideal media strategies shifts, then people who are buttoned-up in other aspects of their life can be more interesting and get more attention.

Why Donald Trump won in 2024

Re-upping my election post-mortem, so that we don’t forget.

Noah Smith
Oct 11
 
READ IN APP
 

Everyone except the die-hard faithful now realizes that Donald Trump’s second presidency is a colossal failure. The president is doing his best to gin up symbolic, minor controversies in order to activate negative polarization and distract from his spectacular failures on inflation, the Iran War, corruption, racial harmony, and so on. These include demanding that artificial intelligence be renamed “artificial superintelligence”, bellowing that he should have won the Nobel Peace Prize, and conducting an execution on live TV. The goal is to get Republicans fighting Democrats over these controversies, in order to trick everyone into focusing on how much they hate the other team instead of how much they hate Trump.

The trick will probably fail, just as Trump’s promise to give every American $5000 for voting Republican backfired. All of these little tempests-in-teapots simply reinforce what a cruel, selfish, petty buffoon Trump is. And Trump’s approval rating just drifts lower and lower:

Trump will probably lose the midterms, and become a lame duck president, spamming increasingly grandiose, unworkable executive orders while battling a stream of Congressional investigations.

That means the window is closing on my ability to force Democrats to reckon with their failures during the Biden years. If and when Trump loses a national election, there will be far less pressure for soul-searching on the left. And once the GOP is no longer in control of all three branches of government, the Democrats will be able to influence actual policy instead of sitting around rebuilding their brand.

So before that happens, I want to summon the last fading scraps of the self-reflection that Democrats and progressives were briefly forced into after Trump thumped Kamala Harris two years ago. When Trump won, I wrote four blog posts trying to explain where the Democrats had gone wrong:

Identity politics isn't working

Noah Smith
·
November 7, 2024
Read full story

Americans hate inflation more than they hate unemployment

Noah Smith
·
November 8, 2024
Read full story

The educated professional class is out of touch with America

Noah Smith
·
November 10, 2024
Read full story

The blue cities must be fixed

Noah Smith
·
November 12, 2024
Read full story

So today I’m going to repost all four parts of my election post-mortem, so that the progressives and Democrats among my readers can take one final moment to reflect on how not to enable the rise of authoritarian rightist leaders in future election cycles.

Identity politics isn’t working

I’ve made no secret of the fact that I think Trump is a terrible choice for America, but there’s no denying that the American people have made their choice. Trump is currently projected to win every single swing state. He outperformed his 2020 performance in every single county in the country. He’s projected to win a solid majority of the popular vote — the first time a Republican has done so since 2004. I still don’t like the Electoral College as an institution, but you can’t blame it for this result like you could for 2016. In fact, Trump’s victory was part of a more general Republican landslide — the GOP took the Senate and improved its majority in the House. A map of political shifts between 2020 and 2024 shows almost solid red.

I suppose a small silver lining here is that we won’t have to spend the next two months enduring waves of “Stop the Steal” election denials, lawsuits, and threats to repeat January 6th. Democracy delivered Trump a victory, and so Trump has little incentive to attack democracy.

In fact, that silver lining might extend to the long term too. Trump and the GOP won because nonwhite voters and working-class voters — traditional Democratic constituencies — shifted his way. Dems still won Hispanic, Black, and Asian voters overall, but their margins fell significantly from previous elections, while actually improving with White voters:

In fact, exit polls show Trump winning a solid majority of Hispanic men!

Update: Over at Matt Yglesias’ blog, Jed Kolko shows that heavily Hispanic areas swung harder toward Trump than any other parts of the country:

Ronald Reagan’s prophecy that Latinos would become Republicans is coming to pass.

Income has realigned as well. Democrats are now the party of the educated upper middle and wealthy class, but have lost their appeal to the middle and working classes:

This largely destroys the narrative that nonwhite immigration will demographically drown White Americans under a tide of imported minority votes. In fact, it vindicates my guest poster Wally Nowinski, who observed that high-turnout elections like this one now help Republicans, because marginal voters — working-class Americans and Hispanic Americans — now lean to the right:

Democrats benefit from low turnout now

Wally Nowinski
·
July 21, 2024
Read full story

At some point, Republicans are going to realize this, and hopefully become less anxious about America’s racial future. Hopefully they will also realize that any attempt to make voting harder actually hurts them in the future, because the impact would fall disproportionately on their own base.

I expect these realizations to take some time to sink in, but ultimately their effect could be very salutary for American democracy. In the days of Nixon and Reagan, Republicans never worried about democracy itself — it was obviously on their side. Even in 2004, Republicans could tell themselves that we lived in a “center-right nation”. Now, Trump’s victory, powered by lower-income Americans and Hispanic men, will hopefully convince the GOP that democracy is still a game they can win.

A democracy needs both major parties to believe they can win via persuasion rather than by organized resistance, and 2024 showed that Republicans can still do that — even if the method of persuasion is one that I personally wish hadn’t worked so well.

If you want an optimistic take, there it is.

So what other important lessons can we learn from this disappointing election result? I didn’t title this post “Why Trump won”, because I don’t think I really have a convincing answer — I’m not a political scientist, or even a political pundit. In fact, there are probably a bunch of reasons, not just one.

Nor am I going to be one of those pundits who tells you that if only Democrats had listened to my policy priorities, things would have gone very differently. In fact, few Americans care about my own policy priorities. My top issues are industrial policy and pro-democratic foreign policy. I definitely don’t think emphasizing those more, or doing more of those things, would have propelled Harris to victory. (I don’t think they would have hurt; I think voters just don’t care.)

But I do think there are some important lessons that we can already learn from this election, especially at the intersection of economics and politics. In particular, I see three big ones:

  1. Identity politics — viewing racial groups as homogeneous “communities” to be targeted with appeals to collective grievances — is not an effective way of winning over Hispanic (or, probably, Asian) voters.

  2. People care about inflation more than about unemployment.

  3. The educated professional class has become dangerously out of touch with the rest of the country.

Instead of writing all of these in one post, I’m going to split it into three, because I think the lessons are each very important. Since I’ve already shown the racial and class breakdown of the exit polls, I’ll talk about how identity politics is failing Democrats. Whether or not you think identity politics drove voters into Trump’s arms, it certainly hasn’t done an effective job of retaining Hispanic voters. The whole approach needs a deep rethink.

Americans are individuals, not extensions of racial “communities”

In the 2010s, there was a big debate over identity politics, with scholars like Francis Fukuyama warning that treating the American electorate as a balkanized set of racial collectives was undermining democracy. Stacey Abrams and other progressive writers pushed back against Fukuyama, arguing that all politics is identity politics, and so Democrats should continue focusing on racial appeals.

Abrams et al. were right in the facile, definitional sense that people’s personal identification with larger groups, movements, and ideas — rather than their own personal economic interests — drives much of their political behavior. After all, if human beings were rational calculating machines, they wouldn’t even vote, given the incredibly low probability that any election will be decided by a single vote.¹

But the 2024 election — even more than the 2020 election — makes it clear that most Hispanic and Asian voters don’t want to be appealed to based on the racial group of which they’re supposedly a part. For example, lenient policies toward asylum seekers from Latin America don’t seem to have won over many Hispanics:

In Hidalgo County, in South Texas — a Mexican American stronghold that Biden won with 58% of the vote in 2020 — Vice President Harris and Trump were virtually tied early Wednesday, with Harris leading by less than half a percentage point…In Cameron County, at the southern tip of Texas’ Rio Grande Valley, Trump led Harris, 52-47, according to early results. Biden won that county with 56% of the vote four years ago.

The whole notion that lenient policies on illegal and quasi-legal immigration would win inroads with Latinos was based on the idea that Hispanic Americans identify strongly with others of their same race. Political scientists call this the theory of “linked fate”.

Democrats clearly buy into this theory when they refer to racial groups as “communities”. This term has become ubiquitous in Democratic messaging — for example, Harris talked about her “economic agenda for the Latino community”.

But races are not communities. Our country is not like a segregated 1930-era city, where Black people live in a ghetto, Chinese people live in Chinatown, Italian people live in Little Italy, and so on. Hispanic and Asian Americans might share a sense of “linked fate” with others of their race, but it’s only one of many things they care about, and perhaps not even a major one.

The big exception, of course, is Black Americans, who continue to vote mostly like a racial bloc, despite Trump’s modest inroads with Black men. This has clearly influenced the Democrats’ view of how racial politics operates in America, and they’ve tried to apply the same mental model to Hispanics and Asians. This is explicit in California, where you hear the term “Black and brown” thrown around a lot.²

But it isn’t working. In fact, it’s backfiring. A recent paper by d’Urso and Roman found that use of the term “Latinx” actually made Hispanics vote for the Republicans in nontrivial numbers!

Group labels are political, but little theory and evidence explains how group labels shape politician evaluations…Latinos’ relationship with “Latinx,” a gender-inclusive label, is a theoretical test case. Using several datasets, we find: Latinos are less likely to support politicians who use “Latinx”…Latinos who oppose “Latinx” are less likely to support politicians who used or are associated with “Latinx”…Latinos in areas where “Latinx” is more salient are more likely to switch their vote toward Trump between 2016-2020[.]

One common interpretation of this result — and one the authors discuss — is that many Latinos are conservative, and that this makes them susceptible to “anti-LGBTQ+” labels. I’m highly skeptical of this interpretation. Outside small, highly educated, deeply progressive circles, who even knows that the purpose of the “x” in “Latinx” was to be trans-inclusive? Almost no one who is likely to be offended by the term is even aware of this.

Instead, what they hear is simply someone making up a weird label and applying it to them. It’s what sociologists call ascription — it’s someone making up a racial category for someone else and then stuffing them into it without their consent. The Occam’s Razor explanation for Hispanics’ dislike of “Latinx” is that it minoritizes them — it declares that they’re part of a special “community”, separate from other Americans.

Democrats’ purpose in assigning Americans to “communities”, of course, is not to exclude them, but to reward them — to hand them special prizes or favors via government policy. For example, the Biden administration had a whole policy oriented around giving government benefits specifically to “HSIs” — an abbreviation for “Hispanic-Serving Institutions”, i.e. colleges that a lot of Hispanic people tend to go to. Harris also had a plan for encouraging small banks to give Hispanic people more loans.

This is, fundamentally, a special-interest model of politics — it’s similar to the kind of quid pro quo that historically dominates much of urban machine politics. I’m not sure whether today’s Dems inherit their instinct for this kind of group giveaway from their old Tammany Hall days, but it’s recognizably similar to the way California cities hand out cash to favored nonprofits — especially because the programs are often targeted at colleges or banks or nonprofits or other organizations that claim to serve the racial “community” in question.

But there are notable downsides to this approach. First, unlike in a city, these targeted initiatives probably don’t make it through to the public consciousness. What Puerto Rican voter in Philadelphia even knows what the heck an “HSI” is? But more fundamentally, I think most Americans, including most Hispanic Americans, would rather be treated as individuals than as members of a racial “community”.

Identity politics and minoritization

Identity has many components. For my part, I identify as an American, a Texan, a liberal, a rabbit keeper, a writer, a nerd, a PhD holder, a science fiction fan, a Jew, a white person, a Lithuanian-American, and so on.³ If politicians primarily spoke to me as part of the “Jewish community”, I would be annoyed, because I don’t necessarily want to be defined by that component of my identity. I don’t reject it, but I don’t want to be reduced to it either. And if politicians tried to appeal to me with policies targeted through Jewish organizations to benefit Jews, I would simply not care. In fact, I would be a little conflicted about accepting any of those benefits, since it would pigeonhole me into prioritizing an identity that exists as only one component among many.

Even more fundamentally, being constantly minoritized — being told to think of myself as a Jew first and as an American second — would pressure me to shrink the circle of people that I consider part of my own in-group. Because I think of myself as an American first and foremost, I feel like there are 330 million other people who share my primary identity — 330 million people on my “team”. But if I were to think of myself first and foremost as a Jewish person, that would shrink my in-group to only 16 million, almost none of whom live near me. It would make me feel more isolated, and might even cause me to start questioning whether the 323 million non-Jewish Americans who live all around me have my best interests in mind.

In other words, being set apart from your fellow countrymen and neighbors is generally not a desirable thing, even if the reason is to put you on a pedestal.

I suspect many Hispanic Americans feel the same way. Talking to Hispanic folks (remember, I’ve lived most of my life in either Texas or California) and reading books like The Diversity Paradox, The New Americans?, and The Great Demographic Illusion, it seems clear that most would like to think of themselves as regular Americans — not to give up or forget their national origins or ethnic identity, but to prioritize their American-ness.

The progressive movement of the 2010s told us that this was a bad thing. “Assimilation” became a dirty word in progressive circles, and the University of California told their faculty not to call the U.S. a “melting pot”. The implicit assumption was that given the choice, people would like to prioritize their racial and ethnic identities, and that only forcible conformity pressure from American institutions — or from White people — was preventing people of color doing that. The Democratic party’s embrace of identity politics — its habit of targeting racial “communities” with encouraging rhetoric and specific material benefits — was seen as a way to counteract the pressures of assimilation.

The conservative counter-narrative was that race relations had been fine right up until progressives started making everything in America about race. Conservatives always send me the following chart:

This is a powerful argument. If structural racism was really so entrenched before 2014, then why did two-thirds of Black adults say race relations were good? Essentially, the progressive story is that they were effectively bullied into saying this — or perhaps bullied into thinking it. The conservative story is that progressives created the decline in race relations by making everyone think about race all the time.

I suspect that neither of these stories gets it quite right, but that the conservative story is closer to the truth. Increasing the salience of racial divisions and racial conflict makes people mistrust their neighbors more. And although both sides were guilty of this in the 2010s, progressives were far more zealous and absolutist about it.

Essentially, the progressivism of the 2010s sought to turn American society into a sort of estate society, where people’s rights, privileges, and social roles would be mediated by their identity group. How your teachers and principals treated you, your relationship with the law, what colleges were available to you, what kind of parties you could go to, what jobs you could get hired for, how your bosses treated you at work, what kind of benefits you could expect from your government, and even how people walked past you on the street were to be determined by the race you were born into, rather than your own actions as an individual.

These race-based social relationships were to be enforced by a combination of DEI departments, lawsuits, social shaming, job loss, and so on. Ibram X. Kendi even suggested the totalitarian step of creating a constitutionally mandated “Department of Antiracism” to enforce race-based social relations at every level of society — all in the name of combatting “structural racism”, which Kendi couldn’t even define when asked.

Democratic party politicians never fully embraced this vision of the future, even in 2020-21. Some of these ideas were tried out in 2020-21, but they failed almost as quickly as they were tried, making basically everyone mad in the process. By 2024, Kamala Harris was tacking pretty strongly away from the racialized vision of America.

But that was too little, too late. People remember the individualistic Americanism largely prevailed in public life before 2014, and they remember the constant hyper-consciousness of race in 2014-21, and they know which one they like better. And although Democrats abandoned much of their woke rhetoric, the practice of targeting politics at specific “communities” has persisted. I suspect that it refreshes the bad memories of the racial conflicts of 2014-21.

All of this is a long-winded way of saying that Democrats’ racial targeting probably makes a lot of Hispanic people feel singled out and alienated in their own country, even if the purpose is to help them.

But that’s not all. Democrats’ identity politics flies strongly in the face of the narrative that has defined the American experience for many Hispanics.

The story of Hispanic voters is defined by the American Dream

To the extent that most Hispanic Americans do share a common experience, it’s the immigrant experience. Immigrants come to America seeking the American Dream of upward mobility and opportunity. And by and large, they achieve it. Their children tend to earn a lot more than they do, and their grandchildren earn even more.

This was the path that most immigrant groups have followed — the Irish, the Italians, the Lithuanians, the Chinese, and so on. For a while, people argued that Hispanics were different — that they would be permanently excluded from the American Dream. That turned out not to be true:

Hispanic voters and the American Dream

Noah Smith
·
July 1, 2021
Read full story

For many Hispanic Americans, their salient experience of America has not been one of racialized exclusion, but one of upward economic mobility and social inclusion. Economists have found that Hispanic incomes are converging to White levels across the generations. Once you control for the composition effect of new poor immigrants coming in, there’s strong income convergence across the generations:

We study the sources of racial and ethnic disparities in income using de-identified longitudinal data covering nearly the entire U.S. population from 1989-2015….[T]he intergenerational persistence of disparities varies substantially across racial groups. For example, Hispanic Americans are moving up significantly in the income distribution across generations because they have relatively high rates of intergenerational income mobility…

Hispanic Americans are moving up significantly in the income distribution across generations. For example, a model of intergenerational mobility analogous to Becker and Tomes (1979) predicts that the gap will shrink from the 22 percentile difference between Hispanic and white parents observed in our sample…to 6 percentiles in steady state…

Hispanics are on an upward trajectory across generations and may close most of the gap between their incomes and those of whites…Their low levels of income at present thus appear to to be primarily due to transitory factors.

In fact, despite composition effects from continued immigration, Hispanic wages have grown faster than White wages in America since the turn of the century:

Surveys unsurprisingly have found widespread economic optimism among Hispanics for many years. Hispanics are climbing the ladder of education:

Hispanic homeownership is rising strongly. And Hispanics are starting businesses at very high rates:

New businesses owned by Latinos accounted for 36% of launches in 2023…As of 2023, Latino entrepreneurs have established a staggering five million businesses across the United States, collectively generating over $800 billion in annual revenue…The rapid pace of this growth is further highlighted by the fact that the number of Latino/a-owned businesses surged by 34% from 2007 to 2019.

In other words, Hispanic Americans’ economic path looks reasonably similar to that of Italian Americans or Irish Americans.

In the 2010s, it became taboo to even talk about these successes in some progressive circles. The University of California’s 2015 speech guidelines told faculty not to say “America is the land of opportunity”. This was deemed to be a racist utterance, since it supposedly minimized the economic exclusion that many minority groups have faced.

But the fact is, America is the land of opportunity, especially for immigrants and their children. Hispanic Americans, broadly speaking, have been prime beneficiaries of that upward mobility — they have worked incredibly hard, gone to school, started businesses, learned English, and done everything else they were supposed to do. And America has rewarded them with economic success and social integration.

Compared to that self-bootstrapped success, racial preferences — DEI, affirmative action, preferential government contracts, and so on — are basically a booby prize. Yes, in reality, those policies can sometimes help accelerate Latino achievement. But the mere fact that they’re on offer — and that Democrats seemingly view them as permanent policies instead of temporary ones — sends the message that Hispanics are a permanently racialized, excluded, marginalized group. This message is often explicit — when Democrats and progressives talk about “marginalized groups”, which they often do, that term is generally supposed to include Hispanics.

Being a marginalized group is simply not part of anyone’s American Dream.

The tricky part for Democrats is that this is an approach that has largely worked with Black voters — or at least failed to alienate them. It will be difficult for Democrats to convince themselves that Hispanic voters are not going to work the same, after spending so many years believing they would. But the 2024 election, and the trend of the last few elections, makes it clear that the two are not going to work the same.

After identity politics

Identity politics allows Democrats to hold on to a supermajority of the Black vote, so I suspect it will never go away. But the Black vote is a smallish and shrinking part of the electorate, and even there, the power of idpol may be fading a bit. Meanwhile, Hispanic voters, Asian voters, and Middle Eastern voters are the future. Those groups are all strongly upwardly mobile, and mostly descended from people who came to America voluntarily in search of the American Dream. And although ethnic studies professors and progressive activists will happily tell you all about the Chinese Exclusion Act and post-9/11 Islamophobia, it’s just not the case that Hispanic, Asian, and Middle Eastern Americans have anything that compares to the history of slavery and segregation.

The Democrats need to move away from identity politics. And switching to class-based politics, as some have suggested, won’t really help. Biden was probably the most pro-union and pro-worker President America has had since the mid 20th century, and yet some prominent unions refused to endorse Harris.

Instead, Democrats need to retool their message to be about American identity, as it was in the New Deal days, and as it arguably was for Clinton and Obama. I believe Harris actually took steps in the right direction, but not enough, and not nearly soon enough — and she was probably the wrong person to sell the idea. My advice is not to be discouraged, and to keep at it — Walter Mondale and Michael Dukakis both went down to crushing defeats with centrist, positive messaging, but then Bill Clinton eventually figured out how to make the approach work.

Republicans will eventually screw up. Trump is old, and he has a lot of foolish and bad people around him, and his economic policy program is kind of a dead end. At some point, America will once more call upon the Democrats to save them from Republican mistakes, as they did in 2008 and in 1992. Democrats will have an easier time rising to that inevitable summons if they leave the identity politics of the 2010s behind. Because that stuff just isn’t getting the job done.

Americans hate inflation more than they hate unemployment

In 2021, there was a fierce debate, both within the Biden administration and among the general left-of-center commentariat, about how much to worry about inflation. For example, in May 2021, Larry Summers wrote:

Even six months ago, it was reasonable to regard slow growth, high unemployment and deflationary pressures as the predominant risk to the economy. Today, while continuing relief efforts are essential, the focus of our macroeconomic policy needs to change…Inflationary pressures are mounting…How much does it matter whether inflation accelerates? In general, increases in inflation disproportionately hurt the poor and are associated with reductions in trust in government. Progressives might consider the role that inflation played in electing Richard M. Nixon in 1968 and Ronald Reagan in 1980.

In February 2021, Olivier Blanchard, another prominent macroeconomist, wrote a detailed argument that the Biden administration was spending too much on Covid relief with the American Rescue Plan, and that this would generate a surge of inflation. The argument included a simple model whose predictions ended up being close to what actually happened.

Other economists pushed back hard against Blanchard and Summers, arguing that inflation was due to transitory factors, and that it was important to keep spending in order to preserve full employment. One of these was Paul Krugman, who declared himself “a card-carrying member of Team Transitory” — “Team Transitory” being those who thought inflation was mostly due to pandemic disruptions and would fade on its own. There was even a live debate between Krugman and Summers in early 2022. But by late 2022, Krugman issued a mea culpa, and admitted that Biden’s American Rescue Plan had exacerbated inflation:

In early 2021 there was an intense debate among economists about the likely consequences of the American Rescue Plan, the $1.9 trillion package enacted by a new Democratic president and a (barely) Democratic Congress. Some warned that the package would be dangerously inflationary; others were fairly relaxed. I was Team Relaxed. As it turned out, of course, that was a very bad call.

Economic analyses of the inflation surge of 2021-22 generally assign the American Rescue Plan some share of the blame.

Ignoring Summers’ warnings, and believing Team Transitory, might have cost the Democrats the 2024 election. I’m no political scientist, but there are reasons to believe that the burst of high inflation in 2021-22 was one factor in Kamala Harris’ loss.

Why inflation probably mattered in this election

The first reason we should think inflation mattered is that people pretty consistently said it mattered. On Gallup’s long-running “most important problem” survey, inflation consistently ranked as the most important specific economic problem that people mentioned, right behind “economy in general”.

A lot of other surveys showed similar results. And the percentage of people who told Gallup that the economy was “extremely important” to their presidential vote was unusually high — almost as high as in 2008, when the financial crisis had just devastated the U.S. economy:

And of course consumer sentiment was pretty low, even after adjusting for changes in methodology:

Now, it’s possible that this was mostly just Republicans complaining about inflation because it felt more substantive than talking only about more social/cultural grievances like wokeness, immigration, trans stuff, etc. After all, opinion on the economy shows a very partisan pattern depending on who’s in the White House:

It’s a pretty good bet that Republicans will suddenly “discover” that inflation in America is actually low now, and give Trump the credit.

But if you look historically and across countries, it really looks like inflation tends to make voters particularly mad. Research often finds that cumulative inflation over a President’s term in office — not just the current inflation rate — affects presidential approval and election performance. If you look at Gallup’s long-running survey, you’ll see that the inflation of the 1970s dominated Americans’ complaints even more than the unemployment of the Volcker recessions in the early 80s, or the recession of the early 90s:

And if you look at other countries, you’ll see that governing parties in every other rich country have seen their vote shares go down this year:

There are relatively few factors that are affecting all rich countries at the same time. A backlash over immigration is another possible common factor, but the list is basically just that plus inflation.

On top of that, there was a model that predicted the election outcome quite well. An interdisciplinary team of researchers created a model based on presidential approval ratings and economic conditions in each state, and they ended up predicting each state correctly:

It might be a fluke, but the same model got only one state wrong in 2020 (Georgia), so that’s pretty encouraging. In any case, the model relies partly on economic fundamentals — measures of the labor market and real wages. And real wages depend on inflation. So since labor markets are generally very strong all across America, the erosion of state-level wages by inflation is going to be the main economic factor that led this model to forecast a Trump victory.⁴

So I think it’s safe to say that while it’s possible inflation mattered less for Trump’s victory than people say on polls, it did matter at least somewhat.

Why inflation makes voters even angrier than unemployment

Let’s talk a little about macroeconomics for a second. Most mainstream macroeconomic models assume that there’s some sort of short-term tradeoff between inflation and unemployment. If the Fed lowers interest rates or does quantitative easing or otherwise prints money, the general consensus is that unemployment will go down and inflation will go up. Similarly, if the government borrows and spends money and the Fed doesn’t counteract this by raising interest rates, the general consensus is that you’ll get faster growth, more jobs, and rising prices.⁵

Macroeconomic policy then becomes a question of how to strike the right balance. We want everyone to have a job. We don’t want inflation to go about 2%. But if we have to choose between these two things, how do we choose? In economic models, the relative degree that policymakers should care about inflation versus unemployment is determined by a social welfare function — basically, how much each of these economic ills makes regular people unhappy. A lot of economic research is dedicated to figuring out what that welfare function, and there’s not really a consensus.

But the experiences of the 1970s and the 2020s are teaching us that in America at least, people seem to get even madder about inflation than they do about unemployment. And the question is why. I actually wrote a post about this back in March of 2021, shortly after the American Rescue Plan was passed:

Why do people hate inflation?

Noah Smith
·
May 26, 2021
Read full story

The basic story here comes from a survey Robert Shiller did in 1990. Basically, inflation tends to make people’s purchasing power go down, because their wages can’t keep up.⁶ This makes people poorer, and people do not like to be poorer.

The inflation of 2021-22 definitely made people poorer. In fact, the drop in real personal disposable income from mid-2021 to mid-2022 was more severe than the Great Recession or the 1970s inflation!⁷

This was caused by a combination of the end of pandemic relief, and falling real wages and other income due to inflation. In 2021 and 2022, Americans’ real wages suffered their biggest drop in postwar history, thanks to inflation⁸:

Remember, real wages are a key economic input that went into the model that managed to successfully predict every state’s election result. People really don’t like it when their real wages go down!

One key thing to understand is that this sudden impoverishment happened to most Americans. Rising consumer prices affect everyone, from the rich to the poor, the employed and the unemployed, the old and the young.

In a recession, on the other hand, the negative effects are largely concentrated. If you’re one of the unlucky people who loses their job, you take a huge hit. But if you’re not one of those people, you probably do OK. Maybe your wages grow more slowly for a few years, and maybe you have to stress out about the increased possibility of being laid off. But in general, the harms of inflation are diffuse while the harms of unemployment are concentrated.

If you’re a moral philosopher, an activist, or an economist estimating a social welfare function, you may prefer harming a lot of people a little bit with inflation to harming a few people a lot with unemployment. But a democracy doesn’t vote based on social welfare. It’s one person, one vote. So if unemployment harms 10 million people a lot, and inflation harms 200 million people by a moderate amount, it’s clear that inflation will directly harm a much larger number of voters.

The social welfare function and the “get your butt kicked in an election” function are two very different things.

I actually suspect that there are other reasons why inflation bothers voters even more than unemployment. Inflation is something that’s obviously beyond an individual’s control — if the price of eggs goes up, you can choose not to buy eggs, but otherwise there’s not much you can do. But unemployment is something that individuals do exercise some degree of control over — if you work a bunch of extra hours during a recession and establish a good relationship with your boss, maybe you can avoid getting laid off.

In general, I think people are less worried about risks they have some control over, even if the overall level of danger is higher. Look at how people are more afraid to fly than to take long road trips, despite road trips being much deadlier per mile. The leading theory is that in a car you have some control over your safety, while in a plane you have basically zero control. Similarly, I suspect that inflation makes people feel powerless, like being stuck in a crashing airplane.

In any case, this is probably an important area for survey research to explore. But in the meantime, Democrats need to remember that full employment doesn’t necessarily mean an economy that Americans are happy with. If it comes at the expense of rapid inflation, that price is going to be one that most Americans aren’t comfortable paying.

Democrats should be wary of macro-progressivism going forward

I’d like to say a little more about the debate over the American Rescue Plan in 2021. While Paul Krugman and Larry Summers viewed their argument in purely technical terms, some economists and commentators did come at the debate from an ideological angle. In general, spending more was considered the progressive position, while spending less in order to avoid high inflation was considered more centrist or moderate.

This makes sense — full employment disproportionately benefits the least well-off in society. The lowest-paid workers are often the first to be fired in a recession and the last to be hired in an expansion, so the longer you can keep an expansion going, the more poor people can have jobs. Also, full employment tends to push up wages, especially at the lower end of the scale — in fact, even as most Americans lost purchasing power during the inflation of 2021-22, the bottom 10% of American workers actually saw their real wages rise.

The educated professional class is out of touch with America

I’ve been writing about the lessons that Democrats should take away from the big GOP victory. I’ve written about how identity politics is failing to attract Hispanic voters, and about how Dems cared too much about employment and not enough about inflation. The third big lesson, I think, is about class in America. The educated professional class is drifting away from the rest of the country, in terms of values, beliefs, and their information diet.

This election upended a lot of demographic trends that people had been very certain about only a few years ago. Trump seems to have produced a large-scale shift of Hispanic voters to the Republicans, and big cities swung harder toward the GOP than other areas. But there’s one key trend that this election didn’t reverse: education polarization. Trump was even more dominant among non-college voters than he was in the last two elections, while Harris won the highly educated by about as much as Biden did.

Over the years, the Democratic base has shifted decisively from the working class to the educated professional class:

This shift doomed Harris’ campaign, since people without college degrees outnumber their college-educated counterparts — in 2024, the latter were only 43% of the electorate.

And this weakness looks likely to be a long-term problem. In the past, when college education was steadily increasing, it was easy to think that college-educated voters would own the future. But in recent years, the rate of college enrollment has plateaued and begun to fall:

And the number of new college graduates fell in 2022, even as America’s total population grew.

As for why fewer Americans are getting a college education, I wrote a post about this back in July:
